[[VIDEOID:93362313a270b063085f7e3a8762f80d]] I tried to think of anything that I would change to improve this sports duffle bag, and the only thing I would suggest would be to add a mesh water bottle holder into the fixed end compartment. That's the only thing I would change because with the exception of no water bottle holder, this gym duffle is the most well thought out and best made sports bag I've ever seen.

The bag is roomy enough to handle everything you'd need to carry to a game, to the gym, or for a weekend getaway, and it's also sized just right to work as an airline carry on bag and it fits into an overhead compartment. It's made of water repellant polyester and the material is thick enough to protect your clothing or gear as well as to keep everything dry regardless of weather conditions.

While most of the storage capacity is inside the roomy main compartment, the bag does offer several storage compartments on the exterior as well. There's a zippered compartment on the front that measures approximately 7.25" x 7.25" where you could easily fit sunglasses, boarding passes or other travel documents, and there are zippered storage compartments on each end of the bag as well.

One end compartment is fixed, and the other one has extra fabric lining that allows it to expand inwards towards the main compartment, so you can use this one to stash smelly or dirty clothes and shoes away. Putting dirty smelly shoes, clothes, and towels in the expandable compartment keeps grime and odors away from clean clothes or gear in the main compartment, and there are two air vents on the outside to let the dirty or wet things get ventilation.

Inside the main compartment there's a zippered compartment that measures approximately 6" x 3.5 that would work well to store keys, lip balm, wallet, cell phone, or other small items while you work out, and the main compartment has plenty of room for clothes or other gear as I hope my video shows. You can carry the bag by the carry handles which Velcro together and are comfortable to carry, or by the adjustable shoulder strap which has a thick adjustable shoulder pad. The straps are all heavy duty webbing and the attachments are heavy duty plastic with metal clips that won't slip off so the bag can handle some weight in it and still be comfortable to carry.

All stitching is even, tight, and well reinforced at pressure points throughout the bag. Zippers function well and all pulls have plastic handles to make them easy to operate. The bag will keep your clothes are gear dry as well as keep dirty shoes and clothes away from the clean ones and has an interior that's easy to wipe clean. I'm very impressed and pleased with the design, materials, construction and functionality of this sports bag, and frankly I am surprised that it doesn't cost more than it does.

This sports duffle bag was provided at no cost by the manufacturer for evaluation and review.

Wow, these inexpensive fitness tracker watches have really come a long way! I've used WearOS, Fitbit, Galaxy and Amazfit brand watches, and usually find the cheap ones are cute for my kids but not very accurate or full of mostly gimmicky features.
This one actually looks and acts a lot like a cheaper version of my current Amazfit GTS3 watch. The way the menu works, the way the app works... it's all very familiar. Granted, this watch does not have the high resolution OLED display that my Amazfit does, but the display is capable of vivid colors and looks great!

The accuracy is surprisingly spot on, I even tested my heart rate with this and other smartwatches I own since usually there's a lot of discrepancy, and it often lined up exactly. Steps were interesting- most smartwatches don't count steps unless you move for more than a few steps at a time (disregarding a step here or there as an error). This one goes a step further and actually refused to count steps I made unless I was WEARING THE WATCH! I'm not sure if this is a attempt to prevent cheaters from shaking their watch or something, but I noticed it would not count any of my steps when I held it in my fingers, but when I put it on my wrist, it counted! Perhaps there is a proximity sensor on the back of the watch, I'm not sure. This might be a problem for those who occasionally put the watch in a pocket or something to get steps if, for example, pushing a shopping cart (since your wrist doesn't move, pushing strollers and carts tend to not count anyway- one workaround is to put the watch in a pocket but that might not work now).

Another thing I wish it had is a better notification system. Certain apps which aren't in their list of known notifications won't work correctly (Google Voice, for example). But that's true of all cheap tracker watches. It also can't install apps or extend functionality like the more expensive ones. There is definitely a reason my regular watch costs 5-6x as much as this one, but for what it is on a budget, honestly, it's pretty amazing!

Wow, before saying anything, the screen on this laptop is stunning; bright and sharp. It is not the first nice thing I noticed about the laptop. Out of the box, it has a solid, perhaps a little heavy feel. It has a matte crosshatched finish which is not my favorite, but looks classy enough. The basic shape is elegant, it is thin and sleek and satisfying in the hand.

Keyboard/Touchpad

The keys are backlit, crisp to the touch and typing is easy. It has a slightly compressed full keyboard with a squeezed 10 key which is nice, and at least for my uses fine that the keys are 2/3rds their normal width. Keypad is sensitive but clicking works better than most and I have no problems with fine control of the cursor. The fingerprint reader is on the touchpad but does not affect usage and is a nice touch in general. All in all, inputs through keyboard, touchpad and touchscreen are perfect.

Screen

Like I said, once this one on, the screen is what stuck out for me. Wonderfully bright and crisp. Touch screen controls seem to work fine. Screen size is great. We watched a number of HD nature films on it and felt comfortable. The screen hinges completely around to create a tablet which I far prefer to swivel options. I also liked the way that it tents for movie and presentation viewing. Could not be happier with the screen.

CPU/Performance

This is a nice quick machine. SSD, i7 and plenty of RAM out of the box had it booting quick and I see no problems with performance. I would be amazed and happy to see it approach the 9 hours of battery life that it promises, we'll see about that over time. My son wanted to put it through the paces with STEAM games but I'm passing - It's mine, but it should handle most reasonable games although it is obviously not optimized for hard core gaming.

Summary

This is a well built, solid laptop. It has the makings for a great Netflix platform with it's screen and flexibility of viewing positions of the screen as well as crisp, bright HD. This is hands down the best laptop I have owned as a complete package.

Pros
+ Super Bright, HD screen
+ Nice crisp feel to the keyboard
+ Well powered for standard uses, SSD, i7 and RAM gives it enough muscle

Cons
-The design of the power cord and jack are disappointing, It looks spindly and its design encourages lateral pressures. I really wish more thought went into that.
-The pattern on the outside is not my favorite, but looks nice enough

This is a handy little item if you need power backup for a phone or tablet, when you expect to have an extended period away from a power source. I'm planning to carry it with me when travelling, for example, and it might be handy on a hike as well.

I plugged in my regular micro-usb phone charger (the specs call for 2.1A at 5V) to fully charge it. Then I tested it on a phone (Samsung S4) and a tablet (Tab S), and found the results quite satisfactory. The specs say that the two USB ports will provide 2.4A at 5V simultaneously, and I was certainly able to charge my two devices at the same time without problems.

There's some discussion in the instructions about "smart charging", but I can't verify if that makes any real difference. (The idea seems to be that you can tell the charger to dialog with your device to select an optimal charge profile. Nice idea, but I didn't see a difference after I did what they asked. Maybe it was optimal already ...)

The flashlight is a nice touch, but I don't know that I'd ever use it. I'd carry a flashlight if I think I might one, rather than depending on one charger to provide backup power as well as a light source.

Finally, the charger is well-made, and compact in design. Easy to slip into a backpack for instance. One important limitation to keep in mind: you will probably need to carry a separate USB-microUSB cord (I have a 1 foot cord I use), because the cord that comes with it has a fat rubberized head, making it impossible to fit into some recessed charging slots (such as my tablet when it's inside a case).

This is a review for the Baseus 5-in-1 USB C Hub. I have a few different hubs now because Apple decided I only needed USB-C ports on my laptop. Depending on what I’m doing and how many devices I need to plug in, I’ll either use a hub or adapters.

WiFi signal strength can be impacted by hubs or similar devices, there’s some interference with USB 3.0 and 2.4Ghz networks. It’s a known problem, there’s a lot about it online if you’ve also run into it. I’ve noticed this using other hubs, and I have about the same degree of interference with this one.

I don’t love the design of this hub. I wish the hub’s USB-C plug was straight, not an “L.” While I can still plug in other USB-C things next to the hub, the “L” shape of the plug dictates how the hub sits on my desk.

I've learned a lot about surveillance systems recently, having researched, selected, installed, and tweaked both this and a LaView model with four cameras and eight channels. This Defender model has a price tag more than double the LaView, but its specs clearly justify that. But although this is an excellent product, having experience with another brand shows me neither are perfect:

Overall. The Defender comes with a more solid looking DVR and a couple extra cables (i.e., Ethernet and HDMI), making it appear more premium right out of the box. However, the AAA batteries (worst kind of batteries anything could take price/power-wise) for the remote came DOA which was totally lame. Both units come with very cheap mice, rectifiers, remotes, and cables.

-Most people into this kind of stuff have extra of these things around anyway, so it's not a big deal.
-The cables look and work fine, but they are not actually coax in the shielding/cladding sense. After cutting the ends off mine during installation anyway, I'd recommend planning to buy your coax on a roll (especially when you have some runs >60') and maybe getting a boxed power supply rather than using multiple awkward rectifier packs.
-The Defender had issues pushing HDMI output past 25', which the LaView did not, which could be an issue if you're planning to view your output on your TV far from your Telecom Closet (TC).

DVR. The LaView has D1 cameras, but only the first two channels can record D1@30fps, while the other channels can do CIF@30fps or D1@6fps (bogus). The Defender can record all four channels WD1@30fps.

Using NTSC in N. America, WD1 is 960x480 resolution. This is also referred to as 960H. Or, more accurately, one is a capability of the other, but I'm trying to keep this simple. D1 is 720x480, so basically, WD1 is "Wide D1". The TV Lines (TVL) spec you see is independent of the previously mentioned spec from what I understand, but my full understanding is still a little fuzzy. Suffice to say, higher TVL is better.

But the Defender is missing these features that the LaView possess:

-USB port in front for easy mouse or backup HD access, convenient IF you have the DVR pointed forward (I have mine pointed backward in my TC for cable access).
-IR extender port, which should be great if you have your device pointed backward in a TC or if you want to view this on your TV in a different room. I haven't gotten mine to work, but I haven't researched it much yet, so I'm not sure who's fault that is.
-Alarm inputs, which you can set to turn on cameras when something triggers an external alarm you set up.
-Controls. The LaView has buttons on the front of the DVR while the Defender does not.

It should be noted that the only way to control either of these devices fully and easily is with the included mouse or through their remote viewing software. I attached a little mouse holder to the inside of my TC door so it is available when needed.

Remote Viewing. I could immediately pick up the LaView from my home networked computers. The first one immediately gave me full functionality while the next three gave me limited functionality. I think the difference may have to do with the newest Internet Explorer not working as well, but compatibility mode does not give greater functionality. I had to mess around a little bit to get the Defender working right away, but you basically have to push it to the IP address and then port 5000, but then it was still less easy to get my computer to install what it needed to install (the 1step thing included didn't work for me, and I tend to think they know it will never be one step, they just want to motivate you to go through the process).

But, once I got it running, I like the full featured remote viewing software of the Defender better. For viewing off your local network, both needed port forwarding set up on your router. This can be quirky if you're using a home-type router rather than a commercial router. I'm a network guy, but I believe this is just the reality of the situation.

The local software is great on both devices. They have about the same features, and both are intuitive to use. The LaView software is easier to read on my TV from far away, and the Defender's software looks a bit more like a computer program. The Defender has PIP and PIPx2 options that are really cool.

Cameras. These Defender cameras, with their better specs - are clearly superior, but they are also a lot bigger, which is a small disappointment (as I really don't want to flaunt my extreme paranoia to the neighborhood). You can't hide it either way, but small cameras are a good thing. Anyway, side-by-side, it's hard to get a firm grasp on the resolution difference because the LaView cameras are almost zoomed out further so you see more anyway, but the wider resolution of the Defender is theoretically fantastic because you get more off to the sides (given a same zoom to start with) and less toward the sky. For example, on my porch, the LaView covers it just fine, but you see some of the ceiling. The wide Defender cameras can get more of the yard to the side of the porch while getting the same amount of ceiling. Oddly, it's not as much more crisp as you might think, but lighting and everything plays a roll in this. But at night, the Defender cameras really shine because the night vision is truly excellent and then the lines are much more crisp and detailed. This is especially important in very dark settings (less important when you have city street lights around).

[[VIDEOID:ce9372435451bc2c3bda4d2794c79f4f]] I am really impressed with this camera. The Flip MinoHd package pretty much does everything the average user needs it to do. It takes high quality video, transfers it to your computer, lets you stitch videos together to create movies, allows you to trim your videos, pull snapshots out of them and helps you share them to various websites including Facebook and YouTube.

The Flip comes partly charged right out of the box, but they do suggest that you let it charge for 5 hours before you use it. I plugged it into a USB port on my laptop for about an hour before using it and the battery was fully charged. Operation is a cinch. Turn it on, point and press the red button. The zoom in button is + the zoom out is -. Delete is a trashcan. How much more obvious can this be? The only problem I have with the recording is that pressing the zoom controls doesn't always produce the desired effect immediately and I tend to get a bit of a jitter in the frames where I'm trying to get it to recognize the command. Of course I'm still getting used to holding the camera, so I expect that I'll get steadier as I learn the feel of it in my hand.

Uploading your vids to your computer is also simple. Again, plug it into a spare USB port and there they are. There's software included on the camera's hard drive, and it's a nice little program called FlipShare that helps you label, sort and share your vids pretty easily. Though again, I do have a quibble with the saving part. It will only let you save to your C drive in the video library. Meh, I figure it's simple enough to copy the vids to another drive when I'm done. The software also helps you cobble together shorter vids into a movie, complete with music -- you can use the tunes they've provided or any MP3 on your computer -- which can be softer than the sound on the video, louder or which can replace the sound completely. Their selection of music is fairly uninspiring, but what can you really expect? When you're done, you can upload or email your videos with FlipShare, or make a video greeting card with one of their templates. I've used FlipShare to upload a video to my Facebook account and it works very smoothly.

As for quality, I've looked at these vids in four different sizes and I have to say that with the exception of the ones I shot at night, the quality even in the largest size is exceptionally good. The night vids tend to be a bit pixelated at the larger sizes, but not so much that you can't enjoy them. I haven't checked the quality on my HDTV yet, but I'm going to guess that it'll prove to be surprisingly good. However, you don't have to take my word for this. The video I've appended to this review shows the same Halloween decoration in daylight and at night. I leave it to you all to judge the quality.

The camera itself is compact, light and relatively easy to handle. It comes with a wrist strap and a drawstring bag. I hesitate to use the wrist strap, though, since a free-swinging camera might end up smashing itself into things as I went about my business. It's fine if I'm actively engaged in shooting a video, but not so much if I'm just carrying it around with me in case I find something to record.

Given what this recorder does, and the simple but useful software that comes with it, I really think the SRP is reasonable. This isn't professional grade stuff, but it's more than good enough for most of us. It takes good quality video and makes it easy to edit and share that video with friends. What more could you really ask at this price point? I am sold on the Flip and I think you will be too.

An astonishing example of technology like nothing I've ever seen before.

It's been forty years (!) since I first saw a video camera in high school, a big b/w camera with a backpack that contained the batteries and internals. It was impressive! Then we used a kind of mini-VHS video recorder to share kid videos with our parents maybe 15-20 years ago. Then I got an iPhone which had kind-of video capabilities. So I guess I was ripe to be blown away by this Sony FRAX53/B.

It's small and compact, like a small football. The swing-out screen is breathtakingly crisp and the internal operating system and menus are not only in color, but accompanied by clear, bright sound! I charged the battery and took a video of one of my cats. I could not believe the clarity of the image when I viewed it on the screen! The video is of such high quality that it's easy to overlook the still camera, which is remarkable. High-resolution, bright images. The "Photo" button is kind of oddly placed, it's not easy to operate it while you're holding the device with its right-side hand strap. You can also use a "Manual" mode and twist the lens to achieve custom focus. There's a 20X optical magnification which ought to satisfy anyone.

The Sony software is thorough and functional. The camcorder will transfer photos and video wirelessly if you have a fairly modern computer. I had to use a PC laptop rather than my elderly Mac. That meant using Windows 10, which led to some baffling moments trying to figure out if anything was working.

Between the Sony software and the camcorder and our WiFi setup and Windows 10 I found that the best thing to do sometimes was just WAIT. Windows would give me bad information and I would misinterpret that as an error. Ignore what Windows is telling you and be patient while the FDRAX53/B does its work.

The printed manual is basic and you'll want to spend time reviewing the online documentation. I'm still trying to figure out how to use the Sony FDRAX53/B and a "U-Stream" service to get a live stream going. There is a LOT of technology packed into this camcorder! Expect to spend some time reviewing it all. As I mentioned, Sony packed a TON of features in this device, and there's a learning curve to really understand and appreciate them all.

If you're planning a vacation or expecting a newborn child, BUY THIS CAMCORDER! You cannot take enough videos and photos of your kids when they're young, and the same goes for vacations -- this camcorder is small enough to tote with you (it does not like fog or water, though!) and the QUALITY of the images are incredible! It's not so heavy that it's going to be a burden.

The sound is very good, and there's a "gun" style microphone if you want to A) avoid wind noise B) capture audio of what you're shooting (like at a kid's soccer game) rather than local chitchat.

One thing that occurred to me while I was fiddling with the camcorder in my right hand, that being that if you were holding one of your kids in your left hand and the camcorder in your right hand and they both began to slip... which would you grab? This camcorder is THAT nice. Between the quality of the camcorder and its fantastic lens and the Sony software for image management and manipulation, this could be a major hobby in and of itself. This is my second Sony HX camera. My first was a Sony HX-50 that died after several years of use (lens motor stopped working). This version is improved in a couple of important ways. Most importantly, the popup viewfinder is tremendously useful in daylight conditions. The viewscreen is often hard to see in sunlight, but that is never a problem with the viewfinder. Opening the viewfinder is a little clunky, but you get used to it. The viewfinder does have a focus lever so using it with glasses is no problem. I also like that the GPS locks on much more quickly than older cameras (that often had GPS that were too slow to be useful). Despite the features, this camera is slimmer than my old HX-50.

The main downside to this camera (and probably all compact big-zoom cameras) is that the image sensor is very small, which limits the quality of your images. Even in bright sunlight conditions, my photos are always grainy when viewed on a large screen. They may look fine on a cell phone screen or a low quality viewer (like Facebook or Instagram), but when viewed full-screen on a computer screen, the image quality is noticeably more grainy and less dynamic than photos from a better camera. Photos are still much better than any cell phone camera, of course.

A big zoom camera is great for sports and wildlife and if you want a big zoom in a pocket sized camera, you'll be hard pressed to find anything better than this. For sports and wildlife photos, getting closer to your subject is often not possible. I've taken usable wildlife and sports photos from hundreds of yards away, even miles away for landscape photos. If you don't need the big zoom or can tolerate a bigger camera (like a one-inch or micro-4/3 or APS-sized sensor), however, you can do much better than this (for a bigger price).

I received these phones as a review sample and wanted to test the claim that they are studio quality. In point of fact they are very close. What I mean by studio quality is they are neutral sounding - there is no bias towards any particular frequency band. These are fairly even on the highs, mids and lows.

Of course, if you are listening to modern music that emphasizes low frequency response with a lot of bass you may want to check out other phones that do a better job. I will say that while the frequencies are naturally divided, the separation is excellent so I am certain these phones have a crossover.

Since there are ample specs in the product description (and two video reviews at the time of this one) I will spare you a recitation of that information. I tested these using a few key albums, and also plugged the 1/4 inch connector directly into my Roland RD-300NX keyboard to hear that instrument's natural responses. Both tests confirmed that these are studio quality. However, audiophiles who want unbiased sound will also love them. I played some of my favorite test albums like Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, Ahmad Jamal's Live at the Pershing and some 20-bit mastered CDs. In all cases the frequency response in each band was perfect and the ability to hear nuances (including the natural reverb on Kind of Blue) was a treat. More importantly I heard the albums the way the engineers wanted me to hear them.

To be sure I do have other phones that are at this level of quality, but most are in a much higher price range. I did not expect to be impressed with I accepted a review sample, but not that I've had time to put these through their paces I am impressed. They are now in my practice room/music studio and there they will remain. Definitely recommended.

This small, silent, unmanaged 1000 Mbps Ethernet switch has 4 super fast ports (the other 1 is for your input) that not only provide high speed internet but automatically detect if the plugged in device needs power and, if so, how much!

I did thorough testing on this unit over the last couple of months and I am thoroughly impressed by the performance.

By utilizing the built in chip this switch will provide up to 30 watts to every Ethernet device connected but will not provide any power to devices that do not require power or more than is required. I found that this switch works absolutely flawlessly.

Having the capability to provide super fast internet speed and power at the same time makes this switch perfect for both business environments and as a hub for security systems.

I’ve tested my unit extensively using different security cameras and the results are nothing short of incredible. While most security cameras can be run via WiFi, nearly all of them still require a power adapter be plugged in. By utilizing this hub, security breaches are all but eliminated - by utilizing Ethernet instead of Wifi transmission your local storage unit makes it so there is no easy out of network access. In addition, transfer speed, resolution and picture quality is greatly increased - making the entire system more useful. In my experience, I found power is much easier to manage doing it this way as opposed to having to run separate power supplies to each camera.

This POE switch provides ample power for four security cameras, even those with pan / tilt capabilities. It is easy to install, requires little space and is reliable. While I had not used this brand in the past I will not hesitate to in the future.

This is an all around outstanding product that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend. This unit is sure to hold up well and perform even better.

This MP3 player, which I was given at a discount in exchange for my honest review, is sleek and lightweight yet potentially—via a firmware upgrade that I hope Lonve will consider—very powerful. (See my photo of the player lying on top of my MacBook Pro trackpad to get an idea of its size.) It can be listened to without hooking it up to anything else, either with wired headphones or through the surprisingly good-sounding on-board speakers. The view screen when the player is powered on is quite readable, and I love how the surface of the screen becomes a classy grey-bronze mirrored surface that is so clear you can use it to check your appearance. The ability to add up to a 32GB SDHC card you've preloaded with music or video is a great feature.

The included wired headphones are better than some I've listened to, although I prefer another pair that fits my tiny ears better; unfortunately, those are Bluetooth, so they won't work with this player. I will likely listen to the player my itself, with no headphones, through its speakers.

I can't five-star love this player because I can't set the time to a 12-hour clock and it doesn't allow for adding playlists, which I was thinking it did. Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't even start an album folder playing by tediously navigating to it in the Explorer; it appears you have to navigate all the way into the files in the folder and then start it playing, although I haven't even been able to get this to work. It takes too many steps and is so very aggravating that I usually just quit trying to play either music or video.

What really shines on this player is the radio. I'm sure reception will vary depending on where you are, but in Lexington, KY, I can pull in NPR very clearly and easily. It would be nice to be able to store favorite radio stations—if there's a way, I haven't figured it out after days of fiddling with the player—but I'm happy that I can leave it sets to my main station and it always comes back there even after I've powered off and then back on. If you're a person who likes to listen to the radio at night with the lights off, going to sleep, but don't like fooling with headphones, this will be a great little player for you.

The Game feature has a neat little Tetris-style game that's amusing while stuck waiting somewhere. The Photo feature is nothing to write home about, but it can be used to show off a few photos of your pets or kids or maybe a logo or graphically produced emergency contact info. There is an Autoplay Time setting you can set in the Settings/Photo. The text feature allows for reading text files, so you can take along a grocery list or study notes. I started to knock off an extra star (down to three) because of something I really dislike about this player, and that is the dedicated left-side button (one of only three) that seems to serve no purpose but to turn on the voice recorder. When I press it by mistake or forget that the On/Off button is the button on the right, not the left, the Recorder comes on. Then I get a file format error when I try to get out of it. It would have been better, I think, had they used that button for something more likely to be used constantly (Explorer with the ability to set either the internal C: card or the external D: card as the default for the button maybe) or, better, allow the user to define the function of that button via a Settings selection. I want to be able to disable the Recorder completely, although I know some people will want to have a recorder. But I hate it.

You do have the option of upgrading the firmware, but the instructions are very poor. When I select Upgrade in Settings/System (which you reach by scrolling down to the end, near the Language setting), I am warned to connect to USB. When I connect the USB cable to my computer, however, I get the Connect screen on the player and there does not seem to be any way then to access the System/Upgrade selection. The instructions, such as they are, are clear in how to navigate through the features and which of the two non-Recorder buttons (middle, right) to push in connection with the up/down, left/right arrows. But, needless to say, there are bugs in the player I am reviewing. Lonve has been good about getting back quickly with answers to questions, though, so I'm hopeful they'll work hard to get this one right.

I bought this camera for my wife last summer when she was in China. She was looking for something with less shutter lag than our last generation of Nikon and Canon digital point-and-shoots, and something cute and portable. The Panasonic DMC-FX30 is both of these things.

Out of the box it overexposed and undercolored things, but this was easily fixable after fiddling with the settings menu. Even set up right, photos using the flash still look too shiny whit, and photos taken at high ISOs are pretty noisy. The lack of a real viewfinder also makes capturing action clunky, but this is obviously in part an artifact of my preferences. This camera takes fine outdoor pictures, and the wide angle zoom allows for some cool shots and works well in confined (well-lit) spaces.

The camera is a small, precision-made jewel of a camera, with controls and buttons designed for smaller hands than mine; they fit my wife fine. We both missed the lack of a real viewfinder; pocket cameras seem to making an unfortunate departure from this useful standard (bright sunlight washes the display out, and it's easier to take a picture from your eye, as that's what you're composing with in the first place). The camera performed fine in its role as a city camera in Beijing, and for snapping quick shots back home when lugging the SLR around was inconvenient.

Now, however, we are in rural China for a year doing field work, and I was using the Panasonic as a backup to my Nikon DSLR. It was nice having a wide-angle lens in a pouch in my pocket when I had my normal or telephoto primes on the SLR. The Panasonic worked great in this role for 3-weeks, and then the automatic lens cap froze shut and wouldn't open, despite my coaxing, cleaning, etc. I finally just pried it off so I can still use the camera (I keep a business card over the lens in the soft pocket pouch), but let's say that I am not impressed with the camera's durability, compared to any other camera I've had, film or digital. It never got wet, dusty, dropped, or sat on; it looks brand new, but the lens cap won't work, and failed in a way that renders the camera useless to someone unwilling to take pliers to a Leica lens (failing and staying open would be preferable).

Anyway, if you're looking for a field or reliable travel camera, pass this one up.

Wireless problems:

1.) Instructions with unit said there did not need to be a "line of sight" between the transmitter and the receiver, but the instructions on the website said there had to be a direct line of sight between them.

2.) The website instructions talked about adjusting the "potentiometer" on the back of the transmitter, but there is no potentiometer on the back of it to adjust.

As far as the "buttkicking" goes, we (husband and myself) did not find it a particularly wonderful addition to the home-theater experience. We put in "Polar Express" to test it out and found that it was interesting, but not something we could not live without while watching movies. It was literally the same experience we had when watching the movie, "Earthquake" in the 70's. The couch and floor vibrated on varying levels depending upon the intensity of what was happening in the movie, and loud low frequencies were heard, but I guess we might have been expecting too much. When the train in Polar Express was powering up, the shaking and low frequencies were tremendous, but did not necessarily course through our bodies like others have written about.

I think the buttkicking experience would have been much better if we were able to mount it in the center of our couch instead of at one end. Our couch does not have center support leg so we had to place the buttkicker on one far end of it. Much of the vibration was wasted by going away from the couch. Possibly "buttkicker" could have included an inexpensive substitute adapter in order to place it in the center of couches that don't have a center support. That would have been great.

We will continue to work on the wireless problem, and if we are able to fix it, that will increase our happiness with the buttkicker. Otherwise, we will still use the buttkicker, but not as often as we would if it worked wirelessly. Having to manually connect the amplifier to the processor via wiring every time we want to watch a movie is a pain in the.......butt.

This Surface Laptop 4 model from Microsoft is an excellent premium grade laptop. My prior laptop is an older 17" Lenovo. This one is smaller (obviously), but much, much quicker.

The aluminum chassis is thin, lightweight and solid. The display is looks great- colors are detailed rich and vibrant, and the touchscreen is effective and appropriately responsive. I find myself simply reaching for the button on a given sites screen, rather than maneuvering the cursor and tapping. (Although, the TouchPad is certainly responsive, too). The keyboard is comfortable and responsive - the surface around the keys and track pad has a texture that makes it seem sort of "soft" (even though it's not). Sound is rich and full. Very nice!

Very few ports - only what you need and not much else. A USB Type-A and Type-C, a headphone jack, and the chargers connector. (Or you can charge using the USB Type-C port).

Set up is straightforward, I loaded in some software (Wordperfect suite) and everything just fell right in place and all worked as it should without issue)

5.) The keyboard is good. It’s not the best, a little spongier than the MacBook Pro 16’s, with a slower rebound, but still among the “good” keyboards on the market, - reasonably tactile. It has physical F-keys, something I wish I had on the MacBook Pro 16. I think the TouchBar is one of the worst things to happen to MacBooks (inadvertent touches are the worst!), so I hope Apple reverts to physical keys this coming year on their flagship system. Rumor has it they will.

6.) Ergonomics are decent, though it’s actually a bit tricky to open the laptop as there’s no indent where you’re meant to flip the screen up, - a peculiar oversight. Bezels are a little large for 2021, but far from offensive.

7.) Sound quality is not bad, but a far cry from the bass that the MacBook Pro 16 is able to generate. You could certainly listen to music here, but headphones would be preferred.

8.) Battery life and thermals are absolutely fantastic, decimating the MacBook Pro for general usage, which is just a portable toaster. The laptop just runs remarkably cool with this AMD setup. That said, when the fans kick in, they kick in with a WHOOSH, which can be a bit disconcerting. Battery life is superb, easily giving me 8-11 hours for general web usage, a good 40% longer than my MacBook Pro doing the exact same things at a comparable brightness.

  9.) The SSD is nothing too special. While yes, any SSD is faster than not-an-SSD, this is on the lower end of the spectrum in terms of NVMe performance.

Overall, I really enjoy the Surface Laptop 4, but it’s not hard to see where Microsoft could make some massive improvements and solidify the Surface line as THE Windows 10 systems to buy.

4 out of 5. A worthy alternative to high-end laptops, but not yet at the top of its game.

Somewhere there is an ancient marketing survey that identifies teen-age boys as a prime segment of the gaming market and that says they really like bright, flashing lights. So manufacturers who want to sell to the gaming market still think they have to add flashy lighting to all their products. Well, the gaming universe is much larger than teen boys these days and bright, flashing lights have nothing to do with playing a game. With that pet peeve off my chest let me add a couple of things to give this review some context. First, I do spend a lot of time online playing an MMO but I'm very much a casual player, not a hardcore competitive one. Second, I am not an audiophile. High end stereo gear is wasted on me as the music coming from most any clock radio is good enough for me.

To my non-audiophile ears, the sound from this speaker is fine. It provides a nice range without being too heavy on the bass end or too shrill on the high end. Whether gaming, streaming videos, or listening to music and audiobooks, this speaker holds its own nicely. Though, like the flashy lighting, the sound quality really doesn't make any significant difference while I'm playing in my MMO world. The ambient noise, NPC chatter, battle music and such, all come through nicely but that's a perk, not something that particularly improves my game play.

The under the monitor design of this speaker really doesn't save me any desk space. The mini speakers I was using before were much smaller and were out of the way on the side of the monitor. This space bar basically sits in front of my monitor and takes up more room than other speakers. One strong plus to me for this speaker is the fact that it really is plug and play. I had it up and running in just a few minutes. Other "gaming" gear I've tried with flashy lighting systems require software to control the lighting and sometimes getting that software to install and run properly can be a major, frustrating effort. So I really, really like that this product lives up to its "plug and play" claim.

There is one last negative point to mention. a minor one. The volume and other controls are flat buttons on the side of the soundbar. So to adjust the volume, change the lighting, etc, you need to move the soundbar to look at the side of it so you can see what you are doing. I call that a minor issue because my keyboard has mute and volume control buttons on it and I can just use those to adjust the sound as needed.

The bottom line of all this for me is that I wouldn't buy this speaker as a "gaming speaker" but simply as a nice mid-range speaker who's sound quality I like, one that is easy to set up and use. Oh, and lest I sound too much like a Grinch, the lights really are pretty, the way Christmas lights are. It's just that they have nothing to do with gaming. :)

I am specifically using these to step up 3v to either 5v (for USB devices) or 12v (for a strip of LEDs). I've set up two so far, and they work pretty well. The pot is very sensitive, so that you can bump it up by tenths of a volt or less. The pads are pretty easy to solder to. The power delivery is relatively clean, I have some flicker on the LED strip, but that seems to resolve itself fairly rapidly - for sensitive applications you might want to run through a capacitor to clean things up a bit.

The unit is moderately efficient, but becomes quite warm - when converting from 2xAAA Lithium batteries (3v) to 12v, with an approximate draw of 200mA the converter (both the top of the transformer and bottom of the board) temps at about 116F within three minutes or so of operation. Pretty warm, warmer than I would typically like. I might try hooking up a 9v instead to see if this knocks the temps down a bit, or if that fails, adding a thermistor to mitigate the risk of a thermal event.

Would recommend for general experimentation though.

Having outdoor safe speakers is essential for my household. Not only do I have audiophiles who are addicted to headphones and speakers, I have a husband who insists on taking his speakers to outdoor jobs. that is fine except when the job turns out to have a sudden rainstorm or high dust going on. Before giving it to him, I had our daughter put it through the grind at work (food prep) and in town events. Let's see how this speaker performs..

WHAT IS THIS SPEAKER LIKE?
This speaker is gray in color. The housing is very rubbery in consistency. The right side of the speaker has sealed controls under a rubberized pad over top of the buttons. The speaker stays put and is heavier than expected.

ON/OFF BUTTON/PAIRING
Holding down for over a second powers up the speaker. Next to the power button is the PAIRING button. This is not for pairing the speaker to a device but it is for pairing with another speaker just like it. A coworker with my daughter has this speaker and they tested it out- works GREAT so you now get two synced speakers.

CALLS BUTTON
You can send and receive calls with this button. You can also access your voice commands on your phone with this button.

VOLUME BUTTON
This is plus or minus sound controls. You can also skip by holding down- + is forward, - is backward.

PAUSE/PLAY
You can control pausing and playing with this button.

DOCKING
USB for charging, mini USB port (to use to charge a device if need be), and auxiliary outlet for like an old MP3 player or other device that does not have Bluetooth capability.

CHARGING INDICATOR LIGHT
Red when charging and turns white when fully charged. Will indicate when the power is running low so you will know.

SOUND QUALITY
Sound quality with this is very good. My daughter has a coworker with the same speaker so they both have had a chance to experiment with their speakers. So far it has been a great speaker. The balance of the recording of course affects the speaker, but so far it has not been overly muffled, out of balance, etc. Where you put the speaker affects how it sounds too.

When put on the floor, it really does sound better than on, say top of a box, or couch, etc. A very hard surface seems to really make it sound best.

VOLUME
When using the volume controls on the speaker, the sound is better than when you use the volume controls on the device (tablet, phone, etc).

DURABILITY
This speaker was taken to a huge town chicken and biscuit dinner and was dropped and still is working perfectly.

BATTERY
Two 10 hour shifts at full volume, and this speaker kicked through it all before needing to be recharged.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a really nice durable speaker that is dustproof, shock proof, and supposedly water proof, this is a good choice. It is solid, has decent sound , and even can be synced with another speaker if you get two of these for coverage around a room.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a decent speaker, and I feel more comfortable having my husband use this on his jobs than the other really nice speaker he was beating up.

As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

This MOTOROLA MDC100 FULL HD (1080p) DASH CAMERA (Black) suits my needs perfectly. It’s mounted on the windshield, behind the rear view mirror, with an extremely strong suction cup. The suction cup is made of something that sticks to the windshield, and a ring tightens the suction cup so that it really, really sticks. The dash camera itself plugs into your car’s repurposed “cigarette lighter” outlet, and video recording turns on automatically when you start your car.

The camera requires a micro SD card (not included) for recording the video of your auto trips. I installed a [[ASIN:B00M55C0NS SanDisk 32GB card]] (the maximum size), and filled about 15-20% of the card with an hour’s driving. So the maximum size should record for 5-6 hours before it starts recording over the oldest recordings. The camera’s internal software allows you to “protect” designated recordings (or still photos) if you don’t want them to be recorded over.

Using an adapter, I inserted the micro SD card into a Windows 10 PC, and the PC was able to play the .avi videos without any problems at all. I also deleted selected videos that I made while learning to use the settings. The camera has a “delete” function, but it’s easier to use a PC for deleting selected files.

The camera has three modes--recording, photo, and replay. In photo mode, you can take still photos; in replay mode, you can look at your recordings and photos. You can replay the videos at various speeds (up to 8x maximum). You can also fast forward and fast rewind your videos as you replay them.

The camera takes excellent high-definition footage when it’s set to the highest (default) setting. The camera’s on/off functions for both power and recording are a bit confusing at first, so I strongly recommend that you sit down with the camera and familiarize yourself with all the settings and features before you install it in your vehicle. Of course, the camera is easy to uninstall/reinstall if you want to leave that step for later.

One very important thing to know is that if you turn recording off manually (by hitting the OK button) for any reason, you must turn recording on again manually when you’re done with Settings or whatever made you turn recording off. Otherwise the camera won’t start recording automatically when you start your car.

The camera has a built in battery for holding the settings and powering the camera while the vehicle is parked. I didn't test the Park function, which is disabled by default, because I don't like to leave an electronic device in plain sight when I'm going to be away from my car for a while. The battery can be used to replay videos or to look at photos, but it doesn't last long when used this way.

I won't buy another.

Original review:
I received the Amcrest ProHD 1080p IP PT "WiFi" camera yesterday, 10/30/15.

I downloaded the Amcrest Lite iPhone app. Followed instructions. It would not connect via Wi-Fi using my router's password. Tried again and again. I have a TP-Link C9 dual band wireless router with both 5gHz and 2.4gHz transmission. The Amcrest website says in an obscure forum post that the camera operates only in the 2.4gHz band. I changed my iPhone6 (iOS 9.0.2) from 5G to 2.4G. Still could connect via Wi-Fi.

So I plugged the camera directly into the router via ethernet, completely defeating the purpose for the initial purchase. It finally connected. I saw the picture for about 30 seconds, trying to get the camera to full screen, I clicked around on the mysterious icons. Nothing seemed to work. I clicked on the "X" box. The camera disappeared. I tried to reconnect. It came back with "USER LOCKED." I went to their website to search for an answer. They said (at least for their DVR line -- virtually nothing was about this camera) "users are locked out after two failed logon attempts and that I must wait 30 minutes for the reset." I waited. Still USER LOCKED. No camera. I don't even recall trying to log in. I was in the app, trying to reconnect the camera.

I created my Amcrest user account and received their confirming email. I created a user and password for Amcrest.com. The account is actually for something called amcrest.Zendesk and Accumed.zendesk and Foscamhelp.zendesk. I then tried to log in at Amcrest.com. It won't take my log-on credentials. "Invalid Logon or Password." How many user names and passwords does it take to plug in a camera?

Trying to start over, I deleted the app and rebooted the camera. Still USER LOCKED.

Finally, I found that if you push and hold in the little LED network-activity-indicator button on the back of the camera for 10 seconds, the camera will reset to factory. Deleted the app again, set my phone to operate in the 2.4gHz band. Still won't connect via WiFi. Plugged in via ethernet, then used my router's password and it connected. Per the prompt, I then created a new secure password, replacing the default "admin/admin". Finally, I can see and control the camera. So, I have a WiFi camera that won't WiFi. The camera needs to connect to the router at 2.4gHz band (and in my case, via an ethernet cable) but after getting it set, the phone can go back to the 5G if desired.

They claim their products are "Simple, Reliable, Secure." Not quite. They fail to hook to Wi-Fi and then lock me out. Their website won't let me log on even with a user and password.

I downloaded the camera's big PDF user manual to find what the icons mean. The document looks nothing like the camera's icons. They went into great detail...about a previous firmware version, then changed the firmware to look very differently.

The camera works, eventually, and only via ethernet in some cases, but getting there is a real test of patience.

Great board. Install was simple. Most ports are in decent locations with no real trouble with cable routing. First boot was normal and got me right into the bios screen. Make sure you update the bios before doing anything else. I made the mistake of setting my memory to DOCP1 (to get my DDR5 set to 6000) before updating the bios which resulted in black screen, no post. A quick cmos reset with the back panel button and I was back in business. Updated bios to version 0805 and then enabled DOCP1 and everything else went good with no trouble at all. I did notice that once I had had Win11 installed, my boot times were slow. Did some research and found that there's a bios setting "memory context restore" that needs to be changed to enabled. After that the boot times improved drastically, but still not as quick as my previous AM4 system. I'm sure it will improve with future bios updates. With a 7700X cpu, Cinbench R23 multi-core score is 20k (about the same as my previous 5900X). Timespy score with an RTX4080 is 29k, which I got to 30k with a quick oc. So far so good, it's a fast and stable motherboard.
I do have one con: CMOS battery was DOA! I found this out when I removed power from my sys to setup another pc. I had to go back in and setup all of my bios settings again (then saved my profile until I could get a new battery. I recommend swapping the battery (CR2032) before you set it up and to save your profile in the bios. I guess it costs extra when buying a $500+ motherboard to get a working cmos battery. -1 star.

I am using this strictly to boost the sound on our smart tv- a secondary but often used tv. I had purchased a similarly looking sound bar for my smart tv several months ago that works well. When this item came up as an option for review I figured it would an interesting item to try out since it has the addition of a subwoofer. Maybe it would be louder? Maybe it would sound more dynamic? We would see.. er, hear. So I tasked my husband with replacing our other sound bar with this set. It took him very little time to get it set up (less than 10 minutes, and it only took that long because our cat was helping. "helping").

The sound is definitely better and clearer than just using the speakers the tv comes with (which is usually the case). The sound is on par with the sound bar we had been using, except with the added dimension that the subwoofer provides. Without the subwoofer, it sounds just louder. With the subwoofer, it adds some depth and a nicer overall sound. We really just needed our tv to be louder. Cable is typically loud, but some programs on the various streaming services we have all have different levels of audio, with many being much too quiet. So better speakers have helped a lot.

The subwoofer connects to the soundbar via bluetooth. Both plug in, so plan to have 2 open spots in your power bar or wall receptacle. We have this system set up so the volume can be adjusted using the smart tv remote, rather than having to use the remote it came with. No issues there at all. Easy!

While I have the soundbar directly under the tv, I have the subwoofer set up in a corner a few feet away

The soundbar has spots in the rear in case you want to mount it to a wall. Subwoofer, does not.

Both are basic and minimalist looking. Subwoofer is black on black, soundbar is black with dark gray. No obnoxious branding or colors.

The instruction booklet is thorough, including information about the remote, battery info, placement and mounting, general operation, bluetooth operation, AUX in operation, Line-in operation, Optical-in operation (which is what I am using for use with my tv).

Overall sound is decent. Not home theater experience, but it definitely provides a sound and volume boost to internal tv speakers. I haven't yet tried it as a speaker for music. I really only purchased my original soundbar for use with tv (and replaced it with this for same purpose). I may give it a try anyway sometime soon. If I do, I will report back on how it does.

I like the added dimension that the subwoofer provides. I like the overall aesthetic. And because the combination of the two allows me to hear shows better than just using the tv speakers (on low audio streaming, as cable is always loud), I am pleased to use this.

I don't know hat this product costs, so I can't compare it. But, in short, it is about the same as just about any other low to mid priced soundbar. This is better sounding with addition of subwoofer. Not amazing, but definitely adds to my listening experience. 4 stars so far.

I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

I’ve spent the last month using and playing games on the Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3. It’s a decent entry-level laptop. I wouldn’t consider it a dedicated gaming machine, but more aimed at daily use plus some gaming.

However, I don’t think 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD are enough. In my very first day of downloading games, I filled more than half the hard drive (and only ~236GB is available to start). As for the RAM, my 5-year-old laptop has 8GB of RAM and I’m feeling it. A laptop from 2022 should start with at least 16GB.

The Quad Vent fans vent in the back and on both sides of the laptop. I wish there wasn’t a vent on the right, because it’s right where the mouse sits. After maybe twenty to thirty minutes, my hand gets sweaty, which isn’t great when playing a competitive game.

I actually really like the power input being on the back, as that way the cable isn’t in the way when using the mouse. But I’d like another USB-A port in the back, because I can see using a hub with this laptop.

The keyboard is not my favorite. On the plus side, it’s a full keyboard. I can’t remember the last time I saw a laptop with a numpad. The keyboard has backlighting, but only one color option: white. The keys are flat on top and somewhat slippery. The keyboard itself feels cramped, especially when gaming with WASD.

The laptop is heavy, about 7 or 8 pounds. It’s not something you’ll want to tote from class to class. The battery lasts about an hour if playing games, and about 3 hours for normal use.

Notebook computers can overheat. It isn't a worry when you use your computer sparingly, but it can become a problem with extended usage. This cooling pad was designed to solve the problem by circulating air via two small fans with the power supplied by your notebook's USB. The movement of air is, supposedly, enough to keep your notebook from overheating or at least lessen the chances.

A product like this certainly sounds like a good idea and a practical solution to a problem, but does it really work as promised? Well, it does cause some extra flow of air, as expected, but the cooling effects are minimal. The main reason is because the flow of air is so light. Turn on the fans and place your hand next to them. You will barely feel anything and this is reason enough to suspect that it makes little difference.

Another thing to keep in mind with this cooling pad is that it will not work if you do not set it up properly. It has to be standing on a flat surface so that the air can flow underneath. If you're the type who holds your notebook on your lap, then a product like this will not work for you. There has to be space underneath so that the fans can operate and get the air moving.

The Mac Cooling Pad does fit securely on Mac's of different sizes and can be used for non- Mac pc's as well. I suppose it could make some difference in temperature, but it seems like a novelty product to me. Unless you are already experiencing an overheated notebook, a product like this is a waste of money.

f1 and f2 buttons are primarily used for setting mic sensitivity and voice quality. Under Mic Sensitivity you can choose: Dictate (good for personal memos), Speech recognition (turns on when it hears voice), conversation (good for interviews or conversations, auto zoom (good for large areas where there may be close up voices and far voices), and lecture (good for lectures)

You can choose either low quality at 8kbps in Mp3 format to super high quality 192kbps in mp3. There is also a wave format in 1411 kbps. The higher quality you go impacts total record time. You can add a micro SD card for adding recording time.

There are also 4 index folders labeled A thru D. These are for separating projects. There is also a folder you could place music files if you wanted this to be a mp3 player.

There is also a menu setting where the voice quality and mic sensitivity can be accessed as well as numerous other options such as splitting files, display contrast, and clearvoice (an option that improves the sound quality of the recorded voiec)

The unit comes with rechargable AA batteries that will need to be charged when you first open it. They charge with the included usb to micro USB cord. Any other micro USB cord you own will also work. Once the recorder is connected to your computer through the USB cable you can download and upload voice or mp3 and wave files.

The only thing I wish this had was different settings for each index. For instance I would have liked to set index A for lecture mode at high quality, index B for dictate at a lower quality, etc. Once you set a mic sensitivity and recording quality, they are the same for all index until you change them in settings.

Overall a great quality recorder. Great for meetings, memos, and conversations.

It's not a horrible amp. It's just not a great amp. Maybe the A90 would sound better when paired with muffled/veiled or extremely warm sounding headphones. For Sennheiser HD800's or HD820's though, which are inherently bright, it's a horrible match. The A90 sucked the soul from the music with those particular headphones.

The chain I tested with the A90 was a Naim ND5 XS2 streamer > Nordost Silver Shadow BNC > Schiit Gungnir Multibit DAC > Cardas Clear XLR > Topping A90. There's usually a Schiit Mjolnir 2 at the end of the chain and it sounds amazing. I didn't expect the A90 to outperform the Mjolnir but I did expect it to outperform my little DAC/Amp combo, especially when being fed such a good source

All I can really take away from my experience with the A90 is DO NOT pair this amp with bright headphones. Can't comment on other headphones but avoid this amp if you've got HD800's or 820's.

I have mixed feelings about this stylus. Overall, I like it. There are some very good things about it, but it has a few issues.

I'm using this primarily with my iPad Pro, and to a lesser degree with my iPhone 6s. This is my first experience with a fine-point stylus, although I've considered purchasing one for awhile.

First, the pros:
-- I was able to get it charged with no problem
-- Using the included quick start guide, I found my way to the Wacom website to get more details on set-up and apps that I might want to use with my iPad Pro.
-- Found the apps in iTunes App Store and downloaded a few of them to my iPad, got them installed and ready to test.
-- Pairing went smoothly -- no hiccups or issues at all. This was a pleasant surprise, as I've had problems in the past pairing things with the iPad.
-- Was able to get it up and running with both Bamboo Paper as well as Sketches and ibispaint.
-- Nice look and feel -- since it's the size of a fairly standard pen (ball point, gel, retractable, etc.), it feels "natural" in use.
-- Surprisingly long battery life -- I used it almost constantly for 3 hrs, and still had a lot of battery charge left.

Cons:
-- it skips. My iPad doesn't have a screen protector, so the pen is operating on the bare glass. I thought maybe the problem was the glass, so I cleaned it -- twice. Didn't seem to help. It skips in all three apps, and in different parts of the screen each time. Still haven't figured out if it's operator error or problems with the apps or something with the stylus itself. I'll keep playing with it and see if I can find a common denominator cause. When it skips, it's only a short distance -- maybe 1/4" or so -- but it's enough to be annoying.

-- the tip has an annoying tendency to retract during use, especially if I'm using it for writing longhand. In 3 or 4 lines, it has already retracted over halfway. I'm not exerting much pressure on it -- only enough for it to "register" on the screen, so I think it might be the combination of the motion -- writing loops, "twisting" to make some of the letters, etc. -- plus the minimal pressure. What it means is that I have to stop periodically to twist the pen to move the tip "out" again. Otherwise, I end up trying to write with the hard plastic external edge of the tip, which doesn't work that well.

So why the 4-star rating? Despite the issues, I still like this stylus. I'm not a professional artist, but I do like to sketch, to annotate photos, etc. and it really does work nicely for that even with the skipping (I just move the image a bit and try again). If I were a student and I was looking to use this to take longhand notes in class or something, I'd probably drop the rating to 3 stars. But for my use, it's OK. I can work around the issues. So I DO like it.

I bought two different brands of drive recorders for my vehicles. I bought this one, and I bought the Apeman C420D. Granted it costs a couple more dollars, I am blown away by how vastly superior the Kingslim D2 is compared to the Apeman.

Firstly, the video/picture quality is outstanding on the Kingslim. It’s crystal clear on both the front and rear cameras. Even when moving at high speeds, there is no blur or bounce to the recording. At night, the Kingslim is still amazingly clear compared to the Apeman. The Apeman records terrible footage in low/no light. I have angled my rear camera upwards rather than facing the ground (as a back-up camera would be angled) so that I can record license plates/road ragers of vehicles behind me, and I am able to read the license plates/see the driver almost as clearly as I am able to see from the front camera.

Secondly, the setup was fairly easy, and I think anyone could do it themselves. All you have to do is run the wires through your trim to the lighter socket and back of your vehicle, and depending on if internal or external mounting your rear camera, through the back of your vehicle. You can also splice the wire to your reverse light wire, which will turn the camera system into a back-up camera. I decided not to do this because you can just instead change the front camera’s screen to the rear camera’s feed and use it that way temporarily.

Lastly, and most importantly, the customer service. I had an issue with the parking sensor and headlight sensor on my Apeman C420D and contacted support about it. All they could tell me was that those features were made that way and were functioning properly, and that if I didn’t like it to just turn them off.

I’ve had zero issues with my Kingslim so far, so the only interaction with their customer service was a letter that they sent me (I was surprised by that, as it’s usually just an email), thanking me for my purchase. This shows me the difference between how Apeman sees their customers and how Kingslim appreciates us.

All in all, you will not be disappointed in this camera. It is exactly as advertised!

It could well be that these companies need to shell out a little more money for decent technical writers to produce more thorough step-by-step setup instructions. OR, they could simply design the units so they're easier to set up for those of us who are not geeks or electronics engineers. It's not all that terribly frustrating; just be ready for several minutes of trial and error ...and pray you don't have a power outage! There's a lot to like about this kit, starting with the price. For the money, I've owned similar light kits to this before, but this one comes with batteries and chargers for wireless use as well as the AC plug adapters for constant power. Similar kits that I've owned required me to buy the Sony-style FP batteries separately. It also comes with a soft case, however I found the case very flimsy and not very protective (it comes folded up inside the box, there is no rigidity to it). BUT, I realized that the box it comes it is roughly a similar size to the case when unfolded, and sure enough it actually can fit inside the case perfectly! I'm not sure if this was on purpose, it was not obvious to me that this was the intention so maybe don't throw away that cardboard if you want to give your case some protective strength (see attached photo for carboard box inside carrying case).
As far as the lights themselves... they are pretty good. I was concerned about them being less densely populated than other LED panels I've used, however it appears that each diode puts out more light than I was expecting so overall it is a good amount of light for using with video for something like an interview setting.
Meanwhile, the colors and party mode are a bit different for me. I'm used to using light kits as a professional tool, and I think the multicolor part is a bit too gimmicky. It's cool to set a tone with a color like the way I'd gel a red light for a setting or something, but the party mode? I can't imagine a use for the strobe effect of it changing color constantly. I have DJ lights that can move to music and this has a mode for that as well, however it seems that the only option is to change color with each beat suddenly- no gradual fade or anything like that. The hard cut is kind of migraine-inducing distracting, so I'd honestly rather use a different light for party background style color changes. As a light kit, it's pretty good, but the selling point of using it as a sound-controlled DJ thing is iffy. Maybe a DJ at a bar mitzvah would find that option useful?

My laptop came with a Dell PA1900-02D (9T215) which I still have and works fine. I wanted a second charger for another location. The EasyStyle SK90B195462looks like the original but is much lighter, probably due to being a switching power supply. My laptop had been discharged down to 5% prior to plugging the replacement charger in. The connector fit fine, but the laptop did not recognize the charger and warned that it may not work. I figured that's just Dell telling me it's not a Dell accessory. I permanently shut off the warning (an option) and continued to use the EasyStyle charger. Charging appeared normal and battery status was indicated as charging. However, after a short while it seemed stuck at 11% charge. I came back a few hours later and it was still indicating at 11%. I plugged in the Dell charger and 100% full charge was indicated immediately. I unplugged the Dell charger and the computer still indicated nearly full charge. I plugged in the new EasyStyle charger and the indication was charging and still near full charge.
My conclusion is that the charger works, but may cause the computer to give incorrect charge status under some conditions and it will be best to unplug the charger to get an accurate battery status.
