I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

I've had several pairs of Sennheisers before the momentums namely a pair of HD580's from back in 1999 & much more recently a pair of HD650's. Let me start off by saying I'm not an "audiofile" I'm not a headphones snob. I don't name drop as to act like I know everything about all "cans" as they're referred to as. But I do know music & I know MY TYPE of music, which is pretty much everything except Country/Western. I listen 100% through my iphone or iPods.

I come from an LP, then 8 track (yuck), then cassette, then CD background so when I finally went all compressed format I didn't realize what I'd be "missing" I just thought, "Wow what a convenience"!! Anyway, I ended up ditching all my CD's (about 1400 total, originals!) & ripping them into iTunes, total of about 7500 songs. I long ago sold my HD580 back in 2005 & just listened from earbuds. I got tired of these real quick. So I saved up & did my research & just knew I had to have the Senn HD650's but I knew I had to have a good amp so I bought both (used) & I was thoroughly disappointed. I didn't hear this "wide open" expanded 3D imaged sound that everyone bragged about. After "damning" these headphones for being overpriced I realized, after my anger, I was being angry at the wrong item, it wasn't the can's it was the compressed format that removed all the subtle nuances of the original recordings!

So back to the drawing board to look for a decently priced (new) set of headphones. I bought a pair of in ear headphones from Sennhesier of course & these sounded good, better than than the Apple buds. Then I ran into the Momentums! I did my youtube & google research & the Momentums appear to be the one's I've been looking for. It has the controller but are "can" style headphones not earbuds! The cord is just long enough so i can stick my iphone in my pocket but no so long that it'll get caught on a doorknob or something else. The only drawback is it was hard to find the black with red from any type of discount. I got the brown ones reluctantly but I couldn't argue the price I got them for and for what it's worth the brown looks pretty clean & euro with the brushed aluminum.

I knew as soon as I started listening to some of the typical songs I play that I found my pair. They're paired perfectly for the portable MP3, phone or tablet's. You don't need an amp of any kind, they have great sound quality even for a sealed back design an because they're sealed you won't bother anyone sitting next to you at moderate levels. I was kind of put off of how small the ear surroundings were because my ears are not huge but they do stick out a bit, once I found a good position my ears fit fine.

All I can say is that I"m finally happy with a pair of headphones. I think the challenge is to match your style of music with headphones. Don't listen to name droppers & snobs who only talk about Gredo, AKG's HiFiMan & even Sennheisers. People knock Beats by Dre but hey if your music is like 99% current day hip hop & Dance then the Beats are probably the best suited for you. They're not for people who listen to live rock or classical. I had to find that out the hard way those higher priced headphones that require DAC's & AMPS aren't necessarily suited to my music. I believe the momentums are a great "in betweener" set of headphones. For that person who's aged a bit where they're not looking for LOUD & BOOM any more, they know & want detailed sound but they're still at a stage where they're listening to their music in a compressed 256k or less format, mp3 or wave format & not CD's anymore, but want that CD sound brought back.

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

The still photos in the same situation came out just as bad, also grainy, also often blurry, and often washed-out as well. I tried both video and stills at various levels of zoom--without a zoom the quality of both was noticeably better, but still poor quality. I then took stills out in a well-lit hallway and again was disappointed in the quality and again, the Kodak completely outmatched the Phillips.

I've used it in outdoor conditions and better lit conditions and there's no doubt the picture quality is better in those conditions, but in all of them it comes in quite below the Kodak in quality.

The zoom was very slow to auto-focus and took several long seconds before settling in.

the choice of a micro-SD. Not only is it annoyingly different, which I could live with, but it really took some force to get it into the slot. I eventually used a pen cap to push it in, wincing at the pressure needed to do so. (I won't discuss the times it popped out and I had to search on the floor/desk for it).

it has its pluses, but to be honest, since its primary purpose is taking good pictures and video, and so far it hasn't, I don't see the point in outlining the good points which are so secondary to its primary objective.

I'll use it a few more times to ensure this review is a fair one, but there is no way I will do so at special events or without using the Kodak as backup (or one of my point-and-shoots which also shoot far better video based on the samples so far--two Canon elphs and our larger Canon IS). With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.

This review is for the TP-LInk Mesh WiFi M5 system.
—————
Amended April 28, 2020
Now that I’ve been using this for a couple weeks, I am returning to add these units HAVE NOT cured the dead spots that needed more signal strength. Yes, the WiFi signal is present in those areas of my home. However, the signal strength has not improved over what my centrally located router produced on its own. Essentially for my roughly $125, I got a couple stylish WiFi access points. What I DID NOT GET is the improved coverage promoted in the description.
—————
This IS NOT a plug it in and it works system. You need to know at minimum:
—Your current router’s IP address, the user ID for it, and the password. If you haven’t changed them from the default, you have no business installing a network anything, because you put EVERYTHING on your system at high risk for hacking. Why? The problem is that the default user ID and password are the SAME FOR ALL routers of the same brand (every brand router has a published default user id and password).
—You need to know which of several comm protocols your ISP uses.
—You need to know that IF YOU SWAP OUT YOUR ROUTER for one of the units, the others WILL NOT WORK to extend your WiFi network. For that you need to set these up as extenders, with the first being connected to your existing router.
—To set up a network of WiFi extenders, you need to know how to turn your existing router’s WiFi transmission off. Only then can you use these as extenders, satellites, or whatever you know them as.
—You are highly likely to have to update the firmware on each M5 device.
—You should set aside about two to three hours to set up a network of multiple devices.
—If you set these up as extenders, some of the default security features are switched off. You need to be sure these security features are enabled on your router instead.

A power inverter for your car is a very handy device to have. It plugs into the car's power outlet (which I still call the cigarette lighter) and gives you the ability to plug in an AC powered item. There are limitations, of course - you're not going to be able to plug in your refrigerator, but for low power demand items, it can be very helpful for power when you're traveling or for when the lights go out at home.

I'm very pleased with the Sabrent. It offers a decent amount of power - 300 watts - which makes it far more useful for the things I'd like to use it for than the lower powered inverters. However, the larger capacity comes with a larger size. The unit is about 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, and 1.5 inches thick. It weighs a hefty one pound. Not a small and inconspicuous device by any means.

All the controls and ports are located on one end, which makes it easier to deal with the large size. There's an on/off rocker switch. I wish it had a more solid "click" to it - it has a rather soft touch, so it can be inadvertently switched on/off when moving it if you grab it the wrong way. It has a single 3-prong female outlet to power an AC device, and 2 USB outlets. The USB outlets are a nice addition, since it can be used to charge phones, tablets, etc. without having to unplug the inverter and plug in a conventional car USB adapter.

The housing is plastic but appears pretty sturdy. The plug that goes into the cigarette lighter is decent. Works fine, but feels a little on the flimsy side compared with the overall unit. The cord could also be a bit thicker for greater durability or, ideally, coiled so it does not get tangled. But quite workable as-is and MUCH easier to deal with than an inverter that does not have a cord and plugs directly into the car power outlet.

Performance is very good. I had no problems running a 60 watt cooler using the inverter. Power delivery seemed fine and steady. I don't have test equipment to measure the power quality, but the cooler ran at a steady pace.

The inverter does get pretty warm in use, and has an internal fan that kicks on to keep things cool. The fan can be heard, but the sound is not what I'd consider to be noisy.

It's important to know the power demand of whatever you're plugging in, plus keep in mind that some devices, such as coolers, have an initial surge demand. For example, a 60watt cooler may use 60 watts when running, but will pull 100+ watts when it starts up. If you try to run something that attempts to pull more than the inverter can supply, the inverter will shut down for safety (both for itself and the item attached). According to the specs, this can handle a surge of 350 watts, but I'll keep any surge loads I put on it at not more than 300 watts to be safe.

Although 300 watts won't go far, this is a handy item to keep on hand not only for power on the road, but also to serve as a power source (albeit limited) when the household power goes out. While there are some faults with the unit, overall it is a good performer and a decent value for the price. 4.5 stars rounded to 5.

Though I have a laptop, I decided to use this solid-state drive as a boot drive on my desktop computer. If you are unfamiliar with the difference between a solid-state and a regular hard drive, the solid-state has no moving parts, which makes it silent, fast, reliable, and shock resistant. It has twice the capacity and twice the speed of the solid-state drive I got a couple of years ago for the same price, and blows away a standard drive for speed.

Given the silence and speed, it makes a great boot drive for running Windows, Photoshop, and other programs where speed is a huge advantage. Just to give you an idea, when upgrading from a regular two-year-old hard drive to this solid-state drive, my Windows boot time went from two minutes to about 10 seconds. Seriously, my computer now starts up and is ready to use in like 10 seconds.

What I do is use a solid-state drive as my boot drive and a regular hard drive as a storage drive. Solid-state drives like this are really expensive to purchase if you need any kind of capacity, but a 200 GB drive will certainly hold all of your programs and often used files.

As for this drive specifically, I hooked it up to my desktop and it was immediately recognized by Windows. The drivers installed automatically. In order to make the drive show up as a drive and work in Windows 7, I had to right-click on computer, click manage, double-click storage, double-click disk management, partition it, give it a drive letter, and format it.

As I said, it's a lot faster than the solid-state drive I had from a couple years ago, and there's no problem using it on my desktop machine rather than my laptop.

You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”

To use this SANDISK EXTREME UHS-I SDXC memory card the way it's intended (for advanced photography), you need an SDXC device (camera or camcorder). You also need an SDXC device that's compatible with this new, latest SDXC format. I was disappointed to learn that my older Panasonic Lumix DMC-LX2 camera, which is compatible with many SDXC memory cards, is NOT able to recognize and use this memory card.

A word of warning: If your SDXC or other device is incompatible with this SDXC card, the device may suggest that you format the card. Do not do this! Formatting will ruin the card as an SDXC card. SDXC devices are backward compatible (and can accept SDXC, SD, or SDHC memory cards), but SDXC cards should be used only in SDXC devices. (To learn more about the do's and don'ts of SDXC memory cards, you can Google "SD Association Using SDXC memory cards".) If you have a Panasonic camera, you can find a list of cameras that are compatible with SDXC on the Panasonic web site. Presumably other camera manufacturers' web sites have similar lists.

Although this card doesn't work in my camera, it can be accessed with a USB reader or adapter that is SDXC-compatible; or through a WinXP, WinVista, or Win7 PC card reader slot, if the PC has the exFAT file system update (KB955704) that can be downloaded from the Microsoft Download Center. My fairly recent Win7 PC (ASUS Essentio Series) is not compatible with the above file system update, but already had a driver that enabled it to access the SDXC card without formatting.

One nice feature that I didn't expect is that it doesn't appear to let you switch to an input that doesn't have a device even powered on, at least using the remote.

The nice feature of my previous switch was that it did not need to be powered. The Koopman one DOES need power. It comes with the micro USB cable and power adapter, but if your TV has an open 5v usb output, that might be more convenient. I had to plug it in. It's small and light, so I'll need to anchor it in place so it's not flying off the stand. HDMI cables like to pull things awry. It's almost inconspicuous.

The remote is tiny. The box itself had a button on it, so if the remote goes temporarily missing, you can still tap your way between inputs.
I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.
One cool improvement would be if it had an audio output, even in only a 1/8" port.

Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. Lots of pros:

- very comfortable to wear. I always have ear buds in when working out, and these stayed put through all my cardio work with zero ear soreness.

- sound quality is great. I was listening to Friday Night in San Francisco (John Mclaughlin, Al Dimeola and Pco De Lucia) and was amazed at how much of the mid-range sound I was missing using my old ear buds (JBLs). The bass is not boomy, but more than adequate. I found I was able to get better bass sound by changing the rubber tips to a larger size that better fit my ear.

- lots of nice touches such as a carrying case that is well designed to protect the ear buds, a selection of rubber ear tips, and even a cleaning tool. It also comes with an airplane jack adapter, but I won't get much use out of that.

- outstanding sound isolation. No ambient sound gets in at all. In fact, I had to take one of them out when I was doing road work since I was concerned about not being able to hear cars approaching.

My quibbles are minor and mainly relate to the sturdiness of the cabling. It seems pretty thin and may not stand up to the rigors I often put my ear buds through. Too early to tell if this will be a problem, so I didn't subtract any stars because of it. I'll update the review should the build quality prove to be too wimpy.

Highly recommend that this be on your short list if you're looking for comfortable buds that sound great, and are very effective in blocking outside noise.

I have a Foscam WiFi security camera in a steel pole barn. Even with a high gain antenna on the camera and a fiberglass door, my connection was pretty bad. Choppy video and lost connections were common. I needed to get the antenna outside.

Although this antenna isn't outdoor rated, it is pretty easy to make watertight. Some tape over the mounting screw holes on the back and a little self vulcanizing rubber electrical tape around the antenna joint and no water is going to get in. You could use something like RTV silicone too. Keep the moisture out and you now made it outdoor capable. It was pretty close the way it comes and I'm sure it would probably be fine for a long time, but sealing it completely is pretty easy. The magnet mount works great on the steel siding. The camera I have, like most, comes with a standard SMA connector vs.the SMA-RP (reversed pin), but you can get an adapter here on Amazon. [[ASIN:B005H488Y4 SMA Male to SMA-RP Female Adapter]]

Added a 20 foot cable with standard SMA male and female connectors and now I have a great outdoor antenna for an indoor camera in a steel building that is great for blocking radio signals. It works very well and the results exceeded my expectations.

I've bought another antenna for the same setup on another camera. Although it isn't exactly what they intended it for, it works extremely well.

I've been watching a bunch of electronics repair videos lately and thinking back at my past purchases and the electronics I threw away, I wondered how many devices I could have rescued. Determined not to let electronics repair scare me off from tacking them, I decided to start collecting the tools that I need to do my own repairs.

I started with an affordable, but well-reviewed soldering iron: the Pinecil. A good silicone mat (same one as StezStix Fix), and now a microscope.

The LLIMINK Digital Microscope 7'' LCD, Coin Microscope is a great product. In the box, you'll find all of the accessories you'll need to get started, including any cables that you might need. What I wasn't expecting of this device is that it is actually battery powered and that the battery is removeable (see my pictures) -- very much in line with the Right-To-Repair philosophy. The remote control was a nice addition as well (taking a picture seems to be only controllable from the remote so make sure you don't lose track of it).

The base of the microscope is aluminum with two built-in LED lamps that are separately powered from the microscope itself. They provide additional lighting from other directions if you need it. The microscope itself has bright leds that shine directly downward on the board.

If the microscope mounted LEDs are causing too much glare, there is a collar that can be fitted to the scope. It will block the LEDs and instead, reflect them so that the light is indirect. Kinda like the lamps the dentists use. You're not blinded by the bulb when you're looking up at those lights.

Moving on to the screen, it is a 7" screen with passable quality. The viewable angle isn't great but it gets the job done. Any issues with the screen quality is solved by connecting the included micro-hdmi cable to your monitor. I've included pictures of both the 7" screen and the ouptut from my monitor.

I've already done a couple of simple projects with the help of this device. I built a garage door opener and gate opener using microcontrollers that are connected to my home automation system. I'm building my confidence with electronics and soldering. Hopefully, I can keep more devices out of landfills by repairing them myself.

I purchased this for my Samsung Galaxy S2 8.0, which I recently bought used. The install was fairly easy - I used Supershieldz before and while their smartphone protectors are far easier to install than these on account of the smaller size, the experience was highly comparable. In the end did have a couple tiny air bubbles - so small that they were only iridescent patches - which I could not work to the edges of the screen no matter how I tried. However, I just left the S2 in a warm room overnight, and the next day, they were totally gone and have not yet returned, more than month later.

Responsiveness is indistinguishable from the base touchscreen. Clarity is, so far as I can tell, perfect. Very low friction, though it still picks up fingerprints, science hasn't brought us that far yet it seems. I really like that it comes with two protectors, just in case one breaks in the future. The fact that the screen had a couple (very) minor scratches on it already did not affect the install whatsoever.

Install notes are unremarkable. I followed the instructions closely. Basically, you need a clean area with good light and low airflow. You should wear tight-knit clothing, like nylon or linen, instead of something fuzzy. If you have long hair, tie it back. Wear latex gloves. Make sure you have 15m or so to devote to the install. Remove the tablet from its case, clean the screen up, inspect it from multiple angles, then do the hinge-type install as instructed.

I have also bought the RF-62 II (floor standing speakers) that match this one, the first thing I noticed was everything sounded natural. I have owned Klipsch for over 10-11 years and felt it was time to upgrade. The other thing I noticed was extreme clarity with natural sound. I was surprised since I had some doubts they could improve on my Reference Center 3. Beyond clarity, the highs seem more balanced with everything blending in perfectly with the rest of the sound.

Now, keep in mind my old Klipsch set everyone praised it till no end. When I upgraded everyone (father, friends and neighbors) noticed the sound was natural and not overly expressive. What I mean by overly expressive is "bright sound", this is not a negative since Klipsch speakers are designed to be efficient. But the Reference 62 II lines seem to have been fine tuned and the sound outputs its tone more natural and pleasing to the ears while being dynamic. It truly is an upgrade.

For those of you unfamiliar with klipsch, don't be afraid, they have been around for 65 years and dominate the Mars amphitheater market and movie cinemas. I am 29 years old, and ran into the reference line when they first came out in 1999 (15 years old) and was blown away. I did not make the purchase till 2002 and have been a fan of Klipsch since than. My side hobby is audio and have worked the audio video field threw college and I have Klipsch to thank for catching my interest. it surprises me many are hooked on Sony speakers or speakers they sell in regular stores like Bestbuy, Walmart etc etc (excluding Magnolia high fi). The Reference line is NOT the one in your local Bestbuy. Those are the Synergy line.

Every other speaker sounds like pillows are blocking the sound. lol. I have had friends say that same line to me a few times. The sound is very different from other speakers. The best way to describe it is concert or open field type of sound. I even thought about switching speaker manufacturer. After spending a month listing to other brands. -None- came close. The clarity of the Klipsch speaker design is enough to make you stay.

The upgrades like the magnetic grills are a plus. You no longer have to worry about the plastic stubs breaking off or them sticking. Everything looks more uniformed as in constant; unvarying; undeviating. I also like the speaker design. The copper color on the speaker and design make them stand out instantly with a modern look that is not overly visual. Just enough to catch everyones attention. They look beautiful with grills on or off. Even minor touches like Klipsch logo on top of the grill and etched Reference line at the bottom of the grill are well done.

Note: I am running a high end amplifier with all matching Reference 62 II lines (soon getting my matching back speakers). I have manually calibrated my system, but have everything set to reference level and occasionally pump up the level of my front and center to +3. (reference level is 0. the starting point). You can tell a good speaker when you don't have to alter anything like equalizer or increase speaker levels. Those of you using Audyssey or any type of microphone for calibration you may want to experiment manual calibration since the mics sometimes are inaccurate, or may calibrate your speakers to low or to high. This may be why some reviewers get low volume sound or to loud.

You have to take into consideration that your amplifier, setup, speaker position etc all play a key role in everything.

Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

Our antenna rotor broke and for 3 years we have been waiting for new chips to come through so we could get another one. It has taken WAY too long. I got this to help with the problem in the meanwhile. What I got was MORE problems.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a blister pack. It has a long cord and a double tail plug on it. The idea is that you put the plug into the antenna spot on the TV and the other is a USB port that you put into your TV. There is a sticker to put this on the wall and instructions.

HOW THIS WORKS
I have had no end of frustration with this thing. We do not have an OLD TV but we do not have any USB ports in this that work with the antenna. The outlets are such that I can not fit ANY adapters into the plug to use an adapter for the USB. The cord from the USB to the intersection where the antenna cord is is very short- only 13 inches. Put that together with the other cord for the antenna which is also about 13 inches and you can not spread them tightly so you only have about 22 to 24 inches tops to get from the TV on the wall down to a USB outlet if you don't have USB on your TV.

I TRIED TO MAKE THIS WORK
I have tried many different USB adapters to get this to work and none of them will work with this unit. I am frustrated and have spent so much time on this, I am giving up. I really wanted this to work, but despite this being an HDTV, it just isn't working out with this unit. I guess we will have to go without antenna TV on that TV longer.

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you have USB available on your TV and an antenna hook up, this might work for you. If you don't have a USB port that will work with this unit, you will have to have an available plug that has USB conversion in it, or USB on a power strip that is not more than 24 inches away from the antenna jack on the TV to make it work. You can also use an extension cord and adapter, but honestly, it is a lot of expense for a unit that might or might not work as you like.

MY RATING
THREE STARS. I can not give this a terrible rating like I want to in my frustration. To be fair, three stars is about right. I do not like that it does not come with adapters or alternatives for TVs. Most people who watch antenna TV do not always have the newest equipment. We happen to have this TV that needs the hookup. We have another TV which is newer but the picture is not that great and we already have it set up with another antenna hookup.

I would like this a LOT better if it came with a streamlined USB plug adapter for the power outlets.

UPDATES
If by some miracle, I can find a USB adapter that will fit in this situation and actually WORK, I will update this review and reconsider the rating. For now, it stays as it is. I have put enough time and resources into trying to make this work.

I have been wanting a new MP3 player for a while now. I refuse to waste my phone with cluttered songs and use. I have watched everyone else I know blow through phones from constant use. I wanted to have a dedicated MP3 player. Let's see how this worked out.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This comes in a nice box- great for gift giving. It has a cord with it for charging and attaching to computer if you want to download songs to it. This does NOT have any internal memory, however. All songs have to be stored on a microSD card. There is port for headphones, mini USB, and line out port.

HOW TO OPERATE
ON/OFF
The power button is on the top of the unit. It has to be held in for a moment before it kicks in. There is an issue with the power button being on the top pressed down easily. The design of this has a raised edge of the case so that it is harder to press on the power button accidentally.

MENU
The menu button is easy to operate. It takes you around the menus using the forward and backward arrow buttons.

VOLUME
The volume buttons are on the outside edge on the right as you look at the case. The + and - buttons are separate.

BACK BUTTON
This takes you back through the menu and you can replay songs too.

PLAY PAUSE
Is on the front of the case and it is easy to access and see.

SCREEN
This is not a full color screen. It is simple and easy to read, however, without graphic clutter.

BLUETOOTH?
I had a heck of a time with this at first. I was not having it work well with my bluetooth headphones and it frustrated me to no end. I was about ready to give this an awful review when I suddenly realized- it was not the player, it was both sets of headphones that were not working correctly! Once I got the headphones working, the sound is BEAUTIFUL on this.

I have also used this with a few bluetooth speakers with great results. I like the solid feeling of the body- it stays put but does not take up too much room.

SOUND
You can change the sound quite a bit with this to be what you want. There are presets and fine tuning settings you can use. Once I finally got this figured out, the sound is amazing.

READ OUT
Again, this is NOT TOUCHSCREEN nor does it have fancy full color graphics. It is simple and easy to read and use.

STORAGE
Remember, this stores all of the songs on the microSD card. There is not any internal storage in this otherwise.

AM I GLAD TO HAVE THIS?
Once I got the problems worked out, I have to say I really like this. It is not as intuitive as some items, but it is really nice to have and I love to play it. I like shuffler or single CD artist choices, etc.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a really nice MP3 player. It is a bit more rustic than some might be used to with smart phones, but it really works nicely and the sound is great.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. It does what it says, although I would prefer it to have some internal storage as well as microSD, but that is just me. For what this is- it is very nice. I like it and am pleased with the performance.

I needed a smaller, fast laptop for many reasons to include practical airplane use and general portability. The 15"+ inch size is no longer usable given the seating squeeze on airplanes. I shopped the 13" i5 processor touchscreens (HP, Toshiba, Fujitsu, etc). I thought the HP was `dull' except for the flip display (on more thought, the pivot mechanism looked like a fragile link and to easy to break), Fujitsu was the best but $500 premium was excessive (apparently it's the last laptop built in Japan rather than China). This Toshiba was about right. There are many tradeoffs to consider.

Toshiba good:
I use the touch screen as a mobile cognitive `whiteboard' for sketching and retaining client discussion. Don't waste $ if you don't need a touchscreen. The touchscreen overlay does reduce image quality.

DDR memory is easily user expanded (unusual for a laptop)

Win score is 4.7 out of the box ... far more than I'd think a typical user would need. Expanding memory should push it >5.0. Beyond that, you'd need a zippy video card.

The unit runs on about 25w in battery mode ... won't set your pants on fire.

The optical drive is internal ... no flimsy tray to slide out and take space, just a slot ... excellent! No other 13.3" has this feature that I looked at.

Toshiba has done the best industrial design job ... it has the best look and feel among the units I was looking at

Up for debate:
2 reviewers have problems with the "flimsy" keyboard and I had a similar first take. I would now couch this element a user preference. Personally, the design parameter, cushioned keyboard works better for my typing style after I've had some time on it. I now prefer it over the ridged keyboards. The Toshiba keyboard is a design element and not a flaw or cheapening. As a 'buyer beware' among the smaller format laptops, keyboard compatibility with the user should be the #1 user consideration. You really need to try before you buy. The Toshiba keyboard does not double and triple up key functions to compensate for the smaller space as others are trying. There is no keyboard 'standardization" in this smaller format. Every manufacturer has a different keyboard configuration.

Don't likes:
The `laptops for idiots' bloatware overhead has to go as soon as you're comfortable. This is not unique to Toshiba. There are 40-50 unnecessary overhead programs that slow startup significantly. They are easily disabled to speed the startup cycle.

Battery life is unusually short at less then 3 hours in full operation. The i5 power wattage consumption vs battery tradeoff should be considered. I've been adjusting power schemes with not much success. For trans con flites you may want to carry an extra pack.

Unexpected delight! = Backlighted keyboard means no ambient light required to work in the dark. I've never seen this attribute before.

Anyone who doesn't own an iPod or iPad probably won't see the utility of this device. However, for those who know the limitations of a 16GB iDevice, this can come in very handy to extend your storage.

One caveat is that given the cost of the Airstash at the time of writing, if you haven't yet taken the iPlunge, it might be better to go with the 64GB iPad 3 or 2 in the first place. However, if you already own the 16GB, then getting this device becomes an economical option.

The tech specs are covered in the product description, so below are some of my observations based on my experiences using the Airstash with an iPad 2.

Once the Airstash is powered up (by holding down the power button until the green indicator light turns on, then releasing it to see the light flash rapidly three times), you can connect your device to it wirelessly. However, in order to take full advantage of the Airstash, you will need to install the Airstash+ app which you can download from the Apple AppStore for free. This app allows you to access the files that you have copied to the Airstash. Alternatively, you can use a browser and browse to airstash.net for the same functionality.

While it may look like a flash drive on steroids, and works in a similar fashion when you plug it into your computer's USB port, I found it was not as straight-forward a matter when being used to save files. Accessing the files you have placed there is simple enough, but in order to save stuff to it using your iPad/iPod, your app needs to be WebDAV compatible. The Quick Start Guide supplied with the device briefly mentions that once connected you `launch the WebDAV compatible app of your choice'.

Now, if you're like me, then you probably have no idea what this means. What I've discovered is that WebDAV is some kind of `format/protocol' that allows you to save your files to the Airstash. The problem is, not all apps are WebDAV compatible. Apple's Pages, Numbers and Keynote are, but QuickOffice isn't. So if you're a Microsoft Office user like I am, accustomed to QuickOffice, then this device might not be for you. You can read your Office files from the Airstash, but you wouldn't be able to edit them and save them back to the device.

Other observations...

Without installing additional software/apps, mp4 (movie) files on the Airstash played easily on my iPad, but not avi files. (I didn't try digital movies but the product description says that you can play movies loaded on it on your device.)

I couldn't figure out how to save stuff directly onto it that I had downloaded to my iPad, like apps, attachments, books, etc. Maybe there is an easier way, but I had to sync my iPad with my computer first, then copy the files over to the Airstash from the computer.

The iPad could open epub books (in iBooks) and pdf files saved on the Airstash. Presumably there shouldn't be any problems with music and photo files, but I didn't test these either.

It took about 8 minutes to transfer 366MB from my (old) laptop to the Airstash using USB 1.0. With newer computers this should be faster.

Some pros, some cons - consider this is you have an iDevice that needs more storage space.

This is without a doubt the best looking soundbar I’ve come across so far. The shape is more than just aesthetics – if you have a TV on a table stand the low profile of the soundbar doesn’t get in the way of the screen. Granted, I’m sure there’s a TV out there that sits low enough that the soundbar will get in the way, but if it does it will be minimal. Even if you have a wall-mounted screen, the soundbar shape is still something that can be appreciated.

No complaints either with regard to the build quality. This feels as solid as it looks. I had high expectations given the price point, and I was not disappointed. The remote is also well-done with a straightforward design that makes it simple to use.

A few years ago I ran wiring for my main TV for a 7.1 speaker setup. It took many hours, and gave me a new appreciation as to why electricians charge so much for fishing wire through walls. So, the fact that I was able to get this set up and running in about an hour (including the unpacking and calibration time) was a real treat. I would rate the setup ease, and the included instructions, as excellent.

There are a number of great features, the main one for me being the detachable side speakers. It gives more flexibility than the usual sound bar in that you can position them for rear sound if you want that immersive feel, but also use them as standalone speakers for other devices. I had no problems pairing one to a tablet. One potential negative is the internal battery. While the run time is fine – I ran it for a good four hours continuously without a problem – I’ve had enough devices with internal batteries go bad (e.g., the battery will no longer take much of a charge) that I always am wary of internal batteries.

The sound quality was both good and bad, and in an unexpected way. I was expecting that this soundbar would be left in the dust by my wired system at high volume. While it was bested (especially with bass given the slim subwoofer) it was a far closer horse race than I thought it would be. This soundbar can put out a healthy amount of volume and still remain in control of sound quality.

Where it fell short is when it was not pushed hard. Soft passages were weak; dialog was unclear at times. Running this at a soft volume (such as at night when others are sleeping in the house) was not enjoyable – I ended up having to turn on subtitles since I could not make out the dialog clearly. Now, this issue could be exacerbated by my aging ears, but others in the house, who are younger, also found it weak and unimpressive at low volume.

I think most people who get this will be looking to have “big” sound in a simple to set up, simple to use system. On that end, the Philips soundbar delivers. It misses somewhat on the soft end of the spectrum, but the build quality, looks, and flexibility warrant a five-star rating even at this rather lofty price point.

In my opinion, this unit makes the GH4 into a professional video camera. However, it's certainly not perfect. I begged the Nikon guy at NAB 2013 to build something like this for the D800, but nothing yet. Panasonic is listening. I'm commenting here because as of June 4, 2014, you cannot download the YAGH manual from Panasonic's website for details you may need.

1. Cost

It's more than the camera body, which is to say, really expensive. I can only hope the YAGH will fit future GH5 and GH6 camera bodies. Please, Panasonic: don't obsolete this thing.

2. Power

There is no internal battery. It has to have external power, supplied via the industry-standard 4-pin XLR. This is good and bad. Stated power requirement on the bottom plate is 12VDC at 1.4 amps.

Power is applied to Pin 4, Ground to Pin 1. (Pins 2 and 3 are not used.) The manual says voltage can vary from 11VDC to 17VDC. This means any professional AC camera supply or brick battery like an Anton Bauer 14.4VDC. (I'm using a 12VDC battery pack built from ten NiMH D-cells and supplies 10,000 mAhs.) You'll need a 4-pin extension power cord and drag the power supply with you. Hello battery belt? Sort of going backward. It would be great to have the ability to add lith-ion batteries somehow but perhaps it draws too much power for smaller cells.

The external power powers both YAGH and the GH4 body.

Once the YAGH is attached to the camera, an "Interface Unit" menu appears on the "Motion Picture" tab. There are many options. One setting allows you to set low battery warnings at 11, 12.5, 13.5 and 15 volts. This is very professional.

UPDATE Sept 26,2014: I built a 12VDC power supply from a computer monitor power supply and a 4-pin female XLR jack. I also have a 14.4 volt battery power supply. I found that if I leave the battery warning set to 13.5 for the one power supply the 12VDC power supply won't work. The battery warning settings actually stop the camera from working. Be sure to set the battery warning levels to match the batteries you are using.

3. Fan

Yes, it has a fan. You can barely hear it (can't hear it six inches away), but hot air blows out the left side when it's plugged in. I assume there's a lot of electronics inside to supply all the outputs. Have not demonstrated the fan can be heard by the camera-body's built in stereo mics.

4. Inputs:

a. the 4-pin XLR power plug

b. two, 3-pin XLR audio inputs, switchable between Line (0dB), Mic (-50dB) and 48VDC phantom power. A stereo/mono switch sends the signal from a single mic to both left and right channels. You can select which mics to use: the built-in stereo camera mics or the XLR inputs.

c. time code-in on one of the BNC connectors

d. the micro-HDMI plug that transfers the HDMI camera output signal to a full-sized HDMI on the YAGH unit. This HDMI interface is implemented clumsily; I hope there is a better reason than engineering laziness. It's basically a short Micro-to-Full HDMI extension cord. The dovetailed arm that sticks up on the unit holds the micro-HDMI cord with a plug. You mount the camera to the unit, open the rubber door on the camera's left side so that it sticks straight out of the camera, then slide the YAGH's dovetailed micro-HDMI plug into the camera, then tighten the tiny thumbscrew. The rubber door disappears into the dovetail arm and is not removed or abused by being bent back too far. This sturdy plastic arm with its metal dovetailed very definitely protects the extremely fragile Micro-HDMI socket on the camera body. (I personally would not directly connect a cable into the camera. One yank and your camera is broken. I thought the Mini-HDMI plugs on Canon 5D's and Nikon D800's were bad. This Micro-HDMI is even smaller and weaker. The YAGH solves the problem.) It would have been better if Panasonic had routed the signal through the bottom of the camera, but that would mean another 15 pins down there, and it's already crowded.

e. One drawback of this HDMI interface method: if you screw the dovetail in, it takes up the whole left side of the camera and you cannot pivot the flip-out viewfinder down at all and upwards only about 5 degrees. The whole point of the pivoting viewfinder is the ability to frame low- or high-angle shots. If you don't need to remote the HDMI to the YAGH (say you're using the audio interface and DC in and not monitoring via the HDMI) you can let the dovetail hang there, flopping in the wind, and allow the viewfinder to rotate.

5. Outputs

a. full-sized HDMI socket under a rubber door on the left side outputs 4:2:2 8bit or 4:2:2 10bit. You can't record both internally and externally if in 10bit. You access this setting while in "Creative Video Mode." The 8bit is good for sending to an external monitor while recording to the card.

b. 4, SDI BNC connectors under a rubber door on the right side, marked 1, 2, 3 and 4. They output different signals based on the resolution of the recorded signal.
- any of the four BNCs can output a 1.5G HDSDI signal if resolution is set up to 1080-29.97p.
- 3G-SDI is output on BNCs 1 and 2 if you record in 1080-59.94p or 1080-50p
- 1.5G-SDI Square Division (whatever that is) is output on all four BNCs as a group if you want to output the Cinema C4K (4096x2160-24.00p) or Broadcast 4K (3840x2160-24.00p/23.98p/29.97p). Apparently you will need all four BNCs to get enough bandwidth to send the 4K signals to an external monitor or recorder.

UPDATE: the four BNC SDI outs supply "QuadHD" -- that is, each delivers one fourth of a 3840x2160 picture or, four 1920x1080 streams. If you have a device that can accept QuadHD, you're in business.

6. Plug and socket covers

Minor point, but of some concern. The camera is not waterproof but is touted as "splash proof." To achieve this, rubber doors seal the camera all over. The bottom of the camera has two rubber seals that cover two sets of contacts -- one with five, one with 18 contacts. The YAGH unit has quite exposed corresponding spring-loaded pins sticking up. When you attach the camera to the YAGH, you obviously need to remove the four covers. There's no place to store them. You will want them if you split the units apart, especially the camera seals.

7. Audio Controls

a. two 8-segment LEDs indicating level: 4 green, 3 yellow, 1 red.

b. two approx. 1/2" diameter knobs to adjust level, shielded by a clear cover so they won't get hit accidentally yet are easy enough to adjust during a take without shaking the camera or making noise

c. brightness is adjustable to either "Hi" or "Low" via the Interface Unit menu item under the Motion Picture tab

8. Mechanical

a. two locating pins register to the camera body and are held tightly via the 1/4-20 tripod socket. It really becomes a single unit

b. Both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 threaded tripod mounts on the bottom. There's also a hole for the tripod plates that have an anti-rotation pin. Having both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 allows you to use two screws to mount the YAGH to your tripod plate so it cannot rotate.

c. two 1/4-20 threaded holes are supplied on the lower front of the YAGH to allow mounting a set of matte box rods, once some third party supplier starts making the rod/rail adapter. The two holes are exactly 32mm apart and centered 85mm below the optical center of the lens, conforming to the 15mm Light Weight Support (LWS) standard.

d. It's still not too giant for hand holding, but it's getting there. It's really designed to be tripod mounted.

e. Because the YAGH extends forward of the camera and slopes downward, if you use one, the Metabones Speed Booster tripod foot must be removed for the adapter to fit the camera while attached to the YAGH. Fortunately, Metabones allows this and supplies necessary Allen wrenches and caps.

Overall, the YAGH is useful -- allows (well, requires) external power for long runtimes, protects the camera from HDMI socket damage, outputs all kinds of signals up to true 4K via SDI, allows timecode input and allows professional audio inputs.

However, if you don't need external power, SDI-out or HDMI-out, a simple audio interface like the JuicedLink Riggy [[ASIN:B009YLRZFE JuicedLink RM222 Riggy-Micro Dual-XLR Preamplifier with Phantom Power]] or a Beachtek [[ASIN:B009R89SNQ BeachTek DXA-SLR MINI PRO HDSLR Audio Adapter]] might suffice to get pro audio in.

Got this, my first HDTV, for $749 total delivered. Seems like a great deal. Has the AA01 panel:

PROS: Very good HD picture, which becomes stunning with good source material (after calibrating the picture); excellent SD picture (better than the good CRT TV it replaced); tons of controls for picture calibration; streaming Netflix is great, the Pandora app has become my household's new source for music of all types, either through the TV speakers or piped to the stereo; ethernet makes upgrading firmware and internet apps very easy; lots of connectivity; easy to set up; light; swivel stand works well; power efficient; doesn't get hot; no noise or buzz; no dead or stuck pixels; has analog audio out jack (important for old A/V receivers); functions as an outstanding computer monitor (with DVI-to-HDMI cable); glossy screen helps picture and repels dust; can't even notice the red "Touch of Color" design.

CONS: Though black levels are generally very good, when the screen and room are both dark you can see some flashlighting around the corners and some bleedthrough of the backlight; very fast motion on screen will cause brief pixelization and loss of picture clarity (has to be very fast motion -- football and other sports look great); picture quality degrades quickly as you move off-center (though not as much as in some other LCD TVs); requires major picture calibration out of the box (I used settings found in reviews of this TV on the web, tweaked them a bit to preference, and the picture's much better, though it's hard to get it right); most of the current internet apps are useless; the factory preset modes are useless.

Overall it's a very good TV, with a picture that can sometimes be mesmerizing. And I'm glad I paid a bit extra for the C650's internet connectivity and glossy screen. Excellent product. I get about 35mb/sec transfer times with my Transcend 400x 64GB CF card using USB 2.0.

The biggest culprit with most CF card readers is that the rails that align the CF card to the pins (rails on the side of the CF card) are not deep enough. When you insert a CF card to a reader with shallow rails, it can be easy to bend the pins.

The Transcend P8 has very deep rails for the CF card reader, so a large majority of the CF card sinks into the reader before contacting the pins. This way you can be assured that the pins are aligned correctly without error for bending the pins.

Anyway, great product!

First time using a GMRS system and this was exactly what I needed for how I'm using it. With no modifications or aftermarket purchases, I was able to keep up 2-way comms with vehicles out to at least 2 miles away from inside my Jeep (never got further than that). That was even after resting it at night in below freezing temps. Very impressed with the life so I don't have to carry a separate charger or extra battery.

Setup for basic usage was very easy although getting into more advanced functions is fairly complex. Being able to switch between channel and ferq mode is simple, just turn it on/off while holding a single button. Also, I like that you can turn on high power with a single button push. Anything more than those adjustments and setting a frequency is complex however. Its possible to access the menu on the unit but its really to small to display a lot of text so you need the manual in front of you to really be able to make any useful changes. Not a huge issue for me as I don't need to do much more than set a channel and go, but for those that want to really dive into how the unit operates, its going to be somewhat of a chore.

Overall highly recommend the unit for anyone wheeling in a group that needs a simple comms setup and doesn't want to deal with mounting a more permeant unit. Don't forget to get your callsign to stay legal!

I use canned dusters for a variety of purposes, from cleaning keyboards to cleaning up my electric shaver. These sometimes leave residue behind, so I was interested in trying this electric duster to see if it would cut down on residue and save money in the long run. I will confess that I was not very optimistic and thought it would be underpowered. However, it has proven to be as effective as a canned duster in cleaning keyboards and other equipment, without leaving any residue and without losing power like canned dusters tend to do as they get cold.

This device is smaller than a tea kettle and relatively light. It requires an AC outlet so it does need to be plugged in when you want to use it. I was hopeful I had missed something on the description and that there was a rechargeable battery but unfortunately this is not the case. This was me being hopeful, not a confusing write-up.

It comes with a few attachments to help direct the air flow over the surface of what you’re trying to clean. The most helpful attachment, to me, is the round nozzle, but all of them have their uses.

I took it to my office where we have an abundance of dirty keyboards that need to be cleaned, and I set to work. I was expecting it to do a mediocre cleaning job, but it gave me a very pleasant surprise and blew air with plenty of force to clean out the clumps of dust that collect under the keys. More importantly, though, the power didn’t diminish like what tends to happen with canned dusters as they get cold, and there was no problem with frost buildup either.

So far, this is proving to be a useful and helpful tool. It produces enough force to get the job done without losing power, and it leaves no residue behind.

I am disappointed with these headphones for only one reason: My ears are small, and because of that, these headphones will not snuggly "hang" over my ears like they should. (Children would have the same problem, I expect.) If the over-ear part of the headphones were a little more moldable, I might be able to make them work for me; the extra ear gels themselves are helpful in getting a good fit into the ear canal, but that doesn't keep them from falling off of me. This is why I'm knocking of a star but, again, the problem is not with the headset but with my own anatomy!

With that caveat aside, I love them! For a gardener who wants to listen to something outside while working, the FM radio works just fine and the yellow rubbery cord keeps them around your neck even if you do knock them off. The U.S. Military-grade protection features (against dust, moisture, and shock) make these headphones stand out from the pack.

The Bluetooth pairing and sustained connection with these is better than any other Bluetooth device I've ever used, although I tend not to use Bluetooth unless I'm up and about in the house doing chores. I also don't make or get a lot of phone calls, so we don't even have a cellphone account and depend on the occasional VoIP to get the job done. Meaning I haven't tested the headset features at all.

But the sound is crisp and clear, without mud, more like monitoring headphones used in the music industry. I feel no pressure when wearing them (holding them to my head with my hands, of course, to keep them from falling off of my teensy ears), and I know they would be very comfortable for me in daily use. Maybe I can come up with something to rig them with so they don't fall off. Because I really do like them.

I have used and tested more Ethernet cables than I can remember and there is no question, all Ethernet cables are not created equally. Every one of the AmazonBasics branded items I’ve tested has been excellent and this cable is no exception.

Typically any device requiring an Ethernet cable will come with one in the packaging - it will work (usually). A good comparison is those cables are much like an old car - it should get you there, whereas this cable is like a high end sports car - it will get you there lightning fast, without fail.

This Cat7 is designed to be thin, but don’t let that fool you into thinking that it lacks capacity - within the thin PVC package contains aluminum shielding and 100% bare copper wires for super fast transfer speeds. The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 25 foot cable to run between my router to a unmanaged switch that branches to several IoT hubs - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

You will not find a better Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love. This is a purchase that you’ll never regret.

THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE ZBOX Bi323-U.

DO NOT BUY FROM THIS MANUFACTURER--REASONS:
The ZOTAC WEBSITE happily shows you the line of products available and that's were things stop being great. WHEN YOU ACCESS THE WEBSITE AND CLICK SUPPORT, DOWNLOADS (updated drivers, and so forth) OR OTHER LINKS YOU MUST CANNOT GET IN UNTIL YOU SIGN UP AND SUPPLY SOME PERSONAL INFORMATION, SUCH AS YOUR NAME AND EMAIL ADDRESS. When I was in the middle of installing the software, I needed updated drivers from Zotac and ran into this. I don't know about you, but I don't want to have to give up personal information to get what I need for a product I bought unless I wish to do that, and in this case the OS installation was being problematic so I really don't what to have to register a purchase for an item I may have to return or exchange.

TROJANS-MALWARE-AND VIRUSES ARE INCLUDED WITH DRIVER DOWNLOADS FROM ZOTAC'S website. Once I got in, and was able to download updated drivers, I unzipped the file. My VIRUS PROTECTION WENT NUTS over THREE TROJANS THAT RODE ALONG WITH THE ZIP FILE. I've included a screen shot of this for the review. Worst of all, the download could not be done on the ZOTAC unit because the install wasn't complete. I downloaded on another Windows 7 PC and after my virus software got rid of the infection in the zip file, I had to run a full scan of that PC using the virus app, as well as two others to make sure that PC was clean. Who needs this kind of nonsense from a seller/manufacturer's web site.

GOOD STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX Bi323-U
--It's a decent piece of gear... at least for now. I'll be back if it fouls up later on. The memory and hard drive installation couldn't be easier.
--Once you install an OS, it boots into the software very quickly.
--Windows 7, 8.x and so on install well.
--Debian 8.4.x installs on this unit as well. It takes some tinkering and it finally installs.
--I installed Win 7 Pro, and then removed it and installed Debian. Just wanted to see how easy it is to do that. Notes about Debian are at the end.
--For a very low end item, this isn't a bad choice so long as you're willing to set aside a few hours to set it up and are willing to put up with a poorly designed manufacturer/seller website, and poor customer service.
--For my purposes it was an okay choice. I had a few extra SSDs around as well as memory that were compatible with this unit, so this was a cheap solution to add an extra computer.

NOT SO GREAT STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX-Bi323-U
--BE SURE TO SCAN EVERYTHING FROM THE ZOTAC SITE AND THE CD/DVD THAT COMES WITH THE UNIT
--The documentation is really thin, almost useless.
--At first boot, the BIOS screen appears and you may (likely will) have to change some settings. It's best if you're familiar with what the settings do and what they effect. TIP: the Legacy Boot seems the most reliable. Complete the settings, save and exit.
--The BIOS (after adjusting settings) looks for an OS on the hard drive or CD/DVD. It does not look at USB thumb drives or SD cards. Have the external CD/DVD attached with install disc inserted.
--How to get back to the BIOS or BOOT SEQUENCE settings DOES NOT appear on any boot screens after the first power on, as it does with most other systems. How to access the BIOS settings IS NOT included in the docs. You have to press F8 for the bios or Delete for boot sequence settings. Found it on the web.
--Zotac site uses a squeeze page to get your info before you can access anything useful.
--The combination SD reader/USB port is just weird. You cannot use this port for both at once.

About Linux (Debian 8.4.x)
--I installed this successfully after several attempts. Zotac's site shows Linux drivers, but they download only the Win 7 drivers. You don't really need them for a Linux install. Set the bios for Legacy Boot or it won't boot into Linux after an install. ISO DVD 1 is the only file you need for the install. Graphical install is the only option that worked out.
--DO NOT TRY AND CONNECT WITH DEBIAN MIRRORS FOR NEWER APPS, it fails on all. Later use terminal to upgrade.
--After a successful install, the Zotac restarts and you end up at the Debian login screen for you user id and password. The password is rejected. --Power off with the power button. Power back on and this time you can login with the credentials supplied at install.
AFTER LOGGING IN, your user ID won't be in SUDOERS. Use terminal, SU into root. After that, use apt-get update followed by apt-get upgrade.

Most of the places I have lived have been reasonably safe, so I have never felt any pressing need to add a camera security system to my home. I already have an alarm system, which is useful, but no camera system. I decided that it would be good to be able to see people at the main entrances to my home/property and this convinced me to add the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System to my house.

Setting this security system up is simple enough. You have to mount the included 2 cameras and it doesn’t take much time to complete this step. I placed one of them by my front door and the other one just outside my garage, facing the driveway. The gated entrance to my backyard is right there, and I usually leave my car in the driveway and not the garage, so this seemed like a good place.

There are many things to like about this security camera system, like the wide angle of view that is good for seeing from my backyard gate to the end of my driveway. You can even speak back and forth with someone at your front door and this can prove useful when you want to avoid talking directly, face to face, with solicitors.

With the image quality, although it isn’t as sharp as I expected, it seems sufficient to me. I haven’t experienced any intruders thus far- knock on wood- so I haven’t necessarily needed to get crystal clear details. One limitation I have is that I haven’t owned a camera security system before. This is a first for me, so I don’t have any point of comparison. Still, the picture quality seems good. And I like the notification system. Any motion detection is set up to record, so you can see what is going on and you know quickly.

The app itself is user- friendly enough but one thing to keep in mind is that the Arlo Smart Servive and cloud recording are free for only the first year. After that, you have to pay for a subscription. I will wait to see if the system is worth my while, then decide whether to subscribe. A year of free usage time should be sufficient to make the call.

Security is important and the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System is a good way to keep safe. Two cameras are definitely better than one because I am able to secure the two areas of my property where an unwanted individual is most likely to show up. I find the app and picture quality good and the system as a whole has enough positive points to recommend.

For the relatively little money paid - this is an OK receiver. My previous Sony of the similar basic level has been playing nicely the last 7 years, until it died, so I thought I'll follow-up with the brand. Issue may be subjective, nevertheless... the issue is a quite flat sound, in particular the bass. The non-audiophile (i.e. reasonably priced) receivers used to have a "contour", or "bass boost" function (even the previous Sony model had it), which greatly enhanced the audibility of lower frequencies when played at low decibels. This one lacks it (and it sounds like most of nowadays sold receivers are like this), hence the sound coming out is quite flat (also for treble band), unless you go really loud. In addition, the receiver lacks a sub-woofer output, so there is no chance to improve low frequencies.
Out of the other available receivers, I decided to pick (by recommendation) a little more up-scale (yet still reasonably priced) Harman Kardon HK 3390 (2 x 80W) Stereo Receiver, which has sub-woofer outputs - even though it also lacks bass boost, I am expecting it will revive the bass, even with my old Sony 10" sub.
