This BOSE SOUNDLINK COLOR BLUETOOTH SPEAKER may not be the ideal portable speaker for serious audiophiles--because it has no treble/base buttons, only volume buttons--but I love mine. The volume is controlled by the device the speaker is connected to, or by the plus/minus volume buttons on the speaker itself. The speaker also has an Aux button for the direct cable connection, and a Skip button that lets you go forward or backward in your music selections.

This Bose portable speaker can support two Bluetooth-connected devices at once, so you can switch between two devices (e.g., an iPad and a Kindle Fire) without repeating the pairing process every time. The speaker's voice prompts help you with pairing, and tell you which two devices are currently paired. The voice prompts can be disabled, if you wish.

This Bose speaker is definitely an improvement over the speakers built into my old Sony Bravia TV. Voices are much clearer--including the dialogue from British TV shows--and the sound is far richer. Of course, using this speaker instead of a TV sound bar is only a temporary solution, because the speaker needs regular recharging. When fully charged, it delivers sound for many hours (up to 8) and outlasts the charge on the [[ASIN:B004B8GF7Y TaoTronics® Bluetooth Transmitter]] that I added to my non-Bluetooth-enabled TV.

Whether the TaoTronics transmitter was connected to the TV's headphone jack or to the TV's AV ouputs, this speaker paired instantly. However, when the TV transmitter was connected to the AV outputs, the speaker produced some static unless it was positioned close to the TV. [[VIDEOID:6e49ad5f11d43ea1130e7014d1f00ce9]] I've always been interested in video projectors because I really wanted that theater experience at home. Previously, they have been out of reach because of the price of the devices as well as the price of the bulbs that required replacement.

In the last few years, LED projectors have really come down in price. When it became attainable for me, I started to try out various models and in the last two years, the prices have dropped to the $100-$200 range, even for native 1080p projectors.

As I've said, I have tried out various models and had problems with most of them, problems ranging from not being bright enough, 720p native, unable to fully focus the corners, or even that it needed to be very far from the screen to project a big picture.

The Vimgo Smart Projector is a stylish little projector that has a nice, vertical design that takes up less space than a normal projector. It has a good-sized speaker behind the cloth-covered side panels. The sound isn't high fidelity, but it can get pretty loud. Many other projectors barely comes with a 10w speaker or worse.

It is rated at 300 ANSI Lumen, which isn't going to work well in direct light but quite adequate when the lights are turned down. There are no dark corners and I find the picture to be evenly lit. The keystone functionality is great. You can adjust the "tilt" up and down as well as left and right. You can also zoom the picture out and if all else fails, each corner can be adjusted individually.

I really like that there is a motor that performs the focusing. With manual focus, I often get up and focus the projector, just to get back to my seat and figure out that the focus wasn't that great. With the focus controllable from the remote, I can sit close enough to really see if I got it just right.

The Android system works well for plex and jellyfin, which I have installed. Unfortunately, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video has DRM that prevents them from running on this projector, but that is easily remedied by projecting from your phone or with a FireTV connected to the HDMI (the USB port outputs enough amps to power the FireTV).

Here's a tip: Install the Android TV Launcher by downloading the APK file to a USB drive, then choose the USB app from the projector to install it. It is not only a better-looking launcher, it will also give you access to the full Android system settings. I wouldn't suggest setting it as the default launcher, though because I haven't found a way to launch the built-in launcher manually.

I also found that the Vimgo projector actually has a shorter throw distance than my previous projectors. I'm able to get a larger picture when set up at the same distance as my previous projectors. I actually had to zoom out to make the picture a little smaller to fit my projection screen.

So to conclude, the Vimgo projector does not have any of the problems that I found in my previous projectors. It is stylish and compact with a great picture and good-enough audio (for small gatherings, not for a home theater experience).

This Honeywell smart home security starter kit has a great video and is easily expandable.

When opening the box I was pleased to see that it was packaged very well. The box even has a magnetic closure. Maybe a little over the top but a nice feature to make it feel like more of a luxury product. I also have the Honeywell thermostat and that box wasn’t as nice.
Each item in the security kit was simple and clear to find since they were labeled in their own little box. There is an instruction sheet that is quite large for the info that it holds. The base station could be a little smaller but it looks very nice in my kitchen and blends in very well. It’s a nice design with only one button, for the speaker. You can touch the top to check how it is working and run your finger around the top to change the volume. The camera is small and has a privacy ring that can be twisted to block the camera. It would be a nice feature if I could twist the camera from the app in case we forgot to open it when we left.
The middle mesh part is the speaker and it has a good range of volume and the sound is good.
The bottom has a light inside and it changes colors when you choose the different settings. It also lights up to help when you set up new devices.
The base has a backup battery. You will get an alert when it doesn’t have power. This has been handy when there is a storm so I know when the power goes out and when it is restored.

To start the set up I downloaded the Honeywell app. It was easy to use and is a nice looking app. The main page is very simple. When you go to the settings that’s where all the extras are.
My husband also has the app on his phone so he can use it just as I can.
Set up was very easy besides having troubles with it connecting it to my WiFi. I decided to wait till the next day and it worked after a couple tries. I don’t have a fast internet so that might be why. I haven’t had any issues with the connection since set up. Besides the WiFi wait it was about 15 minutes to set up the app and base.
The key fob was very easy to pair up and only took me a couple minutes to have it ready to use. Nice to have when a babysitter comes over.
The access sensors were very easy to install and set up. I didn’t need the extra piece. It only took me a few minutes to stick them on and pair them. I did use painters tape to attach them to my doors and frames. I am worried about the tape they have ruining my stained trim. I haven’t seen any comments about it. I also wanted to try it on other doors and windows first.
When you open a door or window in home mode it chimes and sends you an alert. When you open in away mode it will sound the alarm. I wish the door sensors were a little smaller or gray. They stand out too much on my wood trim and door. If my trim was white they wouldn’t be very noticeable.

The camera is very clear and has a wide angle so if you position it right you can see a lot. You can switch the video to full screen and the picture is still good. You are also able to zoom in on the video in the app and it has options to take a snap of the video, talk through the base or have an alarm go off. Sometimes it takes a while for the video to load or it will just turn off. I am assuming this is from my slower internet. Usually after a few tries I can get it to work. Also there is a delay in the video and the movement is jumpy, this could be due to the slower internet also. You still get a good picture of who is there. I was impressed with the night vision.

The motion detection is a nice feature when you are away. I have been trying to figure out the best setting while we are at home. It will send me alerts all the time when we are home. Most of the alerts are during the people detection time. Maybe because our camera covers so much of our main area. I do like that how the people detection can let me know who is in the house and I don’t have to look at the video. When it detects motion it will take a short video clip and save them below the live video. You can scroll down to look at the older ones. It looks like the clips are saved for a day. The people detection is limited to 2 hours. But I did notice that you could set it for the morning then when that time was over you could change it for later in the day. You would have to remember to change it but good to know if you wanted it on for longer or multiple times in the day. Not sure why they don’t have an option for more time.

The geofencing didn’t work well for me. It would switch to away mode even when the phone was close to it. We’ve decided to turn that feature off. It’s easy enough to turn it to away with the app, key fob, or talk to it. We are at home a lot so it makes more sense to do it manually. But I could see it being a great feature for people gone more during the day.

The kids like the Alexa feature that it comes with. They can ask the weather, time, kids jokes. I use it for the timer and to ask it questions. We had problems with playing songs. It wanted us to subscribe to amazon music. We have found other ways of playing music but it’s not very easy. Alexa seems limited but still useful. This is my first Alexa enable device so hard to compare.

I like that the security base links to my Honeywell thermostat (it was very easy to pair it) and I can tell Alexa to turn it off or change the temperature or use the same app. I would like to get other devices that link to it. This is a great starter kit and I like that it is expandable for your needs.

You are able to do two way taking with the app. It’s not always easy to understand and you have to talk slower.

The box says you get free 24-hour cloud storage. I’m not sure if that’s for the video clips or what you are actually storing. I haven’t found where the cloud is accessed.

Overall it is easy to use and looks nice. It’s nice that you can have a security system that is easy to use and it doesn’t have a monthly fee. I don’t usually need all the security features that this security system offers but it’s nice to have it set up and ready for when I do.

There's a lot to like about this monitor, but also some clear drawbacks. Let's start with the good news.

In typical HP fashion it comes very well packaged to survive pretty much any measure of rough handling in transit. There's a "quick start" guide that is taped to the front of the monitor that walks you through the setup (which is very straightforward). There's also an excellent user guide in PDF on the included disk.

The overall design is very attractive. It's very slim, lightweight and easy to position. I'm using it with the included table stand since my wall-mount options can't handle a monitor this large (it does come with a metal plate with VESA-compatible holes should you want to use it with a mount).

I used this on both a PC and as a video monitor hooked up through my AV receiver. For both situations I used the HDMI interface.

The sound quality is very good compared with the typical built-in speaker. It lacks bass "punch" but is quite acceptable.

Now for the so-so news: picture quality. It's good, but not "wow" good. Picture quality was somewhat drab looking, lacking crispness and contrast despite spending a lot of time tweaking the video quality with the many options available. It becomes worse when viewed off center (although it does have a decent viewing angle).

It comes with a remote which could be very handy for switching inputs, tweaking the picture, adjusting the sound, etc. I say it "could be" since the remote it comes with is horrible. It's small, which is good, but all the buttons are flush mount and have black on black lettering. It is very, very hard to see which button is which even in bright light. Forget about finding the right button in dim light. Truly horrible design work.

While there are pluses, and it is hitting an attractive price point, I can't see this being worthy of anything more than a little above average (3.5 star) rating. It's a decent, but not exceptional monitor (with a total design failure of a remote). Worth considering if you are looking for a large monitor without breaking the bank, and have moderate expectations as to video quality.

This AMFILM PREMIUM SCREEN PROTECTOR FILM CLEAR is an excellent choice for protecting your Google Nexus 7's touch screen. It's easy to install, absolutely invisible once installed, and doesn't interfere with the sensitivity of the touch screen. I was able to achieve a bubble-free installation on the very first try.

The installation instructions (printed on the retail packaging envelope) are easy to understand. The film itself--the middle layer, which is sandwiched between two masking sheets that are removed at the beginning and end of the installation--is stiff enough to lay down easily. Unlike some protective film, the adhesive doesn't aggressively grab dust motes from the air while you're installing the film. You get two sheets of film (giving you two chances at a perfect installation), a microfiber cleaning cloth, and a stiff cardboard square for smoothing out bubbles.

Because Google Nexus 7 protective film needs only one cutout (for the camera), it's especially easy to install. Just be careful that you center the film with the hole over the camera, and align it parallel to the tablet's top edge so that it lays down perfectly straight. When I got a tiny overlap at a top corner, there was a bubble at the edge that wouldn't smooth out. Rather than remove the otherwise bubble-free film, I raised the corner and trimmed the film with scissors--which fixed the problem.

Yes, the UI and apps are very clearly Android. No, it isn't a mini tablet.
Players like this are an interesting market that is hard to pin the audience down for. There are music players that are cheap on the market for those that would rather have a dedicated player (ie, not their phone). However the user interface tends to be wonky and slow, and newer generation features like bluetooth 5+ and streaming are often a mixed bag, if even available.
The idea behind players like this one, is that it is based on a supported operating system (Android, in this case) so it can play almost any format you throw at it, has plenty of support for popular streaming apps and features, as well as a familiar user interface that is already so polished, it seems silly to reinvent the wheel like the super cheap older media players.
Is it a mini tablet or phone without service? Not exactly. This is not a Google certified device, it does not have the play store or any Google apps on it. Unlike some other Android based players, I couldn't even get sideloaded apk files to install (it kept throwing errors at me). It seems like this device was purposely locked down to keep it an mp3 player. That's good in some ways, my kids aren't allowed unlimited screen time and their schools don't want them bringing smartphones around, so this is a strictly music-player oriented device (especially once you remove things like the browser for them, which it allows you to do). But I also know there are more capable players out there, some of which have quad DAC audio chips. Also, what happens when an app gets updated and goes out-of-date? Sometimes streaming services make changes and updated clients are required for it to work, however you are largely stuck with the version that this came with unless they issue a firmware update or something.
This is still cheaper than the higher end mp3 players that support high end DAC and app updates, but not by much. It seems to be a sort of in-between product. If you have a use for something like this, it could be a pretty good option. But if you're expecting a handheld tablet or alternative concept to an ipod touch, it is not exactly that.

One thing we have a lot of use for in this household is Bluetooth headphones. Whether it is for work, keeping privacy in the house, using with phones, exercising, running, walking, or other uses, everyone in the house goes through headphones. I was very interesting in these especially for exercising as it is hard to find a good pair that stay in.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These earphones are meant to be used for activities that are rather intense- hence exercising, moving around, etc. These earphones come with a short USB cord for recharging and a few sizes of gel type fittings for different sizes of ear canals.

HOW ARE THESE TO USE?
They hold a charge for six to eight hours depending on how intense the listening time is and if it is consecutive or not. The controls are easy to use on the right ear wire. It does not tell you who is calling, but it does ring in the ear. Answering was easy and the call went through well with decent volume. They do stay in the ears quite well for more intense activity. Once in a while I might knock one out if I am intensely exercising, but most of the time they have been good.

SOUND?
The sound is good, but tends a little toward the flat side compared to other earbuds I have used. We have found that breaking them in by using a lot has helped them to sound better than they did at first, so they are really not bad.

COMFORT?
That is where the stars come off. Yes, they stay in the ears, but after wearing about an hour or so, they really begin to hurt. It is not the size of the cushions, but the hard plastic under them that presses against the ears. Two of us have tried them out and it does it for both of us.

WHAT ARE THESE BEST FOR?
These seem to be the best for exercising, running, walking, or an activity that is limited to an hour or so. They are good as far as sweat and water resistance goes. Recharging time is pretty good it can take from one to two hours to fully charge, depending on the day.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For really cool looking earbuds that stay in the ears during more intense activity, these are a good choice. Any time over an hour, however can be uncomfortable. Music playback is good, but not overly dimensional if that is something you are concerned with. We like them for exercising, walking, or running.

MY RATING
Four stars for these, due to lack of dimension in sound and discomfort after wearing a while.

My mom ordered 2 of these thinking she'd be able to play music out of both of them at the same time from her iPhone. They come in the mail and we cannot figure out how to do this at all, and the instructions that came with them were unclear, as well as what we found online.
After a few hours of trial and error, this is what we figured out:
Pair both of the speakers to the iPhone
Make sure *one* of the speakers in connected (the other may not show anymore/doesn't have to be connected)
On the *connected* speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (a sound will play)
On the other speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (the same sound will play with some additional beeps)

Play music and they should work! This worked best for us when only one iPhone was connected/paired with the speakers at a time.

Hope this helps someone else!

I got my Kindle Fire HD for Christmas and ordered this case because I wanted a keyboard and the price seemed right. There are some annoyances that I listed under Cons, but to me they're not dealbreakers. I am happy with this case and really like having a keyboard with the Kindle.

Pros:
The case securely holds the Kindle. I definitely feel better about letting my kids play games on the Kindle while it's in this case than when it's not protected.

I like the look of the case overall. The stitching is sturdy and the leather is nice. It's like a little dayplanner when it's folded up. (I kinda wish it came in a solid color though. All black or all white or all red would look better to me than highlighting the closure in a second color, but that's just my personal opinion.)

I love how light the keyboard is and how it can "clip" on and off magnetically.

It was super easy to set up even though the directions were written like they were translated into English from a foreign language.

I thought the little red flap at the base would get in the way of typing but it really doesn't. It can fold underneath or just be held down with my wrists without any discomfort.

Cons:
I am not sure how to tell when the keyboard needs to be charged other than to plug it in whenever I remember. A red light appears while it's charging then goes away, so I assume it's ready at that point. I haven't used it enough for it to wear out completely, but I wish there was a way to tell how much charge it has left since I use the keyboard here and there and don't want to charge it all the time, especially if it doesn't need it. (But I also don't want it running out on me.)

The keyboard is small and I haven't gotten used to it yet. One example is that the apostraphe is made by hitting Fn+L, and I keep forgetting that then hitting all kinds of wrong buttons trying to backspace and fix it. This is frustrating because I can type 108 wpm on a standard sized QWERTY keyboard without many mistakes. I think this will just take some getting used to due to its small buttons/size. The keyboard is in great shape though, and I haven't had any sticking or falling off keys like some other reviewers have mentioned.

The Kindle seems to take a while to recognize the keyboard each time. It gets a little annoying when I just wanted to type something quickly and be done. (I am still unclear if I am supposed to go into my Wireless/Bluetooth settings each time I turn on the keyboard or if it will in fact recognize the keyboard eventually if I just wait. I usually lose patience and open up the settings.)

In order to charge the Kindle, I have to either take it out all the way or lay the case flat and open the bottom velcro flap. So it can't really be used with the keyboard while it's charging.

The case doesn't really work vertically. If you fold it in half, the keyboard gets in the way and needs to be removed. And it doesn't stand up vertically on its own.

This review is for the Uniden BCD436HP I see reviews here for other radios, so not to be confused.
I used Amazon Prime Now to get the radio to me, in less than 1 hour (about 45 minutes) the delivery person was knocking on my door with my new receiver, wow, I was highly impressed and I will always check to see if Prime Now is available for all my deliveries from now on.....
So, the radio....
This receiver has a 4 gig SD card preloaded with every known frequency with text for the entire US and Canada. They have software called Sentinel you install on your PC and this is your gateway to all updates and firmware and it can control your radios SD card any way you like. Sentinel has an extensive database of all frequencies and let me say this again, all frequencies have text description included which is the most highly advanced scanner database system I have ever seen and I have owned scanner receivers most of my adult life, (long time)..
This is a digital receiver using the latest technology available. It can monitor any analog or digital TX (with some exceptions, like encrypted signals) and gives you extensive control over what you're listening to. There are FCC laws regarding what is legal and not legal to monitor and Uniden has got us right up to the maximum legally allowed to be monitored by civilians. If you are law enforcement persons you will have much more powerful receivers available to you capable of Cell phone conversation monitoring etc., things no civilian should even be interested in.
There is another version of this Uniden radio, the BCD536 which is a tabletop version. If you have large powerful outdoor weatherproof antennas the BCD536 is a good option and it is completely transferable to vehicle dash mount and back from your work desk to your vehicle.
I like this handheld BCD436 best personally for my purposes.
This is basically a plug and play receiver. It comes with 3 2300 milliamp rechargeable batteries, load those, charge them or just leave radio plugged in, enter your zip and you're in. Well theoretically that's how it works, in the real world? No.
When you first receive the radio I would suggest positioning yourself in front of your PC. Have the paper manual, the radio, you and your PC right there in front of you. Get ready to read and learn your radios keyboard layout and what these great, well thought out keys can do for you. You will learn, trust me, you will quickly come to love this radio.
Some cons:
No wall charger adopter included. You can charge from your PC's USB ports but you will need a wall charger with USB port. Most of us have several of these around the house from old cell phones etc. They work fine.
This unit should come with a nice wall charger adopter. That's really the only con, not to bad really.
Antennas:
Your ability to scan and receive signals on any scanner is proportionate to your antennas. The more robust and correct (correct meaning size, materials used etc).. You will need some nice antennas for this nice radio to increase your scanning powers. Amazon has some nice antennas, scannermaster.com has some also. Your local radio shop retailer will have some also. The included rubber ducky antenna is garbage, toss it from across the room to your garbage can, see if you can make a rim shot. Like I said, I have been playing with scanners for many years so I have many antennas to pick from.
Verdict:
This is without a doubt, the most powerful handheld scanning receiver available from any manufacturer. It is the luxury sedan of the scanning receiver world. It is easy and robust. It is backed up by Uniden's Sentinel software which will future proof your radio for many years to come.
I give Uniden 5 stars for this winner.
I give Amazon 5 stars for Prime Now 1 hour shipping, also a winner.

The Condor all band antenna is unsurpassed.

The device works as both a USB charger (1 USB-C port, 1 USB-A port, and retractable USB-C charging cable) and as a power strip (3 AC sockets) with surge protection. 65W max power output (when using only the USB-C output cable) is plenty to charge my laptop (which has USB-C charging). The charger is smart enough to allocate its power output among the different USB ports, depending on which ports you are using (I really like this feature). The included documentation is kind of sketchy about how effective the surge protection really is, so if you live or travel in an area with regular surge problems, this may not be the best device for you.

The charger supports all the latest fast charging protocols, including QC4, PD3, and PPS. Samsung smartphones use PPS for their "Super Fast" charging mode. Apple and Google smartphones use the PD fast charging mode. In my testing, it charges up my gadgets as fast as any other charger that I have tried and it is smart enough to reduce the charging speed as the devices become fully charged to reduce overheating (this is part of the PPS protocol, if your devices support that).

I really like that this charger has an ETL electrical safety certification printed on the bottom of the device. ETL is an independent safety testing laboratory. Many US companies will not buy electrical devices that do not have ETL or UL safety certifications.

If you are using all of the features, I think $80 is a reasonable price for what you get. I have a few other Baseus products and I am impressed with the features and build quality of all of them and prices are generally cheaper from other popular brands like Anker, Belkin, and Satechi.

The build quality as well as the fit and finish of this amplifier board is better than most of the cheap TPA3116 bluetooth boards on eBay and AliExpress. When connected to decent speakers and a 24V switching power supply with sufficient current drive capability, the performance of this amplifier is quite impressive for its size.

Four potentiometers in the front, from left to right are: bass level, treble level, treble volume (volume for the two stereo channels) and overall volume. These pots, as well as the speaker outputs in the back are clearly labeled on the PCB. Tone and volume control circuit appears to use a couple of 072 opamps and an SGM358 opamp. These are not high-grade audio components, simply a low cost solution for a product in this price range. Except for the electrolytic capacitors, most components are SMD.

I tested this amp by connecting it to a pair of Sound Appeal 6.5" 2-way bookshelf speakers for the stereo channels. I did not have access to a passive subwoofer at the time, so I connected the subwoofer output to a 15" bass guitar amplifier speaker cabinet. I used a 24V 5A switching power supply. A 24V 5A power supply may not be sufficient if you are driving 4-ohm speakers and a 4-ohm or lower impedance subwoofer, but all three of the speakers I used were 8 ohms, so 120W of power input was sufficient. With the right speaker setup, the volume output of this set-up can get quite high, even in a big room. Partly due to the efficiency of the 15" bass speaker I was using, it was possible to achieve a quite impressive "thump". Distortion levels are not low at high volume levels, but having the subwoofer output on a separate TPA3116 chip makes it possible to keep somewhat reasonable distortion on stereo channels even when playing bass-heavy music.

Connecting to the bluetooth interface was easy and straight-forward. The amp remembers the previous bluetooth pairing after being powered down.

A few observations about the shortcomings of this amplifier:
- The heat sinks are quite small, and they don't have any mechanical support. Even when driving 8-ohm loads, the heat sinks get really warm at high volume levels. If you are driving 4-ohm speakers at high volume levels, thermal shut-down is possible. If you are using a 18V or lower power supply, you probably won't have any thermal issues.
- There is only a 1000uF 25V filter capacitor at the power input. 25V max rating is a bit too close for my comfort, I would have preferred a 35V capacitor. You really need a well regulated DC power supply to drive this board.
- Bluetooth has a built in antenna on the PCB, but no external antenna interface, making it impossible to mount this board inside a metal case without doing some surgery to the board.
- There are no line level inputs. Bluetooth is the only input option unless you are willing to do modifications on the PCB

Overall, for the current price of $26.99, this is a very nice bluetooth 2.1 amplifier. If you have a couple of decent bookshelf speakers and an old subwoofer lying around, the volume and quality of the sound you can achieve with this amp will be better than any integrated bluetooth system that sells for less than $100.

Update: I recently tested this amp with [[ASIN:B00NOA58RS Dayton Audio B652-AIR 6-1/2" Bookshelf Speaker Pair with AMT Tweeter]]. These speakers are 6-ohms, so it's possible to get a little power out of the amplifier, and especially the high frequencies sound noticeably better.

I received these as a free review sample eight months ago. Since there are a lot of detailed reviews I will focus on my experience with these and also compare them to other sports phones.

First, these are good quality for twenty buck phones. But do be aware that sports phones are designed for comfort more than sound quality. Not that these are marginal - they have a typical bias towards the mid range, with compressed highs and adequate bass. They are not going to win acclaim from audiophiles, but do reproduce music that is clear and perfect for background listening.

Another thing I like is comfort. I can wear these for a few hours at a time without even noticing them. For sports phones that is a major plus. These allow in a little ambient noise for safety, but it does not appreciably affect the quality of music. Volume is somewhat limited. If you like music super loud these are not going to make you happy. On the other hand, high volume defeats the purpose of sports phones since you need to be aware of ambient noise and your surroundings. I cannot emphasize strongly enough that these are NOT general purpose phones.

Finally, the specs claim about four hours of music play time. That is true with the volume at about a third. If you crank the volume to max you can cut that time in half.
Just what I expected from Anker, another fine product.

I have run extensive tests on this camera over the last several months and I must say I’m very impressed with the performance.

Personally I have been working with security camera products for over 15 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from large systems to single camera nursery monitors. I work with a group of security professionals and we regularly consult on large corporate projects and write about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well - I understand what to look for in quality cameras and the places manufacturers tend to try to save money on which makes an inferior product.

Over the years the security camera technology has vastly improved becoming less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install residential security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings.

This is advice any professional security analyst will provide and what we tell everyone of our clients. If you are new to home security camera systems, we recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with PoE cameras run off of quality PoE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

While this camera is not natively a PoE camera I’m happy to share the 5 Pairs Passive PoE Injector and PoE Splitter Kit with 5.5x2.1 mm DC Connector RJ45 Power Over Ethernet by Exgoofit ( https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07F82YK6P/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 ) allow for this camera to operate almost identical to a PoE camera. The power adapter must be plugged in where the Ethernet cable is plugged in with the first pigtail adapter while the second adapter plugs onto the cameras power port and Ethernet jack. By utilizing this you can avoid the security concerns associated with WiFi cameras and still only have minimal wires run to the camera.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. This camera is 2MP which is ideal for the vast majority of installation situations.

Highlights of this camera include:

Awesome Pan Tilt Zoom - Utilizing a 110° wide-angle varifocal lens and the head rotating 355° horizontally and 90° vertically, a 360° view is easily obtained. This makes this camera an outstanding choice to be placed on a corner of an eave where it can constantly monitor the largest possible area.

3.6mm Board lens - in my tests over the last couple of months I have been fairly impressed with the performance of this Fixed Focus 6mm lens coupled with the 1/2.8" Sony IMX307 CMOS with ICR image sensor. While this will not allow for near as clear zooming as a varifocal lens it is adequate in most circumstances.

Low Light Capability - this lens is decent in low light. Images are ok at low light, far better than the vast majority of similar cameras in this price range. IR lighting is dependable and nighttime / low light images are better than expected. My tests showed accurate images within 75’ of the IR lighting. By using both 4 IR lights and 4 bright LED lights this allows the camera to capture more details than many of the others on the market.

ONVIF Compatibility - critical for using with software such as Blue Iris. I have set it up with advanced features such as Patrol and Watchdog utilizing multiple detection zones.

2 Way Audio - I have had no issues utilizing the 2 way audio through Blue Iris - sound is accurate, clear and minimal lag.

Video Compression - This camera utilizes Smart 265/Smart 264/M-JPEG compression allowing for the smallest file sizes while maintaining the highest quality.

Great build quality - this camera is well built and will hold up outside in all conditions. That being said this is not a small camera in any way.

Over the course of my testing this product for the last several months I’ve been thoroughly impressed. It loads into Blue Iris without any issue and advanced features work without any trouble. By using the PoE splitter kit (referenced above) you can easily make this a secure camera by avoiding the use of WiFi. Build quality is excellent - this is made to last and hold up even in severe conditions.

This is a product I would definitely recommend. While this is the first ENSTER camera I have reviewed I look forward to seeing other cameras they create. All indications point to this being a manufacturer that builds high quality security cameras that are dependable and made to last.

I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. It's comfortable in the hand -- I have a large hand, some in the family have larger hands, some have smaller hands, but everyone finds the mouse comfortable to use. It's precise, easy to configure, and I'm very fond of the tiny usb adapter.

I particularly like the fact that you only need use one usb adapter for multiple devices (the "unifying receiver"). In fact you can switch between different Logitech mice if you need to do so (e.g., for a portable).

As for the keyboard, I was a little wary of the "wave" shape, not having used one before, and having some mild carpal tunnel issues. But to my relief, the keyboard is really comfortable to use, the wrist rest is well placed, provides support just where I need it. The keys have a nice touch, not too light, not too heavy, so perfect for me. There are a number of programmable buttons on the keyboard, most of which I tend to use only occasionally, mostly because I forget I have them. But the volume control is very useful, as is the button to bring up the calculator.

Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. If you just want one or the other, I still recommend the M510 mouse, and one of the many Logitech wireless keyboards that you can buy separately. (For instance, I also have the K270 keyboard, and find it to be quite good.)

Disclaimer - I've only had these for about a week so far and these are the very first Truly Wireless Earbuds that I have ever owned.

I purchased these earbuds on a great sale while waiting for another more expensive brand to get restocked, and honestly didn't expect to much from these. First impressions were that they were quite cheap however after using them for a little while now, I've come to appreciate them even more. Even though these are my very first Truly Wireless Earbuds, I feel that after tons of research and watching reviews, I know what to look for in sound and quality. There are so many budget wireless earbuds on the market right now with so many more on Indigogo (which from comments and reviews I've seen and read, I will NEVER buy from). This makes it quite hard to know what to buy. For me, I have been waiting for that perfect very small and discreet Truly Wireless Earbud with amazing sound. The Iyesku YK-T02 TWS Sport Earbuds didn't hit that mark for me but at the price I paid, I honestly can't complain.
Pros:
1. Bluetooth 5.0 - This was one of my main requirements when searching and the YK-T02 has it.
2. Easy to pair (I am using the Samsung Note 8) and pairing was very easy. Once the buds are initially paired, they connect super fast once you pull them out of the charging case.
3. No loss of connectivity to either earbud. I've seen a bunch of reviews where this is an issue with MANY other wireless earbuds on the market. Even some of the more spendy ones.
4. Fit is very comfortable and seem to be very secure though I have not put them through the test of running nor exercise. However I don't think this would be an issue at all.
5. Sound quality is decent. More about this in the Cons.
6. Tons of ear tip options. Most earbuds come with a few extra sizes but these come with a plethora, for that perfect custom fit.
7. Quite small and discreet.
8. Small pocketable charging case.

Cons:
1. Sound. As I stated in the Pros these sound "good" (for the money) but the Highs are quite loud (Mids and Bass are not) and almost hurt when the volume is turned all the way up. Mids are not to bad but the bass is nearly non existent which was a huge let down. HOWEVER let me say, once I played with the ear tips and found the right fit, Highs, Mids, and Bass are much better, but still not what I would have hoped for but again these aren't "High end" earbuds right?
2. Because the volume of these buds are quite low, Audio books are hard to hear when in a loud environment.
3. No satisfying magnet to hold the buds in the charging case like many others on the market. (The case does click shut to ensure the buds wont be falling out.)
4. Speaking of the case, my first impression was that the case felt very nice and lightweight, but it does feel cheap.

Final thoughts:
Like I said earlier in this review, if you can get these from Amazon on a lightning deal or with a coupon, I would say grab you a pair, but just don't expect these to compete with higher end buds. These would be great for the kids and anyone that just wants a good pair of Truly Wireless Earbuds that wont break the bank.

I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this.

These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more.

These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire.

In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these.

Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable.

The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones.

These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

Reviewed by my husband, a photography enthusiast.

Over the last 20 years, my husband has purchased several LowePro camera bags/backpacks (i.e., Mini Trekker & Micro-Trekker 100). He has found that they have been some of the best he has ever owned. He prefers backpacks because they are easy to carry and keep up with, especially if you are on the go. Backpacks also allow for easy storage and are super convenient. They give you freedom of movement and your hands are free to capture those special moments that you may not otherwise get if you were holding a bag in your hand. The Viewpoint (LowePro) BP 250 is the perfect addition to his bag collection especially since it is specially designed for small video equipment.

Here’s what he liked:

• This bag is attractive. The design is smart, functional and full of surprises. The Viewpoint BP250 is well-made with plenty of room for your Go Pro and accompanying equipment. There is a ton of storage (inside and out). There are several compartments where you can store your accessories, cords, lenses and other equipment. On the outside of the main bag, there is a zipper pocket (which allows for small items like a memory stick/card or thumbdrive). There is a pocket on the other side of the bag which will fit a small tripod or other item (like an umbrella). The entire bag can be zippered so you won’t lose any of your accessories.

• It is ideal for those who use (small) video and other digital equipment. There is a space dedicated to a small computer. While this backpack will not allow you to carry one of the larger sized laptops (our 17” didn’t fit), it has adequate space for the smaller ones (about 15”), a SurfacePro, iPad or other small notebook or tablet. He finds that the option of carrying a computer is great because it will allow you to quickly upload and edit your videos wherever you are. There is no reason to wait….just review, edit (if needed), and upload!

• The straps are unlike the traditional ones that come straight down the shoulders. The BP250 LowePro’s straps are curved which he found to be less stress on his shoulders. After some adjustments (he’s 6’1, average sized with average shoulders), it was a good fit. The straps are slightly padded and comfortable. There are small snaps that lock the straps in place to ensure that they don’t fall down when walking or hiking.

• There is a small (lunch box sized bag) that can be removed and can hold your GoPro camera and equipment. Once closed, it fits directly into your main LowePro Bag. It is padded and once inside, will protect your camera and smaller lenses. Or if you want, this smaller bag can be used instead of taking the large one.

• This bag comes with a rain cover. Not sure how much you will use this feature, but if you are ever caught in a drizzle or rain storm, there is a plastic cover that can be removed (unzipped) from the bottom and cover your bag. This is perfect for keeping your bag and equipment dry.

• The price. While this bag may seem a little pricey (about $130) it’s worth it. The craftsmanship and functionality will prove invaluable for the amateur or professional photographer. It’s a small investment with some heavy returns. You’ve got protection and functionality.

Overall, my husband gives this bag 5 stars. He finds that it is not only good to use for a GoPro, but other small video and photography equipment. Backpacks are useful for photographers because they allow your hands to be free to capture those moments or events as they unfold. In the past he has purchased Lowepro equipment and found them to be sturdy and durable, and the Viewpoint BP250 is not different. It looks good and he won’t leave home without it.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential. Unfortunately while the hardware has improved dramatically the software often has not - which is the case with this set.

The set I got did not come with a hard drive which wasn’t a big deal as I always have a few around. A suitable SATA Hard Drive can be purchased for $25-$400 depending on size and quality.

In terms of this system it should be clear based on the price - this is a budget system. That doesn’t mean it won’t work but these cameras are not going to pan, tilt or zoom (the lens is fixed).

If these are installed with this in mind they can still be very effective they just need to be positioned correctly.

For instance if these cameras were placed up high on a second floor overhang you would see an overview of the surrounding area but would not be able to zoom in to see facial characteristics. In terms of wiring any POE (Power Over Ethernet) camera is excellent. The cameras are powered and transmit data over the same Ethernet cable. NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

This is a fairly standard surge protector with 12 outlets with only two of those set apart for the larger adapters. The selling point that it attempts to sell consumers on is the usb ports, including one type-c so this review will concentrate mostly on those ports.

As far as the surge protector portion of this product, the face outward, which means that the longer style chargers that comes with some electronics will not plug in without taking up an extra socket. With only two set farther apart for power adapters, this power strip will not work well for a location with routers, modem, and NAS.

Now on to the USB ports. Five USB ports share a total of Five amps. It means that is the power strip is completely filled, it will only deliver one amp to each port. The type-c port is only useful if that is the only cable you can find because it does not support any fancy features such as quick charging or type-c pd, although it does support up to 3A so some phones may actually consider this "fast charging". Do not expect to replace a true 5-port usb charger with this power strip.

I'll admit, I'm a fan of Sony. I've owned all sorts of things from the brand, from the aftermarket stereo in my car to my professional camera equipment I use at work. They just make reliably good products. However I've mostly owned Samsung television sets just because it's what I had access to on a more regular basis.
I was therefore excited to try out this TV and see how it compared. To be honest, I really REALLY like Sony's color science. It's part of why I prefer their camera equipment, and it shows on this display. The contrast ratio and dynamic range are everything I wanted it to be and more. The skin tones as well, however the average consumer probably wouldn't notice or care about these things. Where the big differences lie in major TV brands these days is going to be features. The latest crop of Smart TVs have so many bells and whistles, you practically don't need anything other than an internet connection anymore. Unlike Samsung's UI which has embraces Amazon's Fire Stick style UI, Sony has gone the Google TV route. There are pros and cons to both approaches, although I think perhaps arguably there isn't as much free included content as Samsung (Samsung actually includes free live TV channels via "Samsung TV", which Sony does not have). But for all the content I actually WANT to see, Netflix, Prime, Disney+ etc, it works perfectly!

So why only 4 stars? This isn't the fault of Sony's TV, but I really wish they'd make it easier to spot and turn off... I really REALLY hate the default motion smoothing (aka "soap opera effect") that all the big brands use these days. As a content creator, I shoot videos in a particular frame rate on purpose. The motion blur or lack thereof helps tell the story in some kinds of scenes. But most TVs want to show off their high refresh rate and therefore use realtime smoothing algorithms to create fake overly-dramatic effects to pump out extra in between frames. The motion looks too smooth to the point it seems CGI (because it sort of is). It just looks off once you notice it, and Sony is no exception. You have to dig around and figure out what they call it on every TV just to make it look normal again, on this set it is called Motionflow and it can be confusing to turn it off. I wish manufacturers would make it a simple and easy to understand toggle switch... maybe even present it as an option to the viewer upon setting it up so they can understand what they are enabling and decide if they want it or not (I strongly recommend not!).
But again, that's true of all modern Television sets, on its own right this is a solid TV and I would recommend it.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

Personally I really like the flood light security cameras. Flood lights are a natural deterrent for criminal activity - when the light comes on it startles the person trying to sneak around and having the light almost guarantees that you will receive a clear image.

I have tested and reviewed several similar floodlight camera systems. As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

In terms of this particular floodlight WiFi camera by FREECAM it comes with a 16GB SD card but while the manufacturer claims the camera can accept up to 64GB, I’ve been unable to get mine to accept anything but the included 16GB.

The app, while certainly not the worst I’ve used, is far from the best. It is not particularly user friendly and support is non existent. I was able to achieve a reasonable reliability in terms of video capture although the alert system is not reliable.

The bulbs are bright - 1400 Lumen and while they are not replaceable being LED, they should last a long time.

Installation was as straightforward as installing any floodlight and required around 15 minutes.

In terms of WiFi flood light cameras, I’m disappointed with not being able to get anything but the included 16GB SD card to work - this tends to point to the company trying to force buyers into their cloud services. I have carefully monitored all traffic and if the camera was attempting to access the internet independently - my internet blocks will prevent this but I have not detected anything in my testing thus far.

The app is not dependable nor is it user friendly.

All around this is a product I would avoid.

Considering the price, I'm giving this little cam 4.5 stars. The half star off is for a user manual that is not as clear as it could be, and for the non-existent buttons mentioned therein.

As Sean Carter wrote elsewhere on this page,this cam is small, cheap, and "set-it-and-forget-it".

I opened the box (which contained everything in the parts listed in the product description), took the stuff out, inserted a 16GB San Disk class 10 microSD plugged the camera in, and had it working in no time. I set the resolution to 720, set the time and date, and left the other stuff pretty much at factory default.

The bracket is dead easy to mount (vac cup). I ran the power cord up into the roof liner, down the inner rubber gasket of the A-pillar, then used a couple of clips to hide it under the bottom of the instrument panel. It comes out on the driver's side center console and plugs into the power port. I used black duct tape to cover the massive, glowing red LED that is on the plug.

So, basically, once you set it up you just leave it plugged in. It comes on when the car is turned on (or the key is turned to Accsy). Note that the cam will stop recording after a few seconds of no motion - like at stop signs, traffic signals, etc. So you may want to set it so it runs all the time.

It comes off the bracket fairly easily, so you can take it indoors and connect it to a computer to view the video. I connected it to a WIndows 8 laptop and the camera came on and queried if I wanted to use it as storage or as a cam. Since I wanted to playback the video I had just shot, I selected storage.

WIndows recognized it as a removable drive. The video is AVI format, stored in DCIM sub-folders within dated folders.. I played the videos back on the PC. Didn't really look for details, so I'll have to check again for things like license plates, etc. The first couple of videos were very fuzzy. After I took the factory protective film off of the lens it shot very nice clips.

The sound is very soft.

Again, this is an inexpensive camera, but it does every thing it's supposed to do.

* * * * * tl:dr;

Pros: Cheap, Easy to install, set up, use;

Cons: Sound is very soft;

Idiot point: Don't forget to take the protective cellophane off of the lens.

I've had these earbuds for a few months now and thought I'd revise my review.

My main gripe with these expensive but ultimately underwhelming earbuds is that they make a "thwomping" sound inside your ear drum whenever you jog or walk fast with them. I was at the gym recently and the sound of the earbuds jostling about in my ears was distracting. I don't recall ever having that problem with cheaper earbuds. This sound persisted even after I customized the buds to fit the shape of my ear.

On the positive side, the sound is decent though the bass and treble weren't that impressive. Its most effective feature was the noise-cancelling feature, which effectively blocked out any other noise. It worked so well that I would never use these buds while driving, crossing traffic or walking alone home late at night. With the spate of iPhone robberies, it's better to be able to hear a stranger's footsteps behind you. It's perfect, however, when you're on a subway or a bus and you want to block out that annoying person next to you who insists on complaining about her day.

The set includes a microphone for your iphone, which I don't use that much but works well enough - I heard my friend's voice on the other end of the line in very crisp, clear tones.

What's convenient is that the buds work with even the oldest ipods around. From the classic 2009 model to the most up to date Nano. Sony was smart to do this - that means a lot of people, not just techies with the most up-to-date devices, can use this. As an example, a friend of mine still has a working iPod mini (don't laugh, he's a Luddite!) and we tested the headset on that too. Surprisingly, it worked! - though the volume controls did not work with such an old, outdated model.

Another convenience is the location of the controls, which are located on a box located on the cord, which prevents you from having to reach all the way down to your iPod or iPhone to adjust the volume. My second favorite feature is the included clip, which allows me to wind up any slack on the cord and prevent it from getting tangled easily. In the past, I've killed so many earbuds because I pulled too hard on the cord by accident, so this is a welcome feature.

This deluxe model includes a pouch that offers an array of different sized earbuds - one set is noise-cancelling, while the other isn't. This is overkill, though. I tried out different sets of buds but none of them fit just right. And the "thwoping" sound I mentioned earlier still remained.

So I have mixed feelings about this product. The "thwomping" (sucking) sound is its biggest drawback for me, as the buds work best when you don't move around a lot.

I've said it a thousand times: "I think I could really get into (real) photography, but I just can't take another hobby that requires me carrying a whole bag of equipment across the world. If I get a DSLR, I won't take it to the places that I'd like to use it the most." Well...I think they made this camera just for me. I believe this camera to be capable of "real" pro photos, just the same as if I bought a DSLR and a single lens, which many people start by doing. It also makes a startup punk like me look like a pro, much to the chagrin of the real pros.

My other cameras include a DSC-H20, which is an older Sony model with a 10x zoom lens, multiple point-and-shoots, and a waterproof/shockproof Panasonic that I really like for my basic, worry-free shots.

My main question about this camera was, why does it appear to be Sony's flagship compact camera in every way, but yet it doesn't have the 30x optical zoom lens that some of the other Sony's have (or even the 10x of my DSC-H20)? I knew there would be an answer, but to find it, I had to start digging into camera specs, something I've been meaning to do for a while.

First, pro photographers tend to think that if you're using much zoom under most circumstances, then you're just being lazy. You need to get closer. In a landscape shot, zoom tends to flatten things out. I may have never noticed this, or WHY this is. You know, you go on vacation, take a lot of pictures, come back and some look great and others look bad. Maybe it's true that every time I zoom in on a landscape, I'm really just ruining my shot.

The other thing is aperture. Aperture basically tells you how clear the background of your picture will be versus your foreground (I'm just learning this myself, so camera pros, feel free to comment with better verbiage), a lower number being better if you want a totally clear picture, and the lowness of that number being what you use to compare the quality of lenses. It's also good to have a high end on the range because that allows you to take those artsy photos with something super clean up front and a blurry background. I've also seen some neat head shots taken that way, where even some hair starts becoming blurry.

Anyway, the low aperture on this camera is 1.8 all the way zoomed out, and 2.8 all the way zoomed in (you can set it as high as 11 in either case). This is a tight range with great numbers (notice that even here, you lose a little bit by using zoom). My camera with the 10x zoom has an aperture equal to 3.5 all the way out, similar to the 30x zoom cameras Sony has now. It makes a big difference, even to my amateur eye.

This camera, and my subsequent research, has allowed me to let go of the 10/30x zoom. Yes, those cameras are great, but this is the flagship mini for a reason. Now I understand. Just taking random pictures in my neighborhood, although so boring compared to my favorite International backgrounds, I can clearly see a quality difference.

The other main spec for cameras is shutter speed. This can be set for 1/32000 of a second all the way up to 30 seconds. The quickest shutter speeds will capture an instant in time without blur, while the slower ones will capture more action with some blur. They are also good for low light scenarios to expose the shot to more light. Very slow speeds should be used with a tripod or the camera set down someplace. This camera makes a noise (not an obnoxious one) when on auto and using a slower shutter speed, to keep you still. It's very intuitive and works well.

While you will get better shots than you ever had before using this camera on auto, the dial wheel allows you to set either aperture or shutter speed as a priority and leave the rest on auto, perfect for people that want to understand what a real camera can do, and who want to set up pro shots without yet knowing everything.

The controls on this thing are awesome. I love that there is no touchscreen to fight with and that everything is so intuitive. Great praise to Sony for knowing what fads aren't worth it. (One fad they did latch onto is that 180 degree rotating screen, which really is fantastically convenient and feels quite strong and well done). While we're talking about it, they also put in the fantastic viewfinder and the pop-up flash, which all completely recess into the body of this thing (an amazing work of engineering art).

Speaking of the flash, you won't use it often. Even on a cheap camera, I try to keep the flash off, but this thing does an amazing job of using ambient light for exposure (I believe this is the third pillar of photography). I swear, I have never seen such clear pictures in very low light. Instead of being grainy, I can pick up minute details (even zoom-able), and they appear brighter than the actual place they were taken. This, I believe, is because of the 1" image sensor they are touting. I'm impressed.

The 960fps thing. With only two seconds, this may be hard to set up the shot you want, but 2 seconds seems a lot longer in 960fps. Even just shaking your leg on camera, you'll see the odd aftereffects of your socks moving like you never did before. Stupid example, but that's the point: the details you get from 960fps slow-mo are amazing.

4k video. I really didn't care about all this until some guy at a conference pointed out how 4k has been used for pro video for years. Instead of multiple cameras to cover a hockey game, for example, you could just use one and zoom in on anything you want and still have high-def video. I realized we probably will move over to actually using it at some point. Well, here's your chance to actually use that 4k TV. It's awesome. It really is.

A note on SD cards. While most devices can read SDHC cards, which went up to 32GB, the reason they want you to have a SDXC card (which can be from 64GB to 2TB in theory) is because the speed ratings are higher. You need the speed rating of 3 (>100 Mbps) to really use these big data transfer functions. I suspect the 960fps is all that can be held in RAM, and that those speeds are way too fast for even the newest and best card (hence the 2 second limit on 960fps).

Suffice to say that I love this camera. I appreciate each of its mechanical and electrical features and how they're perfectly integrated to make this small, marvelous camera. Even in the leather case (not included), it's about the same size as my H20, certainly portable enough to have it when you want it, but with enough features and technology that you're not sacrificing anything in your photography.

Enthusiast of World of Tanks BEWARE! I am not the only one out there to report serious problem with the game vs. this card (and more nVidia cards in general).
I have had World of Tanks crashes on EVGA GeForce 9800 GT and they, unfortunately, continue to happen on this very card - my newest MSI N650Ti-1GD5/OC GeForce 650Ti. They happen regardless the driver version (usually at the beginning of a battle), and they do still occur with the newest 314.07 drivers, though less frequently and at a different moment.
Worked with World of Tanks support and we went through several iterations, including clean re-installations (incl. registry cleanups) of the game/drivers in different combinations, underclocking, etc., but that did not help at all.
To be fair - the card never gave me problems with Portal 2, Order of War, Medal of Honor and a few other games needing solid 3D rendering - it appears to be issue with World of Tanks game in particular.
Not sure whose fault it is: 1) may be game developers, with whom nVidia claims to have business partnership), but, equally valid, 2) it may also be nVidia drivers that crash the program (the issue seems to be reported more often with newer nVidia drivers by multiple players).
Anyway - if you're into World of Tanks a lot - I recommend picking up some decent Radeon card - the one I have on the other PC (HD 6870) never gave me any issues with my favorite game.

EDIT as of 08 March 2013:
I added one more star and here's why:
1. The crash of World of Tanks occurs due to client (program) issue, which was admitted couple days ago by the developer's support folks (they're still working to resolve this, with me). So, as this is not the card's fault I am adding one star, especially that graphics is really stunning (especially for such a price point!).
2. Why not 5 stars? Well, I would, but then one thing stands out - if you want to keep that (factory overclocked) card stable, you need to speed up the fan a bit and that makes the card pretty noisy (louder than a fully spinning DVD drive, in my instance)! So if you do not mind it (or you have a well noise insulated computer case) then go ahead with it.
