A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. (*UPDATE: this thing just does not work well, and I am now looking for something else.)

I have had 2 Tom Tom-Go GPS units and have been reasonably happy with this brand. My first Tom Tom Go lasted less than a year at which point it lost its "mind" in the LL Bean parking lot, uttering, "Turn, turn, turn." The 2nd Tom Tom lasted 2 years when it suffered screen damage. When both units worked, they were reliable and paid for themselves many times over in gas savings.
I decided to invest in the 1350 Nuvi refurbished Garmin to try out a new brand, to be reassured of having up-dated maps and to receive a 1-year warranty on this refurbished product whereas Tom Tom provides only a 6-month warranty on its refurbished GPS. I also liked the prospect of using the GPS for walking tours of NYC, Philadelphia, Boston, etc.
My Garmin 1350 arrived quickly and in perfect condition. It could be used right out of the box.I was impressed by the sturdiness of the case and by how well the suction gripped the windshield. The unit seemed to turn on a bit more slowly than my Tom Toms but the route planning may be somewhat faster. I liked having the points of interest scroll down the screen. There appear to be many more POI choices on the Garmin than the Tom Tom. The categories are intuitive and it is helpful to quickly see both map location and contact information. Since my cell phone is paired with my car, I did not use to Blue Tooth feature to call up the store via the GPS unit, but this would be very helpful.
I don't think that the default setting gives as much screen detail; e.g., providing names for all the streets. I have found the greater visual detail of the Tom Tom helpful when driving at night, but it is probably a needless distraction most of the time. It is very helpful to have the streets spoken at turns. The volume was perhaps even better than that of the Tom Tom. This surprised me, having read numerous complaints about Garmin being inaudible. I even had to turn down the volume to 80%. The pronunciations were reliably clear with only a few oddities; e.g., the town of St. Davids was spoken as "Street Davids."
Route corrections were made more quickly than I experienced with Tom Tom and it is helpful to know which side of the street the destination is on.
In making comparisons with the Tom Tom Go, there is a feature which I miss: the IQ routing. My Tom Toms had an uncanny knowledge of different routes and respective drive times at various times of the day. Quite fequently, the return route would differ from the original Also-- and more importantly-- the drive time was extremely accurate.
In contrast Garmin seems clumsy and mechanical. Perhaps, this is because I am stil getting used to the Garmin? So far, I am extremely frustrated by Garmin's under-estimation of drive times. Even when I go 4 miles above the posted speed limits, I am seldom able to catch up with the predicted drive time.There seems to be no allowance for stopping at lights. The greater the distance, the more this discrepancy.This is surprising given the Garmin's close attention to changing speed limits.

Unboxing: Wouldn't usually make a section of this, but every once in a while a product makes it a pleasure. Especially a weird one like this. It's like unboxing a little UFO. It starts out in something like a hat box with a couple sticky tabs of tape to remove. Wish they could have found a better closure method, but the box is nice. Inside that you're immediately presented with the odd looking earbuds and a starter guide (also round) that has you immediately trying them on and fitting the best sleeve size for in your ear. There are no extra sleeves obviously apparent, so time to dig deeper. Next up is the UFO. A large earbud like this needs a large charging case. This one is round and unzips like some of the nicer headphone cases, but it's also a hard case with lights and buttons. Nothing inside but a charging dock. Under it is a secret compartment (made less secret by the thumb holes for easy removal). At the bottom of the hat box we have our missing sleeves and a charging cord.

Even with a diagram, putting these on was confusing and took four tries. Once they're on though, they are quite comfortable, and I think I'll learn to put them on after a few more tries.

Back to the book, and ugh! now they're telling me to put them in the charging case to pair. But I just finally got them on! &*^@#!

Ok, after getting things paired and back on, I'm able to put them through some testing. I'm not really an audiophile, but I've tried a lot of earbuds. Comfort is good. They don't rely on being stuck in your ear to hold themselves up, so there isn't a high stress point that's going to get sore first. They sound good. Better than most, but not the best I've heard. The control button is on the back of your ear, and I find it awkward and unreliable. Noise cancellation is solid, but like every other one I've tried, it is hard to tell sometimes because it scales with volume. Turning them on in a noisy room doesn't result in a quiet room, but turning up what you are listening to will result in noise other than what you are listening to disappearing quite a lot. There is a passthrough mode if you need to hear what's going on around you, but it doesn't sound very nice.

I like that it's USB-C. No more having to turn the cord over three times to figure out which end is up, and much faster charging. The case has three lights to show you charge progress for the case Each one represents enough charge for one full use of the earbuds. There's also a light on the top to tell you whether the earbuds are charged yet.

It's a solid product. Not my top favorite, but definitely innovative and a competitive offering.

My parents used to have a Polaroid camera and it was everything that we remember those old cameras for – it spat out a white square of plastic that slowly developed into a grainy, faded-looking picture within a few minutes, it was bulky and it had a very distinct sound. It was a great old camera but when Polaroid quit making film for it it became a paperweight. It's nice to see that some of these old cameras are available with film again. That said, there are some oversights with this package.

I will start with the two negatives (no pun intended). First, the way the camera was packaged for shipment was sub-par and the package was partially crushed when I received it. It did not appear to be damaged beyond the packaging, but it was a disappointment to open the package and find the merchandise box partially crushed. Second, the camera comes with no film or batteries at all. So, the camera by itself is still a paperweight. It would have been nice to have at least a lower capacity pack for film to get started.

The camera came out of the box without a mark on it. It looks to be brand new, in spite of being an older unit. Some of the other reviewers have complained that the camera they received either was scratched up or was partially damaged, but mine is pristine. It's a simple, straightforward device too, and it does not require much thought to use.

In use, it works just like it would have when new. It fires the flash, spits out one exposure with that same distinctive sound I remember and the film develops in front of you. The exposure still looks grainy and old when it is all done, but it is a real photograph that does not need a separate printer or software to get a hard copy. This is not the kind of camera a photographer would use, but rather it is for the tourist or enthusiast.

Why would you want a camera like this? For me, it is a trip down memory lane to a time years ago, when candid pictures were a part of daily life and the exposures were lined up on the pinboard for all to see without needing a computer or tablet. It is not going to make pictures that look like they could be in a magazine, but it will produce pictures you can enjoy right away.

I'm currently suffering from dyspnea and while the fingertip measurement is sometimes harrowing, the wrist measurement is always a comforting 96% approximately. I've asked several medical professionals why this is, and I've googled a bit on my own and the only thing I can tell you is that I simply can't tell you why the measurement can be so different at different parts of the body. My best advice, across the boards, is to make baseline measurements on all the functions, and compare them to recent or baseline measurements from other devices. I live in a family compound which is an old house divided up into several apartments. What makes these walkie talkies useful on a daily basis is the water situation in the compound. All the apartments are connected to the cold water line and a couple of the apartments share a hot water line. That means if you are taking a shower and anyone anywhere in the house turns on a cold water tap, not only will your shower lose water pressure but the cold water flow will abruptly decrease, leaving the hot water hotter than ever. For the apartments that share a hot water line, the same kind of thing happens. Suddenly you are taking a cold shower in a a trickle of water. These walkie talkies have solved that problem. With the group call button you can let the whole house know you are going to take a shower so no one will use any water till you call in that you are done.

Nor is that their only use. Several times a year our town will get a tornado alert. Should a tornado actually appear in our area, the whole family will head down to the storm shelter behind the basement apartment. With the walkie talkies we can make sure everyone got the emergency alert and knows that they need to be ready to move fast if the sirens go off.

One our family members has been sick the last couple of days and these units were in an easy way to check in on her throughout the day to see if there was anything she needed. By assigning each apartment its own channel and having everyone on the same group channel, it is easy to call one apartment or to reach them all, whichever is appropriate for a given message.

The units are easy to use and even our least techie family member quickly got the hang of it. The sound is clear even when calling from apartment to apartment. There is a flashlight function that is fairly bright, one that will come in handy in case of emergency. All in all, our whole family is well satisfied with this product and it deserves a 5 star rating.

Rather than trickling out power to devices that aren't on, the system automatically shuts down power to the energy saving outlet when the main outlet is shut off. This is great if the energy savers are peripherals and the main is a PC, but if you're doing something other than a computer setup it can be a pain to remember to only plug an "always on" device into this slot. If you shut that device off, everything in the 7 energy saving outlets will lose power. The power loss will trigger if you reboot your machine, which means that all of your peripherals will go through a full boot cycle as well.

I'd have preferred a switch to enable or disable this feature, and an outlet for charging USB devices rather than coax.

Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

This is one of the better sounding shower radios I’ve used. Although it’s pretty compact (roughly 3.5 inches square and 1.5 inch thick) the sound quality is pretty impressive given the constraints of a single rear-facing speaker. The volume can be raised to a point where it can be easily heard over the sound of running water.

The overall look is nice. The build quality appears solid, and the colors look nice (a baby blue dial, with the majority of the radio being white). It uses 2 AA batteries which are not included.

Reception was decent. It has an internal antenna, so how the radio is positioned is critical to pulling in the station you want to pull in. It can be hung from a hook or the shower head using the included loop, or it can stand up on a shelf or tub edge.

The big negative is tuning. It uses a rotary dial to set the station. It’s not very precise – it’s very easy to overshoot or undershoot the desired station. Once you tune it to the station you want it stays put, but getting there can be a challenge.

This is a decent choice if you’re looking for a low-cost shower radio and tend to listen to the same station all the time. However, if you like to change stations frequently, the tuning can be a bit frustrating.

I've been working in video production for over 2 decades now, and bought my first teleprompter for infomercial style videos back in the early 2000s. Let's just say, much like camera tech has gotten smaller and more efficient, so has teleprompting!
The concept is pretty simple and hasn't changed- angle a piece of glass in front of the lens with a black drop material behind it to create a sort of 2-way-mirror, then reflect text in reverse (you know, because mirror?) and your subject appears to read their script off your lens while the camera doesn't see the text at all.
Things that are still true from back then:
- Your text has to be reversed. My old one came with PC software to do this, and since iPads weren't really a thing yet, we used laptops that could fold all the way backwards (Thinkpads mostly). This, surprisingly does not come with software. But no matter, there are some free ones out there, and my personal favorite is just using powerpoint. We reverse the images and make a slide show that the subject can advance with a standard presenter remote. None of those things are included with this set, but if you've been doing corporate and commercial video, you probably have access to this already.

- You will have some loss of exposure due to the mirror. This isn't a big deal, if you're lighting a scene properly you should be able to easily compensate for this, you just might need to hit that ISO or aperture to brighten it up a bit more. Just something to know.

- Your subject needs to be comfortable reading without his eyes darting around the camera. This is just standard teleprompter stuff.

Things that HAVE improved with this model:
- It now attaches to the tripod! In the old days, unless you had the budget for a proper display one that was embedded in front of the camera, you needed to do this with a stand for a laptop or monitor lying horizontal while the camera tripod was behind it. Not very portable, so it stayed in my studio. This one can be brought along to a location shoot and set up rather easily!

To be honest, that one improvement makes all the difference in the world. I barely used my old teleprompter because I couldn't take it out of my studio easily, and most of my gigs are on location shoots. This is going to make testimonial / narrated production videos SO much easier to shoot out in the field!

Just keep in mind you'll need to figure out the display mechanics (software, presentation, speed, remote, etc) on your own. This just gives you the physical hardware to get it done, the mechanics of it will need your own creativity. Would definitely recommend!

For streaming Amazon and Netflix videos, playing Steam games, and general web browsing, the screen is beautiful and the computer has been working flawlessly since I got it four month ago. I have no complaints on those fronts. However, there are some other things to talk about.

One of the minor flaws is that the mouse turns off after several minutes of inactivity. You have to click it to turn it back on again before you can use it. That may sound like a trivial thing but it can become an ongoing irritant, especially if you work on several different computers and have to remember to click this particular mouse before usage.

Another minor flaw, one that became a major irritant for me, was that the screen would turn off after 5 minutes without any keyboard or mouse usage. It would even turn off while I was watching movies. In the Windows 10 Power & Sleep settings I would change the screen turn off time from 15 minutes to Never. That would fix the problem temporarily. However, every time I rebooted the computer, the screen turn off time would reset itself to 15 minutes. So I would have to go back into the settings to change it again.

Fiddling with the Windows power plan and scouring the net for solutions turned up nothing. Yes, the power plan was set the way I wanted it. No, the problem had nothing to do with a screensaver. No, there was nothing in the Bios that would trigger the reset. After four months of constant irritation, I finally stumbled across the solution by accident. It seems that ASUS has it's own power plan that overrides the Windows one. The default setting on the ASUS power plan was to turn the screen off after 15 minutes. Changing the ASUS setting to Never finally solved the problem. Why ASUS felt the need to put it's own power plan on their machine when Windows 10 already had a perfectly good one, I have no idea. I especially don't know why ASUS set their plan to override Window's.

That problem touches on the potentially major flaw with ASUS. In trying to find a solution to a minor problem on another ASUS machine, I found that their customer service sucks. When, after much effort, I finally got to talk with a live person, their accent was so thick that I literally could not understand what they were saying. When I asked for someone who spoke clearer English, the service rep got all huffy and I never did get to talk with anyone else and my questions never got answered.

This happened after I had already bought the ASUS Zen Z240-C1, otherwise I wouldn't have gotten a second ASUS machine. Now I've got my fingers crossed that nothing major happens to this one lest I get tangled up in their customer service mess again. So, this machine itself deserves a 4 star review for good performance with only minor flaws. However, ASUS customer service would get no stars from me at all and that will keep me from buying anything else from them.

For the price, this is the 3D plasma to own. Panasonic makes the highest rated, best plasma displays on the market for the middle-end consumer and even higher-end sets. The GT30 has taken some hits due to its black-leveling during scene transitions. This seems most notable to those who may not understand or have the know how to alter the video settings properly; I DID notice this occurring when video output is set to "standard", once you tune the display properly, there should be no noticeable or any flickering between darker scenes to brighter transitions. To go into great detail on how to properly set your TV would be worthless, a "good" picture varies person by person but this preliminary issue should not deter one from purchasing this set.

With that out of the way, consider this: you will not see a better high definition plasma display on the market. At the GT30 price, you are not going to get 3D quality, HD quality, feature set and value any where else. If you have not been to any store to view other brands competing with this set/price, do so and do yourself a favor. Once you see a GT30 set up properly, showing the same content as other brands, there should be no questions left to answer. The display owns. From blu rays to PS3 to Wii to regular DVDs, I have not scene until this plasma a more OUTSTANDING visual display. Blu Rays appear as though people are standing in your living room.

the most noticeable attribute of this plasma, at least to me, is the quality and richness of the depth in the display. Its simply amazing. Looks like you can reach your hand into the background and touch things. And no, I am not talking about when 3D is on, that is another story. In pure HD form without 3D, the depth, black, and richness of this display is simply jaw dropping. Your friends will not understand what they are looking at. To note, a HD gaming system looks simply unbelievable. You will be playing your games for the "first time" all over again.

The bad: THE SPEAKERS ARE DOWN RIGHT AWFUL. if you do not have some sort of surround sound system, or at the very least two channels (front left/right) the speakers sound terrible, they may as well sold it without them and saved a few bucks. You will need some sort of sound bar or extra components to get anything other than dialog. And the dialog is barely satisfactory; no bass, tiny highs, bad spacing and underpowered.

3D: Panasonic has the best 3D on the market. Compare it with Samsung or Sony. There is no comparison. View them back to back and you will find that Panasonics 3D technology, although requiring ACTIVE shutter glasses, reproduced 3D images in HD form where as others may not. Samsung for example, 3D reproduction looks like cardboard paper cutouts with no depth and lacking resolution. Not in the GT30 however. The 3D is amazing and even the 2D->3D reproduction (taking standard 2D video and artificially creating 3D images) adds incredible depth to your viewing experience, albeit not so much "pop" off the screen. Worthy to note is that 3D viewing does produce a somewhat dimmer display, not sure if this is due to the glasses tint or how their system works, but overall when 3D is on, expect a less vibrant picture from non-glasses viewing.

Overall, theres not much out there for the GT30 price that offers screen size, content and value. Above all else, picture quality should take the cake here. Please check it out in a store and make your decision. Cant beat this set. On a side note, internet connectivity works flawlessly, I wired the TV with a ethernet cable, which, you should do if you expect the highest speeds and purest connection. The TV synced up with zero glitches and loaded youtube, pandora and amazon with the ease of touching 1 button.

Excellent buy, sound is its largest demerit but can be remedied for a couple of bucks. Good luck!!

I bought one of those very small ASUS VivoMini UN62-M037M computers. It has an HDMI out port to connect to either a monitor or your nice HD TV. (I have mine connected to my TV.) I am running Windows 8.1 on the computer.

Microsoft has acknowledged that there is a bug in Windows 8 and 8.1: When you turn off your TV but leave your computer on, the OS will always give you an Out of Memory error message. There is no software fix whatsoever. Many people are complaining of this issue on boards over at Intel and other places.

The only fix is to either never ever turn off your TV, or always turn off your computer when you turn off your TV, or fool the computer into thinking there is that HDMI monitor connected even when said monitor is powered off.

I bought this ConnectPRO for just this purpose...and it works.

Out of the box I did not get a green light, per the instructions. The light was orange, which implies it had a memorized EDID from the factory.

I reset the box and cloned the EDID from my TV.

I can now leave my computer on always if I desire and turn off my TV at any time, and no more problems.

Sad that Microsoft never offered their own software fix via an update, in spite of the fact they confirm the issue, which forced me to have to spend an extra $70.

When I first purchased my 3 TB MBL some time ago I was quite pleased. Network access, remote access, even an android app. In short, everything my DLink had plus the app and a nicer look on the shelf. I used it extensively for pulling up photos on my cell phone when I was bored as well as to store my most important files. I didn't back them up, a back-up drive is something I kept saying I would add later...

14 months later (note the 12 month warranty had just expired) the drive stopped being accessible over the network. I spent a week and at least 40 hours of my time going back and forth with tech support by e-mail and trying every option they could offer, and the result was that they deemed the unit broken. They said that the unit can not be opened because that would break the drive inside, and they said that they can't fix it. They "kindly" offered me a referral to one of several companies that give them a kick back for data recovery services. Incidentally, I asked two for pricing by e-mail and they didn't respond.

So I took the unit apart and bought a new unit and took that one apart and swapped the drives. Neither one worked. After talking to support again it turns out that WD didn't want these to be upgradable because if they were upgradable you could buy a cheap drive instead of a new unit so they code each board to the drive that will be in it. TO make matters worse, they encoded the drive in a Linux format that no known version of Linux can translate. Attaching it to my Linux system I couldn't mount it using any utility. Several Linux recovery programs couldn't do anything either.

Okay, having told you why I will never buy a WD NAS again, I should now tell you how to fix this if you have the same problem that I do: DiskInternals makes a program called Linux Reader. That's right, Linux can't read the drive but a program designed to read Linux drives from within Windows can! Recovering the data to a drive is time consuming though. I tried it all at once but that froze after a few days. Then I tried one major directory at a time and that worked better. But recovering nearly 3 TB of data has taken a very long time! I'm about 3 MONTHS into the recovery effort and I have about 400 GB remaining. After starting on my wife's computer because mine is a laptop and causing a few crashes and a lot of delays I finally had to pull out an older computer and set it up just to run this program.

If anyone has the same problem and can't get this solution to work, I'll do my best to help if you simply reply to this review and give me all the details. If anyone is considering buying a WD NAS, I want to encourage you to buy a DLink model 323 (I think the 325 is the current version but it is missing some features so I'd get an older one) instead. I've had that thing running for 5 years without a glitch!

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

When I saw this camera at this price point I knew it was something I needed to check out. I appreciated the fact it was 2MP because with this lens you are not going to want to be eating up the hard drive space required for a 5MP.

I upgraded from a year-old, previous-generation Paperwhite, mostly to gain the new inverted white-on-black screen mode that Amazon insists requires new hardware and to have built-in Audible playback over Bluetooth.

This unit ticks most of boxes, and after some debate I've decided to give it five stars, but there are some imperfections worth knowing about. It's mostly good, though, and often great.

Battery life
No complaints. In several long international flights, I've yet to run it down more than about 30%, either in long reading sessions with the front-light or in lengthy Audible playback sessions over Bluetooth.

Audible content
The Audible player works brilliantly. Excellent sound, simple controls (including playback-speed adjustment). It does work best if you don't have a screen password enabled, though-- that will get in the way if you just want to rewind a few seconds to catch something you missed. Playback proceeds even if you have a case closed, which shuts off the front-light and saves battery charge.

There's no headphone jack-- this is for Bluetooth only. Fine with me. I have Bluetooth-enabled hearing aids (cochlear implants, actually) and it's a true joy to be able to listen to books on this device. Thanks, Amazon.

Screen
The screen is pretty much the same as my previous-generation Paperwhite's, meaning not bad but could use more contrast when reading in a dark room using the front-light. Outdoors or in well-lit areas, it's fantastic and mostly glare-free.

More seriously, the lack of contrast mars the new Paperwhite's valuable ability to invert text to white-on-black. This is a marvelous accessibility feature for those with "floaters", vitreous separation and other vision issues. Unfortunately, when used with the front-light in a darkened room, such as when reading at night or in a darkened airplane, the black background is more of a medium gray. So this new feature is less helpful than it could be. In fairness, poor contrast is characteristic of today's e-ink displays, which provide perhaps 8:1 contrast. If Amazon can significantly improve the contrast, I'd upgrade again in a flash.

The screen is plastic and will scratch. Keep it clean and use a case. Even with a case (I prefer one of the various "origami" cases available here, which allow the Kindle to prop itself upright) it will fit nicely into a pocket.

The touch-screen user interface is the same as the previous-gen Paperwhite's. I'm not a huge fan of it; too easy to touch it when you don't mean to, and end up on the wrong page. But, the earlier button-driven Kindles had sort of the same problem, so whatever. I recommend a simple fix, perhaps as a Settings option: require a double-tap rather than a single-tap. How about it, Amazon?

Connectivity
The 4G/LTE capability is a nice speed upgrade from the previous 3G connectivity. Downloading Audible content requires a WiFi connection as before.

Unfortunately I'm finding that global connectivity with the new 4G hardware is inferior to the previous-gen's 3G radio. For example, my year-old 3G Paperwhite connected without issue in Saigon, but the new one won't.

The user interface for turning Airplane Mode on and off could be improved. As it is, engaging Airplane Mode cuts all connectivity including Bluetooth. So if you're in the middle of listening to a book when the time comes to put your gizmos in Airplane Mode, it will cut your connection. Better to do what the latest iPhones do, and have the device learn if your usage prefers that Bluetooth remain active.

Browser
It's high time for Amazon to replace the minimally-functional "Experimental Browser" with something more useful. I get it that Kindles are all about battery life and browsers can be major energy hogs, but c'mon, it's 2019, and this browser feels like a relic from 1996. Probably is.

Step two, reboot and change my boot sequence because Samsung Magician felt it was necessary to change it for me and made this new SSD my boot drive, even though it had no OS on it to boot.

I had heard that an HFS+ driver was available for Windows7 that allows read-only access to HFS+ formatted drives, but Paragon has at some point released a driver that allows read/write access for $20. It appears that when you buy this drive, you are allowed a license to this $20 driver: you have to have the drive connected to the computer to download the driver for free, but I was unable to test if the driver would then work for other HFS+ formatted drives. The driver then appears to run in the background as a service, not an application (thankfully). Suffice to say the NTFS formatted version of this drive is significantly less expensive...

FYI, FAT file systems can also be read by both Windows and MAC, but they have a 4GB file size limit.

I also dislike that if I am to disable the sleep timer on this drive, I have to first install the software on my computer. Most current external hard drives suffer from this problem, however.

So...it works, it's beautiful, 2TB is enormous when you're used to less. The dual-O/S compatibility is a good idea, but I'd personally prefer to get the normal version and put in some legwork to achieve the same results (but of course the other versions may not be as aesthetically pleasing and scream your love of Apple). Either way, it's a good drive.

I've been an avid fan of ebooks since the long gone days of the Rocket and the eBookman, and a fan of the Kindle since the very beginning. This is miles and away the best there has ever been. It is a luxury model, no doubt, but oh is it luxurious.

I like:
The weight. Even in the case it's very light, though if it gets much lighter I'll worry about it blowing away in a strong wind.
The size. It's not going to get much smaller without shrinking the screen.
The interface. I'm sorry, I like buttons. Call me old. I never bent back the spine of a book (horrors) so I can't compare the feel of this to that, but I can say it's nice for a long reading session. The touch screen takes a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial will guide a new user. The tutorial is intrusive at first, but provides useful information and goes away quickly. I will suggest customizing the screen. I hated the default, but you get a lot of options to make it just the way you want.
The lighting is now all but invisible. I was unhappy that you can't completely turn it off as you could with the Nook Glowlight, and turning it down casts an odd yellow light over the page, but it's so even now as to be so unintrusive I barely notice going from sunlight to tunnel on the bus home. With the Nook I'd be thrown out of the book to go turn on the light. With the Kindle, I can keep reading without a pause. It does not have adaptive lighting, but I'm not sure it needs it.
The download speed. I don't know if it's supposed to be faster than the Kindle Keyboard (the last one I had with 3G) but it certainly seems that way.
The battery life. Maybe with this thing going for months we'll finally hear an end to the "but my dead tree doesn't run out of power" nonsense.
Next in series. When you're almost done with a book, it tells you where the story continues. Now the next feature I want, and if it does this I haven't seen it yet, is an alert when the next book in a series I'm following is published. Yes, FictFact is great, but I'm greedy and want it right on the device.

I don't like:
It's not waterproof. There was a lot of hope it would be after the Nook went that route.
It's not solar, yet, but there are rumors of a solar cover coming soon.
It doesn't support Audible and the excellent immersive reading between ebook and audiobook. I have a weird love of that feature, seeing what changed print to audio.
Recommended Content and Reading Lists. I shut this feature off. The information seems scattered at best and gave me no useful information, especially considering how precious screen real estate is.

Getting to the earbud case itself, it's lower and wider than the previous generation earbuds I've tried from them. Opening it up was a treat. The earbuds and whole interior look like some kind of stealth technology. So matte black they absorb light. Controls are easy and intuitive. A clickable button instead of gesture control, so you can tell what you're doing, and don't trigger it every time you brush the hair away from your ear. They're my favorite way to talk on a cellphone too. Nice to have both hands free.

This little monocular/camera has an unique design. Canon made lots of compromises to build it for this size and price. As with any gadget that is full of compromises, it is not for everyone.

As the product description states, this camera has 2 optical lenses (nominally 100mm and 400mm equivalents) and one digital crop to 800mm. These are paired with a very small image sensor (1/3 inch) to get the camera down to this size. Because of the small sensor, the camera is really only usable in bright sunlight; image quality is mediocre to poor indoors or at night or even early or late in the day or on cloudy days when the sun is not strong. The 100mm and 400mm are fixed lenses, you cannot zoom to levels in between those 2 values.

The viewfinder has pretty good brightness and resolution, but is somewhat small, so looking at it for long periods of time was uncomfortable to me, especially in lower-light situations when the image quality was not so great.

The minimum focusing distance is 3 feet with the 100mm lens and a huge 15 feet with the 400mm lens. That makes this camera impractical for most closeup photography.

Battery life is a mediocre 1 hour of screen-on time or about 150 photos. You have to beware of the time limit if you are using this device as a monocular. While you can recharge the device in the field via the USB-C port, that is awkward at best since you have to hold the fragile battery door open while recharging it.

Those are the main limitations to this camera, so who is it really for? The 100mm and 400mm lenses are equivalent to about 4x and 16x zoom levels on a smartphone or point-and-shoot camera. The Canon camera has no wide angle lens, but if you are carrying a smartphone with you, you can use that for your wide angle camera. I believe today's top-of-the-line iPhone has a 2.5X optical telephoto lens, so the 4X and 16X lenses on this Canon are huge improvements if you like telephoto photography. Samsung and Pixel Android cameras are little better, but the Canon still beats them at 16X.

I think this Canon camera is useful for casual photographers who want to take telephoto snapshots of wildlife, daytime sports, architecture, etc. This camera is small and lightweight enough to easily fit in a purse or coat pocket or even a big pants pocket and it takes better bright sunlight telephoto photos than most smartphones. The camera lets you wirelessly copy photos to your smartphone for editing and posting to social media.

What are your other options? Companies like Sony and Panasonic sell good compact point-and-shoot cameras with 720mm telephoto lenses and better sensors than this Canon camera. These cameras are a little more expensive and a little heavier, but about the same semi-pocketable size as this Canon. Of course, interchangeable lens cameras like SLRs or APS mirrorless camera will let you mount huge expensive lenses that can take fantastic telephoto photos, but are usually too big and heavy to carry around if your primary purpose is not photography.

I'm giving this camera 3.5 stars because of list of limitations is maybe too long for most people, but I think it does have its place for some people. I do wish they had used a bigger image sensor to improve the image quality and low-light ability, even if that meant making the camera a little bigger and heavier. Even many smartphones have bigger image sensors than this Canon camera.

Full review:
I'm familiar with the higher-end earbuds from RHA (such as their model MA-350, which I use almost daily), so I was very interested to see what they could produce for at the lower end of the price scale.

The overall build quality is quite good. They are just as comfortable as the MA-350 in my ear, which is to say they are nearly perfect. They have the right amount of cushion so they don't get tiring but still fit securely so I don't have any problems with them falling out while exercising. The MA150 comes with three sets of ear cushions so you can adjust them to fit what's best for your ear.

The cord is less stout than the MA-350 (it's a conventional rather than woven cord) but still seems durable enough for typical use. I very much like the plug connector - nicely made, and is angled to alleviate stress points (the connection is where many of my buds end up failing).

The sound quality is good. I used them on my Kindle Fire and a SanDisk MP3 player. No, it won't knock your socks off, but it's a lot better than I expected for the price. The bass is clear and more than plentiful for my taste. Where I noticed the most difference between these and the MA-350's is in the mid-range and treble. Definitely less crisp, which I would imagine is due to the fact that these are made of plastic rather than the aluminum construction of the MA-350s. But it didn't cause any significant problems when I used them when movie watching - the dialogue was quite clear.

Noise isolation is excellent. Very little ambient noise leaks in when wearing them.

The biggest miss is the same complaint I have with other RHA `phones - the R/L markings are on the stem in raised black letters on a black background. VERY hard to see. So, the first thing I do is to color in the RHA logo on the right bud with a Sharpie so I can spot L & R easily.

But that quibble aside, these are excellent and a great value. Very good sound, comfortable to wear for extended periods, good noise isolation and nicely made. I also like the packaging - rather than a blister pack with lots of plastic, these come packed in what RHA calls an "eco pack" - minimal thickness and packaging that is mostly thin cardboard. Much easier to recycle and open.

Definitely worth a look if you want a low-cost set that provides a very good music listening experience, and an excellent movie sound experience.

I have a growing interest in photography and I have been learning as I go. Features are also more than I expected for a twenty buck light. For one thing you can easily get seven hours of continuous use on a single charge. I did a rundown test on mine and it remained illuminated for a little over seven hours before it started dimming, That was with both LEDS in each head switched on. I ended the test when it started appreciably dimming, but even at seven hours this is more than adequate since I actually do use this as a music stand light and the longest performances are less than three hours.

Another feature that I love is the LED indicator in the USB A end of the charging cable. It will be red until the light fully charges, then it will turn green.

Note: there are two things that I do not care for: (1) the charging end is a barrel connector instead of a micro USB connector, so if you lose of damage the included cable you are going to have difficulty replacing it, and (2) the barrel connector does not completely seat into the charging port. It charges, but I would be hesitant of using this light in a studio where you wanted to suppress all electrical interference. I am not sure there is any from this light, but the fact that a conducting connector is partially exposed gives me pause.

Bottom line: for stage performances this light is better and brighter than most other two-LED models and illuminates sufficiently to read music or lyrics. It holds firm when clamped to my music stand, and the flexible arms allow me to position the lamp heads for optimum reading while staying put.

I love the look and feel of this VERSO "DARWIN" CROCCO standing cover for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablet. Red is my favorite color, and the faux crocodile texture is really fun.

This cover holds the tablet firmly with silicone-enhanced elastic corner bands (patent pending). The bands have a rubbery material on the underside of the elastic that grips the surface beneath it, so the tablet does not slide around inside the cover or want to fall out. (I have screen protector film on my tablet, which seems like a good idea when a tablet is held in place by elastic bands rather than a hard plastic shell. This [[ASIN:B009NHU556 3-Pack Ultra-Clear Screen Protector)]] is easy to apply, and you get three chances to get it on right.)

The cover's built-in stands are quite intriguing. There are two of them attached to the inside of the front cover. One stand supports the tablet at a low angle for typing; the other supports it more or less upright for watching movies. Both provide comfortable viewing angles. The stands themselves are flat, microfiber-covered pieces that match the rest of the cover's interior. You pick the stand angle you want, and open out the appropriate stand. The stand is connected to the cover on top and also with a ribbon underneath, so that the stand converts into a triangular support for your tablet. This design is very clever, and I would consider it perfect if I hadn't already tried the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case]], which is a little easier to set up and offers more viewing angles.

This Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover has an elastic band that holds it tightly closed inside a book or tote bag, as well as an automatic magnetic wake/sleep feature. For the wake/sleep feature to work, you must insert your tablet with the camera at the left and the charging port at the right. This I don't like, because the charging port ends up at the tablet's bottom edge when you use the stands. This means you are limited to using the low-angle stand whenever your tablet is plugged in, because the plug contacts the table top. (With the Marware Vibe cover, the charging port ends up at the tablet's top edge, so you can use the tablet at any angle when it's plugged in.)

According to the accompanying retail literature, this Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover is "compatible" with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9", the Nook HD+, "and more". Because the cover holds the tablet with elastic bands, it should fit any tablet near in size to the large Fire or the large Nook. However, it is definitely too small for an iPad 2.

For me, it's difficult to choose between the Marware Vibe cover and the Verso "Darwin" cover. But in the end, as usually happens, good looks win out. My 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet is going to stay in the red faux-crocodile-skin cover, which is eye-catching, looks and feels luxurious, and is extremely well made.

I received this as a free review sample. This is NOT a bluetooth device. These phones are strictly for 3.5mm stereo connections. That means that this will work with a wider variety of devices.

The sound quality to my ears is why I awarded it five stars. There is definitely a crossover built into these phones because I could hear the separation of low and high frequencies, with a prominent bass in one ear. Also, there does not seem to be any compression at the high end of the frequency spectrum, which gives these phones a more natural sound. I listen to mainly acoustic jazz (piano jazz trios, vocalists, and similar), so I appreciate the realistic sound these phones provide.

There are a few areas that I would love to see improved: the cable is long and would be nicer if it were flat, tangle-proof. Also, the controls are a little too high up on the cable in my opinion. I can easily reach them, but when testing them I could not see the buttons. Of course, those are not show stoppers - just my own preferences. And regarding the controls, I already am familiar with their placement from use and memory, so that is really a non issue.

The phones are comfortable. They ship with small, medium and large tips and I used the ones that were already installed. The fit was perfect. These also ship with an extra set of premium, noise blocking tips. I have not tried them since the regular tips are more than adequate for me.

Other nice features are the zippered, hard case, velcro cable wrap and shirt clip. To be sure, they are value-added items, but the real value is the sound quality and these phones have that without a doubt.

Bottom line: if you want hard wired phones that allow you to listen critically to music (or transcribe it), this is a surprisingly inexpensive solution. I have used everything from high end studio in-ear monitors and premium phones, and these come close at a much more affordable price. I am not saying that these are as good as the expensive phones, but am saying that bang for your buck these are hard to beat and will surprise most audiophiles.

I own ALL of the kensington line of trackballs (clearly a trackball nut). From the original Expert Mouse (using a serial connection) all the way to this one. I can see how some purists are very touchy about their trackball performing and as it becomes an extension of interfacing with the computer, it's critical that it performs well.

PROS:
* Nice compact footprint; Not too demanding for space.

* The ball 'stays in' the unit even if you turn it over! This is a new concept for their trackballs! (you can pop it out if you need to condense for travel)
* Scroll wheel is nice; A feature present only in the higher-end trackballs.

CONS:
* BUTTONS! YUK! The button has some kind of contact issue where if you press it gently enough, you hear and feel a little 'click' but you didn't actuate the button! You must press it harder, and get a louder firmer CLICK! (really kinda mushy) to click it! I have tried different spots on the button and it's all the same! This is ALMOST a deal killer for me, but I'm going to give it some time, see if the button wears in and that false-click goes away over time.
* Scroll wheel is not free-flowing like on the modern expert mouse. With that sucker, you can fling the wheel and it will roll atleast for a half-second or so! This one really resists movement so it's more like a mouse-wheel than a scroll-wheel. It does not have a 'ribbed' feel, it rolls smoothly but it's not a 'on rails' as other models.

My personal favorite is still the modern expert mouse. It's massive (like a little tank on your desktop!) but you can navigate quickly with it, and use it in the manner a trackball was designed to be used.

This is a great, mobile, easy HotSpot device that works just like any Wi-Fi on any device with a great connection. Mobile supposedly for 10 hours, less than hour recharge.

There's only one caveat: AT&T will tell you the pre-installed SIM card it comes with, sealed in new packaging, is INVALID. AT&T will give you a good one for FREE. You simply have to replace it, or if you're like me, get someone that can. :) That simple, and you're ready for set-up. *NOTE*: Both the pre-installed SIM card *AND* the SIM card being sold by a separate seller on Amazon that is suggested as being a good companion purchase with this device are INVALID. This according to AT&T themselves. They will send you a new, free one you can use; tell them what device you have and setup a data plan.

All you need then is to add a Data plan. This device, according to AT&T, *only* works with a postpaid plan ($50.00/month for 5 G's minimum), however there's no contract. There is a credit check. It will not work with prepaid, it will not work with a lesser plan, no matter what the packaging or Amazon description says. I just spent like 20 minutes on the phone with a very helpful, patient, and knowledgeable AT&T customer service representative who also consulted another department for verification.

The one exception is if you already have an AT&T cellphone plan (I do), you can "share" your data package you already have for only $20/month. So that's what I did. It still is postpaid, and there still is no contract on that part of the plan with your new HotSpot device. You'll be given a new number that's only for the HotSpot without a cellphone (Voice) plan component.

I'm really glad I bought this great device, I was a little apprehensive because I'm not techie and I've never tried a mobile HotSpot device before. To make it simple, get AT&T to install (instore) or send you a new SIM card that they say works with this device, and then you can set up the device (supposedly) online with ease. You have to add a data plan for it. I love GPS units. Ever since first using them when they first came out for the consumer market years ago (and were horribly expensive) I'd no sooner drive a car without a GPS than I would without a spare tire. For me, it's a must have.

Given this, plus my enjoyment of anything that has buttons, I've owned several, and have tried out several more. So far, the Moto is the hands-down winner.

GPS' have matured quite a bit over the past few years, so the days of having one manufacturer being worlds better than another is pretty much over. What I mean by that is that a GPS from any of the major manufacturers (TomTom, Garmin, Magellan, etc.) will do the basics of getting you from point A to point B just fine. It's the fine-tuning that has begun to matter.

This is where it gets difficult to provide a recommendation, since what's important to me may not be important to others. For example, I've always shunned units that didn't "ding" at an upcoming turn, or always display the next turn direction regardless of how far away that turn is. Others may find those features not all that important.

So, what makes the Moto best for me? Basically the form factor. I love, love, LOVE the extra wide screen! You can maintain a good map view but still have a portion of the screen dedicated to all sorts of useful info, such as the complete turn-by-turn list, an aerial view of your trip (both close distance as well as the entire journey), all sorts of stats such as arrival time, elapsed drive time, traffic notifications, upcoming POIs and so on. Absolutely wonderful. Plus it has the upcoming turn ding and the always-visible next turn direction.

The build quality is solid, routing is good, the PC interface (the Moto Toolbox) is far more stable than the TomTom Home software (at least for me - running it on Win 7 64 bit), and I love how they have integrated the POI database into the address database. For example, with other GPS if I wanted to go to the XYZ store and didn't know the street address, I'd have to open up the POI database, then select the store category, then find the store. With the Moto I just type in the name of the store using the same screen as I use to type in an address.

Also like that it has real buttons on each side rather than be forced to use the touchscreen. For me, that makes key features (such as muting it) a lot easier to use. The screen is very clear and easy to see even in bright sun. Excellent refresh rate. In fact, very speedy in every aspect, from searches to plots to route recalc's.

The Moto gives you a lot of value for the money. I must confess, however, that I didn't purchase it at Amazon, but rather at another online store when they had it on sale for under 2 bills. At that price, it's a fantastic value. But, even at the regular price of less than 3 bills, it's a solid value.

Can't comment on the services such as the Bing search or Google connectivity since I have never used them (those are some of the features I don't see much value in). But, the traffic info is solid, and just as good (if not better) than the XM traffic feed I have with my built-in GPS (in an Infiniti EX35).

Downsides are that it runs hot. You can toast a sandwich on it after just a short while in use in the car. Doesn't seem to cause a problem, but don't know if that's a long-term reliability issue. Moto is also relatively unproven in the GPS world. So far so good - they've provided software and map updates at no charge without any problem, and have responded promptly to an email for support info. Lastly, the quality of spoken directions is just OK. You can understand them, but it's not the best out there by any means.

For me, this provides the best mix of features I've seen so far. Granted, in a few months I'll be looking at the next newest and greatest one out there, but for now, I could not be happier with this.

Summary:
I bought this kit because I needed to recover the data on an 80GB Hitachi 1.8" Drive from a dead Vaio notebook. No setup was required after I finished installing the drive in the enclosure, and it was recognized and read on my XP machine without a fuss. The enclosure is a thin aluminum extrusion with channels on the inside. The end caps appear to be pot metal castings. One end cap contains the interface board with LED activity light and the USB connector. A USB cable is provided. The kit is cheaply made but did what I needed.

Installation:
Installation consisted of mating a flex cable and connector, sliding the drive and active end cap into the enclosure, and screwing in the end cap(s).

It takes a bit of care and patience to insert the flex cable into the connector on the drive, but I was able to get it done in a few minutes.
The cable needs to be made to assume an S-bend after attaching it to the drive so that the entire assembly will fit into the box. That is best accomplished by gently pushing the end cap and HDD together and guiding the cable into an S. I suggest you place the assembly next to the enclosure first so you can see how much length the bend will need to take up. It's not much. Then, slide the drive into the enclosure followed by the cable and end cap, gently guiding the cable bend as needed. Make sure the end cap fits properly in place before and while you install the screws.

Here's the part I deducted a star for: The screws go into unthreaded channels in the enclosure and their alignment is less than perfect. It took quite a while and a better screwdriver than is provided to get the screws fully seated. YMMV.

If the drive rattles around more than you like front to back, you may wish to install one or two of the stick-on rubber bumpers that are provided onto the far end of the HDD or the inside of the blank end cap. Be aware you'll have to deal with two more screws if you put them inside the end cap.

(2) the apostrophe is on the L key and you have to press the Function button to use it. You will type "it;s" way more than you want to. (3) there are extra keys on the keyboard such as cmd, alt, option, and a weird symbol that looks like a swirly for which my iPad has no function that I am aware of.

Now, the positives. They keyboard is smaller than usual (of course) but pretty easy to use with a little practice. The screen tilt function is fantastic. It can hold the tablet at an unlimited amount of angles. The screen can spin 360 degrees so it can be used with the keyboard as a prop in a triangle format, with the keyboard in the back for movie watching, or out flat for typing in bed with the tablet propped up on your knees. The case is very sturdy, made of a rubbery feel type material, and nice to look at and touch. Not cheaply made at all. It has lights for charging, battery, and Bluetooth pairing. All the holes, speakers, and cameras are exposed where they need to be. I have a tempered glass screen protector on the iPad and it does not get in the way of the case at all.

The keyboard does add some weight to the tablet, but this does not bother me. Overall I am very pleased with this product.

This was one of the last Ultimate Ears earbud lines before Logitech bought the company which resulted in an immediate drop in product quality and increase in product price. Yes, these are still wired headphones, but the sound fidelity is unmatched, and instead of complicated noise cancelling algorithms this simply employs noise isolation to block out ambient sound. These headphones have been out of production for some time, but for whatever reason you can still find them NIB from many vendors. They charge about a little more than what cut-rate vendors charged when they were new about 6 years ago, but they were way ahead of their time and frankly nothing on the market in this price range sounds even close to this good. Plus, these original UE headphones (I don't evangelize anything UE after Logitech bought them) have a lot of great design features. The earbud units are modular, so if you ever destroy the leads, you can always replace them for $10. Also, the standard leads these ship with do NOT have the mic and volume/start-stop control on the leads, but you can buy them in various levels of quality for about $20-60 aftermarket and swap them out. It's money well spent if you want to make calls on them. Also, the lead up to 6" from each bud is cased in memory metal so they can be bent to shape and hold in place to are a comfy fit on he outside of your ears- great idea.

I do a lot with photography and I always keep my eyes open for good lighting solutions that will help me get the lighting effects I want or need for given situations. I saw this one at a reasonable price and decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it. It meets the biggest requirement I have for lighting - it does not strobe.

So many LED lights have an issue with strobing, especially when they’re low-cost. This light is not expensive when compared to a lot of others, so even though it is marketed as a video light I was only cautiously optimistic. To determine this for sure, I set my camera to use the electronic shutter only, sped up the shutter speed as high as I could and pointed directly at the light when it was powered on. Strobing lights always show banding in pictures with higher shutter speeds when using the electronic shutter; this one did not (though the display on the camera sure did but that’s a different problem). This test proved to me that this LED light does not strobe, at least not slow enough for my camera sensor to see it at high shutter speeds.

This is a fairly large LED panel, designed for video use of course but I also can work just fine for photography or even general lighting in the right setting. It comes with a clamp mount and a pole so it can be attached to a desk or shelf, then the mounting head allows for angling the light as needed so it can light a surface at just the right angle desired. The mount is sturdy and there should be no issues with stability when it is set up properly.

The light is super-easy to adjust. There are two dials on the back for tweaking the brightness and the temperature range, and there is a remote included that does the same. The temperature can be adjusted from a warm 2800K to a blistering white 8000K and everywhere in between so you can get the lighting just right.

Power is via an AC adapter and there is no battery. So, this is not a travel light by any means, If you need a light to use in the field, unless you have a power generator with you then this light isn’t it. For a static setting in a studio or room, this light is very good.

One design decision that would have been nice would have been a detachable mount so it could be used with a standard tripod instead of a clamp mount. That’s not a big deal, especially at the price point, but it would have made this light so much more versatile. I have other lights that I can mount on a tripod, so I am not too concerned.

This is a very good video light, especially when considering the price point. It has excellent temperature range, it has a solid mount for stability, and it does not strobe. If you’re looking for a solid video LED light that won’t cost a fortune, this one is better than could be reasonably expected at the asking price. It’s an easy one to recommend.

I've included a picture of the Paperwhite (on the right) and Oasis (left), both set at the same brightness, but with the Oasis's warmth setting on. You can also see there is no white Kindle logo on the Oasis, which I found ever so slightly distracting on the Paperwhite. The quality of the screen on the Oasis is also much better than the Paperwhite - text is more clear and crisp. I was really overwhelmed with the Oasis at first, just because it was so new to me. You can organize things in to 'Collections', but it still doesn't feel like enough. I recommend looking up Calibre and going from there.

My biggest gripe is the ergonomics of the Oasis. Although it's not much heavier than the Paperwhite, it feels like it because of the shape of it. It just feels heavier because of the weight distribution towards the center, and is awkward to hold with that bump/excessive weight distribution that sticks out. I am a 5'9" woman with 'normal' sized hands, so I can't even imagine how this would be for someone with smaller hands. I bought a case immediately because the shell is ridiculously slippery, and in my opinion, a horrible choice of material for something you're going to hold for hours. Looks pretty, but not very functional for an e-reader. I bought the 'Ayotu Skin Touch Feeling Case', and it is awesome. I ordered a couple of others and this one stood out among all of them big time.

Last gripe is that the screen is pretty slow and laggy at times. I know it's an e-reader, but it's a very expensive one that doesn't do anything else (which to clarify I am absolutely fine with BUT, see next point), but at that price, it should really be perfect.

A positive feature of this that is nice is that you can flip the device around and the screen flips with you, so if you are right or left handed or just want to switch sides during reading, that is super helpful.

I do like it, but am considering whether or not I am going to keep it due to the ergonomics alone.

I have several mp3 players and I had yet to find one suitable for everyday use until I picked this little gem up.

My requirements were:

-LONG battery life with replaceable battery (those embedded batteries are going to need factory servicing after 250-300 charge cycles...you can use rechargeable AA or AAAs and easily replace them)

-Color screen...more than 256 colors.

-USB 2.0 transfer

-Ability to drag and drop

-Ability to play OGG files

-FM tuner

-FM recorder

-Solid construction

I have another unit I use for in-line recording, so that wasn't a big deal to me. I came across this unit for a good price so I gave it a shot. Well, at first, I was upset because I couldn't get the player to be recognized under Windows. I called iRiver and a tech walked me through the steps of setting up the appropriate user account and permission in the registry. After that, I hooked in and updated the firmware.

This syncs with Windows Media Player 10 and does so seamlessly. You can set it to sync up automatically or manually and WMP10 can convert to 64kbps wma files to save space if you want. I updated the firmware and transferred a couple of music files with WMP10-no sweat. I then was able to open up the player and drag and drop files into it (requirement met!) Next came the key part-SOUND.

The sound on this unit is very good, even with the included earbuds. I connected a pair of active noise cancelling headphones with big magnets and the SRS sound was FULL and RICH, even though I was just playing OGG files (remember to put those in the DATA folder, not the MEDIA folder!) There's a lot of tweakability on sound, even though there are no user presets you can save to. The screen is nice, if not really large, and it's easy to get the controls down once you've had a day to get used to them.

The unit came with a sturdy armband and a necklace to connect to the T10's VERY well-secured lanyard clip. Either choice is OK, but I prefer the armband because I am always afraid I'll drink a soda and spill some on the unit if it's hanging right below my mouth.

The T10 has a good tuner and can record FM in nice quality. I also found the voice recording to be good, if a little sensitive to body noise (if you touch the body while you record, it is very audible.) The battery life is projected to be 45 hours (WHICH IS FANTASTIC!), so I use some AA NiMH spare batteries from my digital camera for power and I never have to worry about finding a plug when the power goes out. In a pinch, alkalines work just fine, too.

Let's review my requirements:

-LONG battery life with replaceable battery *CHECK*

-Color screen...more than 256 colors.*CHECK*

-USB 2.0 transfer *CHECK*

-Ability to drag and drop *CHECK*

-Ability to play OGG files *CHECK*

-FM tuner *CHECK*

-FM recorder *CHECK*

-Solid construction *CHECK*

In short, this player has satisfied all my needs and done so with great style to boot. I'd highly recommend it with the following warnings:

-Getting it to connect with Windows initially might require a call to iRiver.

-The unit is sort of chunky (it's kind of like a triangular prism) and will not slip into a pocket like a flat piece of cardboard. You will probably need to use a bigger case or one of the two included carry options.

-The design makes it hard to see the controls when wearing the armband on the left arm. Wearing it on your right will allow you easy access to the controls.

I'd DEFINITELY recommend this unit to ANYONE who needed a great player that didn't need line-in recording.

After viewing my crabby review (below), they got in touch and offered to send a new set (you get the key finder and several other pieces that you can attach to other easily lost items). Oh, why not? I have nothing else to do during the hours left around the seven 14-hour days a week entailed in running a business. :-D They sent the doodads in the mail.

MEANWHILE... Between the time I first posted my original grutch and the time the new package of goodies arrived, I lost my keys not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES.

Each time, the Key Finder located the things! Inside a purse...on a piece of furniture where I'd dropped the keys to rescue the dog...atop a countertop where no one in their right mind would ever leave their keys...

It's not a matter of standing wherever you happen to be and clicking the "finder" device. You do have to walk around the house, and you do have to point the finder in several directions until it locates and connects with the receiver on your keyring. Its signal will pass through some but not all walls (why, I do not know: possibly electrical wiring or insulation?). Its range is about 20 feet, I'd guess. It requires some patience and persistence on your part, but it does eventually work.

Click 'n' Dig sent me a new set, which I gave to some dear friends who are even more superannuated than I after the Missus expressed dismay at having lost her keys once again. This is one of those tools that makes old age tolerable...maybe even survivable.

Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.

Honestly, I have wanted a pair of good Sennheiser headphones for years, but I couldn't justify it to myself - I mean we have a Denon sound base that connects via Bluetooth and Alexa for music, so a personal pair of headphones seems like a selfish indulgence. OMG. Do it. Be selfish. I have been wearing these things for days now every chance that I get and falling in love with music all over again.

First thing, I must correct a misstatement in an earlier review - the HD 579 are NOT noise cancellation headphones. They do not have that technology and are not intended to, not marketed as such and I double checked with Sennheiser directly to be sure. It might be easy to mistake the beautiful sound quality and encapsulation of the sound for noise cancellation at first - simply because the headphones fit very well and at an upper volume, external noise doesn't readily intrude.

The fit is far more comfortable than I remember headphones being. The band is nicely padded and adjustable and the ear cups are very soft, thick and they fully cover your ear without any pinching. I have worn these for thirty minutes and up to three hours consecutively in vary increments, every day for five days now and never had cauliflower ear. Nor do my ears get hot. I'm using these with my Fire Tablet, my LG V10 phone and Sceptre 55" television playing music through our cable provider's music stations. The connection plug is tight and the cord has proven to be long enough for use in bed at night while reading, on the sofa reading & it rolls up to put in my pocket while wandering around cleaning house and doing barn chores.

As to the quality of the music.... simply outstanding. Far better than I really expected. One of my favorite soundtracks is from the movie Hannibal by Hans Zimmer. It has a mix of pure classical and opera. The HD 579 phones let me hear the French horns and the soft build of the clarinets as crisp and clearly as the big cellos and trumpets in other, louder movements. Simple acoustic vocal pieces from James Taylor, Tracy Chapman and Paul Simon are beautifully rendered and you can appreciate the realism of a live performance. These headphones are very nice and I wish I had bought something like them long ago, but now that I have these, I won't be far from them and I definitely will be grabbing them every time I want music, which is daily.
