As convenient as this product makes hooking up networking cables, the cheap screws that come with this wall plate make installation a nightmare.

Do yourself a favor, if you have an extra light switch plate laying around, use those screws instead. I've installed two of these ethernet wall plates into two different low voltage mounting brackets. There are no threads in these mounting brackets. You're essentially creating the threads as you go. This necessitates a greater amount of torque and the screw heads are shallow. If using hand tools, this will require immense amounts of force to prevent stripping the heads. Normally, only a small, flat blade screwdriver is all that is required. But this installation works best if you have a powered screwdriver that will provide the necessary torque.

If you can run the screws in and out prior to installation, it may prevent some headaches. I did something similar to the first low voltage mounting bracket I purchased too.

You'll also find that if you have some screws from an existing light switch plate, that they have a deeper slot and are half the length. The provided screws were much longer than necessary. I replaced the screws on the second wall plate I installed after backing out the originals with a set of pliers after the heads were damaged.

To put this into context, I have the right tools and do more DIY than most other people I know.

I wanted a wired connection in a far room out of reach of my router. This works perfectly for that by allowing me to use any power outlet in my condo as a way to extend my wired network.

I tested my upload and download speeds with a network cable plugged from my laptop directly into my router and compared it to a wired connection with the Netgear Powerline Outlet. There was no discernible difference either positive or negative. I even ran video under both scenarios and I detected no difference in performance.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the router, my ping was 12 ms, download was 17.08 Mbps, upload was 5.17 Mbps.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the Powerline using my electrical house wiring, my ping was 12 ms, download was 16.63 Mbps, upload was 5.20 Mbps.

Although these speeds are not great, that is the performance I usually get with the router and service provider I have. Based on my results, this works as designed. Below is a list of what comes in the package and the PROS and CONS.

The package includes two Netgear Powerline 1200 Outlets each with an extra outlet and one Gigabit Ethernet port, two 6.5 foot Ethernet cables, and a quick start guide. For the initial installation of these units, both outlets have to be used because one Powerline must be plugged into an outlet near the router so that the Ethernet cable from the Powerline can plug into the router. The other Powerline can be plugged into an outlet anywhere else in the home. The other Ethernet cable is then plugged into this unit on one end and an Ethernet-enabled device such as a laptop, SmartTV, etc. on the other. If additional Powerlines are purchased then both units can be used for two additional wired connections.

PROS
- The LEDs on the Powerline enable the user to diagnose if there's power, Ethernet connectivity, or the ability to "Pick A Plug" (a.k.a. electrical outlet) with the strongest performance.

- There's an extra outlet on each Powerline. This unit covers the second outlet if it's plugged into the top outlet of a two-outlet receptacle. However, I do not see that as a problem for two reasons. First, there's an extra outlet on the unit. Therefore, I am still getting the ability to plug in two items like I would have had I not been using the Powerline. (In this case the Powerline is one item and a light is another.) If I want to turn my outlet into a three outlet receptacle, then all I have to do is plug it into the lower outlet. This would allow me, for instance, to plug in a lamp in the top receptacle, the Powerline in the bottom receptacle, and another item into the extra outlet on the Powerline.

- According to the manual, the network can be secured by pressing the security button for two seconds and then pressing the security button on one of the other adapters in the existing network. If additional adapters are added throughout the house when security is already enabled, then ALL the adapters should be factory reset. To re-enable security, all that has to be done is press the security button for two seconds on one adapter and then select any ONE other adapter (it's not necessary to do all adapters) and press that security button for two seconds. Both security buttons have to be pressed within two minutes time.

- There's a 1 year warranty plus 90 days basic customer support.

CONS

- I see none at this time.

I will write Netgear to find out what is meant by security with these security buttons. Up to 16 adapters can be installed in a home. I know if I were to install another set of these, I would actually be able to use both Powerlines for extra wired connections, thereby increasing my wired connections to three from one. It's only for the first installation that the extra Powerline is lost because that is used to connect to the router.

In summary, I feel this Netgear works as designed with no discernible difference in speed over a wired connection whether I was plugged directly into the router or the Powerline. Installation was simple and turning any one of my electrical outlets into a wired connection was practically instantaneous.

UPDATE April 27, 2015 - I contacted Netgear for an explanation of why there's a security feature on these adapters and exactly what that means to me. Below is Oleg Fishel's (of customer support) response which I slightly paraphrased.

The security refers to encryption between each of the Powerline adapters on my network. A random key is generated and shared among the adapters when the security setup button is used. All traffic is then encrypted using the highly secure 128 bit AES encryption protocol that prevents any unauthorized person from accessing the communication on my network. The reason enabling this security is recommended is to prevent someone from coming into my home with another Powerline adapter and connecting directly into my network to get information or for free Internet access. Although this scenario might be rare, this may be a concern with apartment buildings and offices where electrical circuits might be shared and in the case of homes that have outdoor electrical sockets. In summary, it is best to enable security. It is especially important when the Powerline is on a shared electrical circuit where someone can come along and plug one of these adapters in and piggyback off the network.

In regard to another question I had regarding the use and installation of 16 adapters all at once, he said "The HomePlug standard (HPAV2) used by the PL1200 supports up to 16 adapters on the network working together simultaneously. So if you purchased 7 kits (14 units) in addition to the original kit, you could have a 16 node network."

I have worked with a lot of different sets of headphones and ear buds and have gotten a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Specifically with ear buds I pay attention to the fit as well as the sound, which are two areas where many manufacturers get it wrong. Anker did a good job with these though there is a soft spot in the sound profile.

I used these with an iPhone 7, and initial pairing was very quick and painless. The buds found each other (another issue I have seen with other sets on occasion), and these paired without much fanfare or issue at all. That’s really all you could ask.

These fit like a dream. The package contains several silicone plugs of different sizes so you can get just the right fit for yourself, but I found that the ones already on the buds were actually a perfect fit. I popped these in, gave them a turn to lock them in place and they sealed perfectly. I am especially happy with how well these fit in my ears and actually stay there.

The sound isolation is on par with what you’d expect. When not powered on and streaming music they are the equivalent to a cheap set of ear plugs – enough to block out some sound but not completely silence the world.

The sound quality is very good but the sound profile could use a tweak. The bass is strong but not overdriven to the point of causing headaches. There is a tendency to overdrive the bass, so having good bass that’s not overpowering is nice. The highs are bright and clear too. The midrange is another matter and feels weak (though not non-existent). Music played through these buds lacks the warmth and fullness that the midrange brings to the table (and if it was overdriven everything would sound like it is coming through a tunnel). I would rather have under-driven midrange than overdriven, but it’s still soft enough to be noticeable.

They case in which these buds are stored also serves as the charger. What is interesting about these is how the case itself is charged. Instead of MicroUSB, this case uses a Type C connector which is not unwelcome but up to this point is unusual for this kind of device. There is a cable in the box so there’s no issue.

These are good ear buds and they have some nice features. They fit superbly and they pair to a source without problems. The sound profile is imperfect, though not terribly so, which is the only complaint I have with them.

Slept two nights with these headphones in their stock configuration and decided I could create something far superior.
For several years I’ve owned and extensively used a pair of the original wired SleepPhones. They are extremely comfortable. The drivers are only 2-3mm thick and sandwiched between two layers of felt. The fleece headband stayed in place without feeling constrictive. It was also easy to wash - open the hook and loop closure on the back, pulled out the speakers and wires, wash, dry, re-install.
By contrast, MusiCozy uses thicker drivers (granted, the frequency response is better than the SleepPhone drivers) then adds a rubber cover, then covers that with a thin jersey fabric. The headband was painfully tight, and I don’t have a big head (22.5”). After the first night, I stretched the headband over a small throw pillow for a day and that helped a bit. But the second night, the thick drivers hurt my ears so bad I took the whole thing off. I mostly sleep on my side and stomach. It’s also tricky to charge because the port is only accessible if you line up the slit in the jersey fabric just right. Some simple product testing would have identified these issues. But for $20, I couldn’t be happier….. why?
SleepPhoness wants $100 for their bluetooth units. I’m sure they are top-notch but I didn’t want to spend that much. Here’s my solutions: The entire MuziCozy headband was disassembled….all two components. The bluetooth receiver / battery compartment and speakers come out easily enough. The fake ‘control panel’ on the front isn’t needed. The speakers have a rubber cover that is not needed. Once that is removed, the speakers are only 3-4mm thick, which is good. I disassembled the wired SleepPhones as well. The felt driver covers were re-used with the MuziCozy drivers, then the whole thing was re-installed into the SleepPhone headband.
This is the best setup - the headband is comfortable, I can still use it to cover my eyes, the sound quality is improved, and the MuziCozy charge port is easier to access thanks to the large velcro opening on the back of the headband.
My girlfriend, by contrast, likes absolute silence while sleeping so she uses the MuziCozy headband to make sure her earplugs don’t fall out and to cover her eyes.
So the entire unit has gone to good use, just not in the way it was delivered. I’m happy with the results but the original product need some redesign.

I bought a Garmin 60CSx GPS receiver as a replacement for a Garmin eTrex Legend for the purpose of geocaching. My eTrex Legend has served me well (and continues to do so) but I wanted a GPSr with more functionality, better operation under heavy cover and expanded map coverage for hiking and road navigation. Researching GPSrs led me to this unit, and I have been very pleased with it. There are a couple of minor negatives that I have found, but these can probably be overlooked.

I am very pleased with the appearance of the screen when the unit is powered on. The display is bright and colorful, and easy to read in the light. This is true of the daytime display. The night display is not as pleasant, with a hard-to-see color scheme. Backlighting the night scheme makes it a lot easier to read but it is still less than ideal.

The unit's software is very intuitive, a menu- and icon-driven interface giving access to all of the features. I have found little need for the user manual since I fist started working with this device, as everything is clear and easy to find. Buttons on the unit make it easy to find the menus and to navigate without too much hassle.

The base map is nothing special but it is adequate for basic navigation. We have used it to follow our path down the interstate. It shows the major roads and also any waypoints that are close by.

The best feature of this unit, in my opinion, is its ability to navigate under heavy canopy. With my eTrex Legend there were times when my unit would simply not be able to get a lock. The 60CSx has yet to lose signal, even inside my living room. The accuracy does drop when there is sufficient cover but the important thing is that it doesn't drop completely.

One thing troubles me a bit about the 60CSx. The accuracy rarely gets any better than 10-12 feet, whereas my eTrex Legend - a unit costing a third as much - routinely can get down to 6 feet. I do not understand why this is the case. I would choose ability to hold a signal over pinpoint accuracy every time, but why can't I have both?

The 60CSx has a Micro-SD card inside and the unit will take a card up to 2GB inside. That's enough room for a whole US street map. This is a nice thing to have available, as it means not having to decide what section of map to load. Load the whole map and be on your way.

The waypoint management functions are acceptable for my needs, which up to this point has meant managing geocaching waypoints. I like being able to mark a point as "found" and then being asked if I want to go to the next closest point. I have noticed, though, that if I am navigating to a point and leave the navigation menus, the point is marked as found anyway. It would be nice to have the ability to specify "not found" without having to go through the menus to locate the point again, just to change the status.

The Garmin 60CSx is a very nice handheld GPS that will serve you well. It is not perfect, but for general use it is plenty close enough.

Pros:
-It’s pretty.
-It’s rugged.
-It feels like it has some drop protection.
-The weight means it doesn’t tip easily.
-The magnet is very strong, and the outer case is sturdy. My last iPad Pro died when it got bent, and this feels like better protection.
-The inner section separates, which offers some heat release.

Cons:
-This is extremely heavy. I’m not sure it could be heavier unless they made it out of lead.
-You cannot charge an Apple Pencil if the pencil is in a sleeve because they cut a slot that fits the pencil exactly with no margin.
-It’s a strong magnet so don’t keep hotel cards etc, near it. It's definitely not safe or OK for those with pacemakers etc.
-The back covers the iPad completely, trapping some heat near the machine for those who run it hard.

It's a great case but I can’t overlook the weight. It can be a plus in that you are unlikely to forget your ipad is there and treat it carelessly, but it also makes carrying it around a literal pain in the shoulder. If you don’t want to feel like you are lugging around a laptop, I would look for a different case. If you are worried about it being bent when you forget it's in your bag or if it’s going to be mostly at home and a magnet on the back appeals to you for things like sticking it to the fridge when referencing recipes, then this may be a good fit.

Personally, I would rather buy a separate stand for when I need it than carry around something this heavy even if it works well.

I have been able to bend them back now to where they aren't so springy and will stay down better but if it's windy, those caps keep blowing in front of the lenses. Tired of cramped cases? Pain in the butt to get nice cable run cases? Having to remove a hard-drive to get a graphics card out? Having to remove a graphics card to take out a HD? Tired of black cases?

I love this case. But it's bigger than it looks in the picture and it's wider than it looks here. Which was not a problem because I checked the size before ordering.

So whats to love about this case. I'm going to try to skip what is obviuos unless it's something I really like about the case.

It's not black
It's quiet even with the stock fans. It wouldn't take much work to make this REALLY quiet.
The audio and USB panels are on the top.
All the 'guts' are on the bottom of the case and laid out in a way that makes it very easy to cable everything together compared to mid/mini tower cases
The rear panel (for all the ports) sits flush on the back of the computer and the computer back is flat. It makes it much easier to see the ports when you bend over the top of the case. Each port has a colored ring around it the same color of the colors of the plug making it very easy to see where what plugs in.
The HDD fit great without a screw in sight and mount in a what that makes connecting them really easy. They are also rubber mounted to help quiet the HDD.
All the screws are in little baggies with a sticker saying what they are for.
The CD/DVD drive mount has to two sets of holes for mounting. One set of hoses is in set positions, and for me they put my drive just about right with the front of the case. But there are also longer slots for the mounting screws so you can slide the drive back and forth to get it to sit exactly where you want your CD/DVD drive fit in the front of the case.
There is room for cabling to run next to the motherboard sides keeping cables away from the top of the motherboard. There is a lot of room under the top of the case (if you don't use extra fans there) to coil up extra wire/cables. If you wanted you could do a very clean cable installation.
It's VERY easy to plug in the ATX power connector and more important easy to take off (which was a real frustration on my old case)
There is a lot of room in general to work in this case for a micro ATX case. You can take the top off and both sides to work inside the case.
The thumb screws holding the sides on are nice and large and both sides come of easily.
This is the first case I have had that has dedicated brackets for 2.5" SSDs. The brackets have rubber grommets you attach to the sides of the SSD. That then slide into grooves holding the drive loosely by the rubber grommets. Seems overkill for a SSD drive that has no moving parts but it works.

A few random thoughts

The top can be a little finicky to get off. But on the good side it fits well when it's in place. Sits nice and flat etc.
The plastic slide that latches the top in place is a very simple plastic latch and can pop out pretty easily. ( I don't know where/when I accidentally popped off but when I went to pickup the top the latch was on the floor) But it does what it is supposed to do and has not come off in normal use.

The bracket to hold the expansion cards in place is a clever design (no screws) but takes two hands to close and you have to wiggle the cards/brackets around a bit to get to get the holding mechanism closed again.

A solid 5 stars from me

Whoever designed this camera and its power source should find another line of work! Why? Here’s my list of reasons to perhaps pass on this camera, or at minimum, get a screw-in physical mount and extra batteries

1) It ships with a very strong magnetic mount that makes it easy prey for anyone wanting a free camera, or just wanting to vandalize something. UNFORTUNATELY, this is the default mounting that ships with it. Yes, Simplisafe does sell an attachable mount (screwed in), yet at this price point a physical, screw-in mount should be the default.
2) Reviews about great battery life—how long a charge lasted are not consistent with my experience. The battery runs down in three to four days, no matter how much or little sensitivity you set for triggering video. In my installation, this means running up and down a ladder a lot. The more traffic in an area, the faster the battery drains.
3) A compatible solar panel charger did not provide sufficient trickle charge to maintain battery function. Frankly, while this facilitates a very easy install, the constant battery charging is a royal pain! It would be great if the solar option worked, as the cameras have sunlight most of the daylight hours.

Best things are:
1) Slam-dunk easy install.
2) Clear videos.
3) Connects easily to the base station (brilliantly designed).

Final notes:
I have a complete Simplisafe system and I love it. The ease of the total install, the base station’s connection to cellular (a standard feature) is flawless, and better is it doesn’t cost anything extra. As for monitoring 24/7, it’s less than $30 a month. The speed of response to an alarm was under 60 seconds when last I accidentally set it off. That’s perfect!

My 3-star REVIEW is FOR THE CAMERA ONLY, and is strictly due to the default mounting system, and the lack of battery life. Recommend if you’re buying one, you get an extra battery or two and a better camera mount.

I purchased my HP m9080n tower from Fry's in November 2007, and have used it for business purposes. Initially, it performed spectacularly. Great speed, handled many programs running simultaneously, little or no noise from the tower. NOTE: That's the ONLY reason I've given this machine 2 stars, rather than 0 or 1 star. When it's functioning correctly, it's very good. But, as you'll see below, I cannot rely on it--so what's the point in having it?

In February 2008, the problems began. The computer had had about 2 months of use by then. I'd do a cold boot (turned it on), and when the welcome screen appeared--if it did--there was no way for me to log in. The icons for each user account appeared but didn't respond, and they didn't open a space for me to enter my password.

I tried many possible solutions before taking it back to Fry's, including reinstalling Vista 4 times, using PC Doctor to analyze any hardware problems (it found none). Had to start it in Safe Mode to do these tests, or used F11 to get into system restore mode. Bottom line is that nothing fixed the problem, despite my reformatting the hard drive, reinstalling Vista, and not installing anything else on the machine. Even with that configuration, it still had nonresponsive icons and no login window on booting up.

Finally took it to Fry's, because it was under warranty. They replaced the motherboard at no charge. When I brought the PC back to my office, it was fine for a couple of weeks, and then I started seeing the same symptoms as before: no window to log in, and nonresponsiveness to system restoration.

Took it back to Fry's, asked them to fix it AGAIN. This time they charged me nearly $200 to reinstall Vista, which I had already done mutliple times. Brought it back to the office, and it functioned well for about 2 weeks.

Yesterday, the SAME PROBLEM STARTED AGAIN: when I turned the machine on, I got no login screen, and the user account icons were nonresponsive. But get this--I was so disgusted that I just let the thing sit overnight, with the nonfunctional login screen still there. When I got into the office the next morning, clicked on the icon for my administrator's account, lo and behold--the login window was normal. I was able to log in as usual, in other words. And I hadn't touched the computer since it booted up with no login window the night before.

If anyone has suggestions as to what I can do about this, I'm all ears. I can't tell you how disgusted I am with HP AND Frys'. The computer is still under warranty, but I've read other reviews here that give me no hope that HP will resolve the situation to my satisfaction. In the meantime, I've sunk $2,000 into an unreliable machine that no one seems to know how to fix. Right now, it's more useful as a freaking doorstop.

In all fairness, we have several other HP desktops and notebook computers in my office. In the 3+ years we've had them (running XP or Vista Ultimate), we have had no problems with them. I don't know if this problem is specific to the m9080n or not.

It says it fits a Nikon D800, but when mounted, the D800 is too tall, barely fitting under the overhead grip arm.

The overhead arm does not extend forward enough to allow the camera to balance, even with the camera mounted all the way to the rear of the baseplate. Thus, even when I'm holding just the front two inches under the hot shoe mount, the camera when mounted with a heavy zoom lens like the 24-70 f/2.8, tilts down. A lighter, shorter lens works better, but you still cannot hold the unit by the foam grip handle without your knuckles scraping the camera's hot shoe mount.

The entire device is of molded ABS plastic and is somewhat flexible in a "springy" way. It appears strong, but remember, your multi-thousand dollar investment is hanging by that little joint in the back of the base plate. If it breaks, it's curtains. You might want to have a safety lanyard attached to a neck strap lug that attaches to your wrist, just in case.

The sleds on the bottom are nice. When you put it down, it's stable, although I had to re-superglue one of the padded inserts on one of the sled rails.

The camera mounting screw is well designed and easy to use, but for some reason, is too long. The threads bottomed out in my camera and would not hold the camera tight. I had to remove the thumb screw and add a washer on the underside of the base effectively shortening the threads. I could have ground off 1/16" or so, too. Not a big deal, but out of the box it didn't work.

One thing's for sure: you need a strong arm to hold this for any amount of time if you have a heavy lens attached. If you are working with a lightweight SLR and a lightweight lens, it's much easier. And seeing the viewfinder is a real problem. And forget about focusing. If you mount a remote electronic viewfinder on the upper hot shoe, it's much easier to see what you're shooting, but now you've added even more weight and your arm will die. (True steadicams went with vests and spring-assisted arms for this reason years ago.)

Overall, the sled is a simple, inexpensive method to hold a camera from above and does smooth out motion well. It's a worthy gizmo to have in your bag.

UPDATE: I attached my Canon HFS-100 HD camcorder to this sled and have never taken it off. It is absolutely the best accessory ever! Perfectly balanced. The overhead handle allows excellent control and fabulous low angle positioning when capturing kids or animals on the floor. The camera's flip-out viewfinder is the key, something the D800 sorely lacks.

I received these as a free review sample. I want to point out that these are hard-wired only. They use a 3.5mm connector and ARE NOT bluetooth. If you want phones for critical listening and transcribing music (or listening to a raw feed before mixdown) these are perfect. Bluetooth always entails some loss of sound quality, but these, and other direct connect phones, do not.

They are neutral enough to pass for high end in-ear monitors (IEMs), but there is a little bias on the low end. As long as you take that into account you can mentally compensate when listening to raw feeds.

One of the things that I found impressive is I could not detect any bias towards the mid range frequencies, nor do the high end frequencies sound compressed. For me this means that I can listen to acoustic jazz and hear the music as originally recorded. This is especially important for a lot of mid 1950s recordings before engineers started playing games with the mix. For these phones I sampled tracks from [[ASIN:B00CJYWUM6 At the Showboat / See What I Mean? / Settlin' In]] and [[ASIN:B000QQV5FM Dorothy Donegan Live]], and listened to the entire two hours and forty-eight minutes of Erroll Garner's [[ASIN:B00ZJ5QXDO The Complete Concert By The Sea]]. That test proved that these phones are absolutely superb for folks for love music.

While this is claimed to be for Android, I tested it on an iPad Air 2 and a ThinkPad T61 - it worked beautifully on both. In fact, on the ThinkPad I was playing from CD instead of an MP3 file and the sound quality was better than a direct connect from my Note 4 phone.

A few notes about the physical characteristics and features: I tested out the control block using my Note 4 phone and found it to be less than intuitive. I prefer controlling functions using those integrated in my Note 4 (including EQ.) I love the tangle free cord, and the comfort of the phones though. Everything about the construction and sound are of the highest quality.

Bottom line: if you are fanatical about sound quality these phones are ones that I highly recommend. I own other IEMs that cost twice as much that are close to these. Granted the expensive ones have completely neutral low frequency response, but if you are not mixing down these are as good in the overall scheme of things.

This is a standard portable external drive with a USB interface. It's small, easy to handle, and works well. Most external drives use the USB 2.0 interface. This has the newer, and much faster, USB 3.0 interface. (But it works just fine when connected to a computer that has USB 2.0. The speed in that case would be the slower USB 2.0 speed.)

USB 3.0 uses a different connector on the drive, so you need to use the USB 3.0 cable that comes with the drive. A standard USB 2.0 cable won't work because it has a different connector on the drive side. On the computer side, it's a standard USB plug, so it fits both USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 jacks on the computer.

I use this to move many GB's of data from my PC to my Mac laptop. The PC has USB 3.0, so it's blazing fast to move data from the PC to the external drive. My Mac laptop has USB 2.0, so it takes longer to move the data from the drive to the Mac. But it works. Drive capacities are now so large that USB 3.0 is a huge advantage. It takes quite a bit of time to move 1 TB of data at USB 2.0 speed.

The main thing about this radio that I really DO NOT like is that it has a permanent battery that must be charged via a USB cable. The cable must be connected to a computer or to a special adapter that can be plugged into any regular household outlet in order to charge it. The fact that the battery can only be charged and not easily replaced as in AA batteries to me, defeats the whole purpose of having such a radio. I consider the ability to listen to shortwave from an emergency aspect, such as if the power grid went down or for some other catastrophic reason. It should work for a while but when the battery dies, so does your ability to get news and information about your local area as well as other parts of the world, unless you have a way to charge it. And if the battery totally dies (I let mine completely expire), you will lose all of your settings including time and date.

I also don't have any use for the recording function, iPod player, and e-reader. They are nice extras but not necessary for a shortwave radio. Most people probably buy shortwave radios for their ability to pick up shortwave radio signals from around the world and not for it's recording function. If you should need it in the event of an emergency of some sort, will you be wasting it's precious battery energy listening to your iPod? And no one takes a radio like this to a pool anymore....they use their iPod, iPhone or whatever for all of their listening needs. Personally, I consider these types of radios to be stored away and used when things look ominous outside or other unfortunate global events are happening.

It's certainly better than no radio, but it's not very practical and there are better ones out there. It looks nice, has a decent overall sound quality for a small radio, is a easy size to deal with and comes with a black pouch to carry it in, but good looks can only get you so far. It's what's inside that counts. Also, for what it's worth, the black tuning knob on my radio fell off. Have now completed the installation and hookup of this antenna. The first test was to listen to Mixed Bag, 90.7 FM which was always full of static. Now this station comes in crystal clear, loud, and strong. Note that I decided to mount this antenna on the side of my house, just beneath the peak of my low roof facing the back yard. I had a quantity of twin 300 ohm cable which I wanted to use. Using a 300ohm/75ohm converter, I simply attached the end of the cable to the two 300ohm screws, protecting the connection with electrical tape. I measured and fabricated a wood mounting plate (see photo) and then screwed the mast bracket to it from the back. The wooden support board was then lag screwed, in turn, to the outside of my house just below the peak using 5" long screws. I then installed the antenna and mast, after reversing it. It now extends upwards vertically yet does not interfere with the roof line. The versatility of the mast permitted me to accomplish that.

(This review is preliminary. I assembled the antenna but am not yet ready to install it.
Assembly tips:

- Both curved antenna segments are secured to the antenna cross bar with the supplied hardware.
- The ends of one (bottom) segment are held in place with two phillips head screws. First, remove the curved metal clamp. line up the holes in the segment and, maintaining hand pressure on each segment end to ensure that it is seated firmly into it's curved metal seat, insert each screw and secure. Do not over tighten these fasteners. This is the "bottom" of the antenna, opposite the 75 ohm connector side. Attach one leg of the segment at a time.
- The ends of the second (top) segment are held in place with two hex head nuts. You will note that each nut is topped with a rubber 'O' ring. This is used to keep the nuts from threading off until assembly. Do not attempt to re-use these as they are not spacers or washers.
- Again, seat the ends of the antenna segment firmly in place, aligning the holes over the studs. Holding down the segment, install each nut. Do not over tighten these nuts.
- The closed loop ends of each antenna segment may now be gently guided in front of the black plastic locking clips. Once the looped ends are in position, firmly, yet carefully snap them into place. The circular antenna shape has now been completed. If assembled patiently and slowly, damage should not occur to the antenna.)

I have had the opportunity to review many headsets and headphones over the years and without question the recent technological advancements have aided this area by leaps and bounds.

I can not recommend buying Bluetooth 5.2 enough over previous technologies if your devices support it. Nearly all devices that are Bluetooth 5.2 capable, including this one, will be backwards compatible with earlier technologies as well.

Battery life is outstanding with these headsets lasting a solid 5 hours each in all of my tests. It is easily charged using the included charging case which will allow the earbuds to be recharged several times from its one full charge. Since the earbuds can be used together for stereo sound or individually you can potentially double play time by using one at a time.

This unique charging case is powered via an included super fast standard USB to USB Type C cable. This case will allow the headsets to be recharged even when you don’t have access to electricity.

After receiving, I made sure the case was fully charged then confirmed each earbud had a full charge. After verifying full power within each earbud I followed the simple pairing instructions and had no problems whatsoever. Once the earbuds are removed from the case they first pair with each other then you simply pair with your Bluetooth device.

The design of these headset makes it so it fits securely in your ear and is relatively comfortable. As someone who has used many of these units, this design is not the most comfortable as the weight is all on the ear canal. I’ve found headsets that are worn only supported by the ear canal can end up being painful when used for extended periods.

[[VIDEOID:1190b451faf9653857f6725f71e2a33c]] THE GOOD:
--------------
* This is the real deal! Every component is high quality, and the NVR unit is externally and internally immaculate. Why do I have to even say this? Because I've tried other NVR systems. I have encountered NVRs with flimsy dented cases, and messy soldering jobs on the motherboard.
* 4TB is pre-installed.
* You get 8 POE cameras! A mistake I made as a newbie was thinking all I have to do is get POE switches, then I would be able to get rid of power adapters for any camera. That is incorrect! A camera has to be designated as a POE camera in order to use POE switches and POE NVRs.
* You get eight 65 ft ethernet cable. If you can run those cables back to the NVR, which has 8 ports in the back, then you won't need to hook up any intermediary POE switches. I plan to use at most four cameras, so If I need to hook up a POE switch, the four extra cables will come in handy. However, more on this issue later.
* Included are also outdoor plugs to protect your wire connections.
* PLUG & PLAY... As long as you run the ethernet cable back to the Ethernet ports of the NVR, it is plug and play. If for any reason, you need to find the IP in your service provider's router admin, look for HEROSPEED DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY. That's the name it shows up under.
* Unlike most security cameras, the live feed of this NVR system has no delay, it's real time, or pretty close to it.
* If you're using a KVM switch at your computer, so you can switch back and forth between different sources... I said in my video that once I get a USB cable to link up the KVM switch with the NVR, then I should be able to use my PC's mouse and keyboard, which are connected to the KVM switch. Well, since then I've learned that what I said is half true. I'll be able to use the mouse, but not the keyboard. The NVR doesn't respond to any keyboards no matter if it's through the KVM switch, or directly connected to the NVR. It only uses the onscreen pop-up. You will need to use the mouse to select the letters and numbers from the virtual keyboard.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Like I said above, it's plug and play as long as you connect each camera directly back to the NVR ports. It goes without saying, but the NVR also needs to be connected to your router or nearby switch to be online. I'm running into issues testing POE switches. If the camera is not directly connected to the back of the NVR, the system cannot find it. There are 16 channels available in the NVR, and only 8 ports in the back, so obviously, this should be compatible with POE switches. But so far, I can't get it to work. I've asked for help from OSI, so we'll see...
* No guidance or instructions on how to install the actual cameras. For a moment, I was SMH. I was looking for the bases. I thought my package was missing them. But I realized the bases were already threaded onto the cameras. For each camera, you need to unthread the base, drill the base onto the ceiling of your choice location, then thread the main camera body back on it.
* Another nitpick is that installing under a ceiling will not always be ideal, or possible. It would have been great if they had included some adapters so that we can install them onto walls like bullet cameras.

Despite the little nitpicks, I still rate this 4-Stars right now. Might bump it up to 5-Stars if we can get the POE switches sorted out. I'm a newbie, so I know this might be easy for experienced networkers. The manual is a bit lacking. There were no discussions on how to install the cameras, and it assumes you'll be directly connecting all cameras back to the NVR, so it doesn't discuss the use of POE switches at all.

I want to give this 3.5 stars- 3 is too low and 4 seems too high, but I'll round up for now. I have mixed things to say about this camera. It isn't going to take stellar photos. They are either going to have a lot of motion blur or if you raise the shutter speed (sports mode) you're going to get substantial noise. The videos side is even worse. A modern cell phone or point-and-shoot is going to snap better photos and videos. BUT... you can take this to a water park and not care what happens to it, which is exactly what we did.
I'm including three examples shots here that I wouldn't have gotten without this camera (excuse the smiley face for privacy). One are kids about to go down a water slide, where I as the photographer am being rained on by nearby sprinklers. Then there's a slightly more epic shot of the giant bucket atop the slides crashing water down on me. This shot froze the droplets of water right before thoroughly drenching the photographer (me) a split second later. The last is from some of our underwater pool shots. These are all cases in which I would NOT have been comfortable using my real cameras or even cell phones- as waterproof as they claim some flagship phones are now, I wouldn't trust them to this. In my experience, even waterproof phones have trouble operating under water (the touch screen doesn't work properly), and we have ruined the charging port of another at a pool previously. But this is totally sealed and has real buttons that work just as well under water as above. For all those reasons, I actually LIKE this camera. It takes photos I literally would NOT have gotten otherwise.
Also, as a bit of personal experience, after going down a water slide and trying to video it, I actually dropped the camera into the pool at the bottom. I was able to run in and chase and grab it, and the entire time I was thinking I'm SO GLAD this isn't my phone!
I'm actually printing some of the photos as I write this and although they appear grainy on my screen, on 4x6 photo paper they look perfectly acceptable.
So why 3.5 stars? Well, the user interface is terrible. More than once I had to turn it off and restart to get back to photo taking because I couldn't figure out how to get out of the mode I was in. Also, it claims to have a 21megapixel mode, but I'm pretty sure it is just upscaling a smaller resolution. The noise at 21mp seems soft, like it took a lower resolution image and then scaled it UP to 21 mp. The 12 megapixels mode seemed much more true-to-pixel size, so that seems like a bit of false advertising. Then there's the video mode- keep it at 720 if you want any kind of normal playable frame rates. It also looks like less-than-HD that has been scaled up to fit, but at least it works at all. At 1080 HD, it was doing a variable frame rate thing that often slowed to a slide show and wasn't playable on my phone or laptop. I'm only able to play it back from the camera, which I wish I had known before I chose it for some things I wanted to remember.
Outside of those caveats, it is good for the specific use as a camera you can afford to get wet.

TLDR: Dropped my GPU temps from 75c to 50c under full load. Reduced fan noise considerably since I went from 5 case fans at 100% to 3 at 30-50% most of the time. LED's are ok. If you want to run cooler temps and less noise, get this!
UPDATE: after a month of use everything was still great. I did make a bad mistake that ended my card. I didn't want to take the cooler off to properly attach the back plate so I was just sitting on top of the card. All was well until I stupidly tried to move a fan from one side on my CPU cooling tower to the other, while my comp was on..... I KNOW, I KNOW, I"m an idiot. I dropped the fan which bounced around my mobo and slammed into the top of my card. Shorting everything out. GPU is toast, rest of system is questionable. Be smarter than me, DONT TAKE SHORT CUTS. TURN OFF YOUR PC WHEN WORKING ON IT AND PROPERLY ATTACH EVERYTHING! Still hyped on the this cooler. Aiming to still use it on my new card IF I can ever get one without taking a second mortgage.

I used this on a XFX RX 580 GTS 8GB Black edition. In a M-atx case, the stock cooler fans would run full RPM just to keep it at 75-80C under load. Add in 5 case fans (@full RPM) to keep the air flow fresh and I had an annoyingly loud heater just a few feet from my chair. Stumbled upon this in a random search and after reading a few other reviews I decided to order it and see how it goes.

Install was straight forward enough. If you can reapply thermal paste, you can install this cooler. Placing the heat sinks on the VRAM and VRM is time consuming but unlike others I found the supplied thermal sticky pads to be fine after applying moderate force for about 10 secs. Only issue I had was clearance on one of the VRAMs as it sat close to the plate and could only be half covered by a heatsink. Getting the placement on that one took slightly longer but by using a few dry test fits I was able to get it placed perfectly.

The MOSs are on the left on this GPU so I was hesitant but after a week of using it I haven't seen any issues with VRM not properly cooling. Board doesn't support junction temp measuring so I have no hard data on if they are hotter or not, but I do feel airflow around them and performance is still great.

The rad and fan were easy enough to install. In a M-atx case it is tight. It was a squeeze and took a few tries to properly get everything where I wanted but once in I have no complaints. I did hear "coil whine" from the pump once, but quickly sorted out that some pressure was being applied to one of the tubes right near the pump, once I shifted it a little, the whine stopped and never returned.

The LEDS are ok. The controller is adequate. The LED along the side of the GPU mount is a nice touch, really adds a higher end feel to the finished product. Obviously this isn't a high end ARGB controller but its got more than enough setting to make it fit into your overall lighting needs. Personally I just wanted some plain old solid white. I do find the white to be slightly bluish in the fans but I chalk that up to ARGB vs the RGB LED case fans I have installed.

Wiring was tedious but it included everything I needed. Other than taking my time to cable manage and tuck it all away out of sight, it was straight forward enough to wire up. Just double check they all get plugged in! I missed the pump power and on my first start up saw the temps just go up and up and got worried I installed it wrong. Luckily I thought to check the cables right before taking it apart and found the problem.

I did add/change a few things,
-Firstly I used Thermal Grizzlys kryonaut paste instead of the supplied paste.
-I also bought a 4-Pin PWM splitter adapter that allowed me to use the GPUs native fan plug to power the rad and VRAM fans. I can't recommend this enough! Using Afterburner to control the fan speeds really is awesome and allows for easy fine tuning for noise and temps needs.
-I did have to cut some of the metal shroud for the front of the GPU back plate. I didnt want to run no plate on top of the board and obviously it wasn't designed to have water tubes go through it. It was simple and easy to cut but is a permeant mod to make it look better. You can see in the attached pics, some are with the plate on and some with it off.

Speaking of which temps are mind blowing! It idles at 28c (ambient is about 22c) with fans set to 3%. in other words, silent! Under my normal full gaming load it chills at 50c with fans at 50%. Slightly louder but still much quieter than the stock blower! If I turn the fans to 100% it will chill at like 35-37c while full 1080p gaming. I've even pushed the OC a bit, went from 1425 Core clock to 1500, and Mem clock from 2000 to 2250. No way the stock coolers would have let that happen smoothly.

I waited a week or so to write this review just to make sure I was still happy. And I am! I'll update this review with any long term issues or problems so if there is no update, expect that its still just plugging along being super chill.

These are around the same price as all the junky Chinese wireless earbud brands on Amazon but sound much better, are much more reliable, and are made by a company with good customer service that stands behind their products.

Ankers has several wireless earbuds with the cords that go behind the neck but only these, the spirit, the spirit pro, and the spirit x are worth considering for purchase. Their other earbuds are older models that cost just as much but have less features and weaker specs.

The bass on these is weak but I use these mostly for working out and for that it is fine.

I already have a pair of Apple EarPods but I wanted another wireless pair of headphones as well so I could switch back and forth while the other pair was charging.

These do not work with Apples w1 chip Bluetooth protocol, only apple and beats headphones work with that standard right now so those wireless headphones brands will sound better than anything other wireless headphones will with Apple products.

They also do not have aptx, which is the best sounding Bluetooth standard for anything other than Apple.

Ankers spirit pro headphones do support the aptx standard and supposedly have better bass than these so those are that models advantages.

However the spirit pro cost twice as much as these and only supports Bluetooth protocol 4.1 while these headphones support Bluetooth protocol 5.0.

Why is that important? Because the 5.0 protocol is the new “low energy” Bluetooth standard. Meaning that if you have both a device and headphones that support it you will get much more play time out of the same size battery.

Ankers other most recent model of earbuds, the spirit x headphones, have the same specs as these headphones in terms of the protocols they support but have a different form factor, obviously, and have 10mm drivers while these have 6mm. They also have a little more battery life.

I think I might buy the spirit x headphones as well in order to have a backup and to compare their sound.

As an Apple user the spirit pro headphones are just not worth the extra cost for me since I will never use the aptx protocol and they do not even support the Bluetooth 5.0 protocol.
If they were Bluetooth 5.0 compatible I might consider spending the extra 25 bucks in order to get that extra bass.

While these don’t sound spectacular they will get great battery life when I use them with devices that support 5.0 Bluetooth and they are very affordable.

I have a sleeve for my tablet that works out very well for me. It provides some protection for the screen and provides some limited protection against drops and bumps. This is the first sleeve I have used for a laptop and so far I like it. It is appreciably cheaper than a laptop bag or backpack, but it also has less room for accessories.

The sleeve I have is the 15.6” version and it fits my laptop almost perfectly. There is a small amount of wiggle room in the sleeve so that the laptop can slide a little from side to side and it’s just enough to make slipping the laptop in and taking it back out much easier. There is sufficient padding around the edges to make this sleeve useful for bumps and bangs but it will not protect the laptop within from hard drops on the edge.

The outer material is a tight woolen weave and it does a good job of repelling water (though it is not completely waterproof). When splashed with water, the majority of the water beads up and rolls off, and of what remains most can be simply brushed off. The end result is a very slightly damp surface, nowhere near enough to get the laptop inside even slightly wet. So, when toting the sleeve outside it will effectively protect the laptop inside from rain.

There are two pockets inside this sleeve. One is lined in a fleece-like soft material that gently cushions the laptop and allows it to slide in and out more easily. The other pocket is zippered and it is lined in vinyl; it is a good place to put papers, smaller accessories like a travel mouse and other small items. This pocket is not big enough to handle a lot of extras like a full laptop bag.

I inspected the sleeve closely and I have not been able to find any problems in the way it is made. There are no loose threads, stitching is tight and straight and there are not crooked material patches. The zipper works smoothly and so far does not catch on the material of the sleeve. Overall I am pleased with the materials and assembly.

This is a very nice laptop sleeve and I am pleased with it. It does a good job of providing some protection to the laptop is holds, it is water repellant and it seems to be made very well.

Most times when I'm taking pictures I'm looking to express myself artistically rather than get a 100% accurate capture. So, color accuracy is not my primary concern - I'll play with color in post processing to get the picture to reflect what *I* want to depict, which may or may not be what others see when they look at what I'm shooting.

But, there are also times when you want the color to be 100% accurate. For those occasions, the Color Checker Passport is an excellent tool to have in your bag.

Using it is pretty straightforward if you're comfortable with working with color balancing charts and profiles. There are a variety of color samples and a white balance card that come in a sturdy plastic case. You unfold the case and include it in your shot (according to X-Rite, the chart needs to take up at least 10% of your image).

The case is well-designed so that it will stand up so it can be properly lit. Construction is solid - it will seems like it will easily survive the usual bumps and bruises of being carried around (unlike the more traditional paper MacBeth Color Checker).

The case alone would make this worthwhile to have in your bag, but the included software extends the functionality so you can create color profiles. It's pretty straightforward to use. First, convert the RAW file that includes the Passport in the shot to a DNG file. You can use Lightroom for the conversion or the Adobe DNG converter. You then load the DNG and the software creates the profile that you can use in Lightroom or Photoshop.

If you're a Lightroom user you can use the included Lightroom plug in which streamlines the workflow a bit. Lightroom will convert the RAW file to a DNG automatically, so you save a step.

You can create a profile from a single illumination (one DNG image) or from two different illuminations (2 DNG images). Using two DNG images allows you to create a more flexible profile that covers a broader range.

My first use was to take a shot of my kitchen counters so I could bring a photo to the store to pick out a coordinating paint color. The counter is ceramic tile with a number of subtle shades running through it (and, of course, I don't have any extra tiles to bring with me). The Passport ensured the shots I took were spot on accurate.

The shortcomings are few. The software seems a bit bloated in size, but that seems to be par for the course nowadays. I'd also like it if the case were just a wee bit bigger. Yes, the compact size is a plus, but I think X-Rite was a bit too focused on getting this to be about the size of a passport (which I'm guessing is the genesis of the name).

Excellent addition to your tool chest, especially if you do a lot of production shooting under controlled conditions.

This is a 3-piece accessory kit for a camera with a threaded lens (in my case, a 58mm thread). I use this kit with a Samsung NX-300 with the 18-55mm zoom lens and it fits that lens well. My experience with this kit has been mostly positive.

Included in the kit are two lens hoods and one lens cap. I will discuss each separately.

The lens cap is, to me, the best component in the kit. It does not look like a particularly exciting item, but in this case this lens cap actually fits my lens better than the original cap from the manufacturer. It is tight and is seated evenly on the lens assembly. As an added bonus is has a lanyard that allows it to hang on the lens barrel so it does not need to be specifically tracked when it is not in place covering the lens.

The second item in the kit is a tulip hood for the lens and it is neither better nor worse than the one that came with the camera. It does an acceptable job of keeping the lens in the shade instead of allowing sunlight to hit it directly. Note that when the tulip cover is in place the lens cap will not fit.

The last item in this kit is a rubber hood that works similarly to the tulip hood and it helps prevents direct light from angling in to hit the lens. This one component is the only one in the kit about which I have anything critical to say, and it’s this: when the lens is zoomed all the way in the edges of the hood can be seen in the picture. It does not take much to zoom out past it but it still merits some mention.

I am satisfied with this kit. It includes two hoods and a lens cap that in my case is better than the original that came with my lens. This is a decent kit at a good price.

I have a TomTom Start and I have disliked the EasyPort mount from the day I got it. I had been telling my wife for months that I was going to get a “proper” mount for my TomTom and that day finally came when I accidentally broke the EasyPort mount. After a little research I decided on this particular mount, and so far I have been very pleased with it.

I wanted a more “normal” windshield mount - a suction cup with a lever instead of a twist ring, and that led me to this particular mount. The design is simple - press the suction cup against the windshield and flip the lever to make the cup stick to the window. In operation this is an easy-to-use mount and it seems to hold the navigator in place without too much trouble. As expected it does not hold well when it the windshield is cold, which is an issue with every suction-based mount I have ever used - including the EasyPort.

The ring in which the TomTom attaches to the mount holds the TomTom in place well enough but I have observed that it does not hold the navigator tightly. That is, the TomTom has a tendency to turn a little in the ring. So far this has not been an issue and the TomTom has not fallen out of the ring so this really does not bother me.

The mount is adjustable and provides for a couple of places where the position can be tweaked for maximum visibility. There should be no issue with getting the position of the GPS just right so it can be seen but not in the way.

So far I am pleased with this mount and am happy to recommend it. It’s a lot easier to use than the EasyPort mount that comes with the TomTom and it’s adjustable enough to make visibility a non-issue, even while in motion. If you have a TomTom and you don’t like the EasyPort mount, this mounting system is a big improvement.

Why is the cable size and breaker on this thing so undersized when it is presumably (due to the fact that it is Stanley Max) for running power tools? 16AWG and 13A is actually a bottleneck compared to a standard 15A 14AWG household circuit. Worse is that it is a huge bottleneck compared to the 12AWG 20A circuits I put in work and kitchen areas to accommodate the many tools (e.g., miter saws, medium sized air compressors, etc.) and appliances (e.g., microwaves) that push the envelope on the 15A circuits.

Point is, right off the bat, I can't run large tools on this thing (and that includes some plug-in-lawn equipment), and I can't run most medium sized tools two at a time on this thing (good drills, planers, grinders, etc. often draw around 9A), so what's the point of the multiple outlets except, granted, that you don't have to unplug one to plug the other in over and over again if working with two tools alternately.

On the flip side, this lighter gauge cable does allow this power hub to be lighter and easier to deal with. It does roll up nicely and I like that the cord can be attached on the side so it doesn't unravel itself.

But I think the outlets should be spaced a little further a part, given that the size could accommodate that. That would allow larger plugs, and maybe even some AC adapters to fit. I also think 20 ft. is way too short, especially for the reel setup (it's not that hard to untangle 20ft.) and the fact that this thing is probably large enough to hold more.

You could use it for Christmas lights or something like that - except it is not a true weatherproof cord - or some low power hobby in the house. This has no quality issues, and there are plenty of uses for it, but the name has me thinking it is trying to be in the tool market. To be really effective in that market, it should be 12AWG, accept 20A plugs, be minimum 50' long, and have the outlets spaced slightly further apart.

I was researching the best way to get high speed NETWORK speeds to a downstairs room. The cable modem was installed into an upstairs room (left side of house) and the WIFI speed in the first floor room (right side of house) was sufficient for most internet streaming services (about 60Mbps) However I needed higher network bandwidth for accessing a NAS.

I sought out solutions that could avoid having to run an ethernet cable from the first floor to the second floor. First I tried ethernet over AC PWR. I received the same speeds as WIFI. Then I found these MOCA adapters, once installed they appeared to work great. I got sufficient speeds but not quite as fast I wanted (about 100Mbps) But once they were installed I would experience constant drops in connection across all devices. It would go out for anywhere from 30 seconds to 10 minutes.

Customer service was great and responsive via email. We verified my setup and hardware were all compatible with the MOCA adapters but the only thing that could cause issues was interference in the coax cables. Since those cables are all inside the walls already, there really wasn't anything else I could do unless I wanted to run new coax.

Ultimately I decided to run CAT8 ethernet upstairs.

I was in the market for a hard drive-based music player and didn't want to go the normal iPxx route, so I began checking into different brands. I had a list of criteria that the player had to meet:

-EXCELLENT SOUND. This is critical. A SnR (Signal to Noise Ratio) of 95db or better

-Excellent battery life. At least 15 hours

-At least 20 GB

-A color screen

-Sturdy build

-As little touch-sensitive controlling as possible. Click wheels are inaccurate and bothersome.

-Ease of use. Drag and drop is preferred.

-AC adapter for charging on the road or from an AC converter in a car

This player meets all of those needs. The SnR is 97db, I've gotten 18 hours out of the battery (remember that increased settings like equalizers and higher bitrates mean lower battery life for ALL players), the case is solid and brushed aluminum, the screen is pretty and quite sharp, only one touch-sensitive control is present, the player CAN drag and drop through Win XP, and it comes with a wall adapter.

I love the powerful sound this puts out and it can drive my big headphones with no problem. It can, like most HDD players, set aside a partition for storage. It has a good FM tuner, recording of FM and a little mic for voice notes. It can even sync with Outlook for contacts and other info. The hard disk seems fast and

Now for the drawbacks:

-You can't watch 15fps video on a tiny screen and reduce your battery life by 67%

-The USB cable is proprietary...no mini USB!

-The wall charger cable plugs into the USB cable...this means two cables for recharging from the wall

-Looking at photos and playing music at the same time is not possible

-Creative software is always iffy. Thankfully, in Win XP, you can open the player from My Computer and access its contents directly with non-DRM music and photos.

-Battery is NON-USER REPLACEABLE. This is odd for Creative.

-No mention of this on the Creative website. Thankfully, updated drivers ARE available from support.

This player would have been state-of-the-art about a year ago, but has been eclipsed by its bigger brother the Zen Vision with 30 and 60GB drives and video...however, if you're not buying into the "kill your eyes with tiny video on tiny screens" and just want a SOLID and RELIABLE player with booming sound, this is it!!! You can tell it's custom-made for Windows (it's MTP, not UMS for any computer), but if you're running XP, then it's a solid choice because you can skip the Creative software and just load music on it.

If you can get it on sale like I did, snatch it up. This is a little gem of a player!

IBI - THE SMART PHOTO MANAGER (US Version) makes it super easy to extract, back up, and share photos stored on my mobile devices. Instead of emailing cell phone photos that I want to share among electronic devices (an iPad Air (3rd Gen), a desktop PC, and a Samsung Galaxy cell phone), I can upload the photos to Ibi via a network connection with only a couple of clicks in the Ibi app.

No longer do I have to address an email, select and add the photos, send the email--and then reverse the process on a second device (open the email, download the photos, and save the photos to the device). All that’s necessary is to take the photos, open the Ibi app, choose “import photos”, select the photos, and hit the import button.

The photos are immediately uploaded to Ibi, and I can access them immediately on all of my other devices. There is no need to clutter up email or to consume precious storage space on my mobile devices, when all I want to do is share photos.

Ibi is extremely versatile. It allows you to sort and organize photos, and create Albums. It allows you to authorize certain people to email photos directly to Ibi. It allows you to set up different areas of Ibi for the use of individuals. It allows you to upload its contents to a PC or other even larger storage device by plugging in a USB cable (not included). It even allows you to stream your videos to a television set (using Chromecast or Roku apps).

Ibi is easy to set up, using Bluetooth. My iPad and my Galaxy phone both found the powered on (plugged in) Ibi in less than 30 seconds. Once set up, Ibi communicates via your home network’s Internet access. When your Ibi app is set up, click on Help, and download the complete user manual (a PDF file). The manual is easy to understand, and will enable you to get the most out of your Ibi.

Ibi is a small drive that easily fits on a bookshelf. It uses just one power cord. I really love this Ibi storage drive. It is simplifying my life.

+++++IMPORTANT NOTE: You should NOT choose “automatic backup” in the Ibi app Settings until you understand how the app works. With automatic backup enabled, Ibi will copy all of the photos stored on EACH mobile device, and you will probably get a lot of duplicate photos. For example, if you have been sharing and storing the same photos on an iPad and a cell phone, Ibi will copy the photos from each device. Worse, if you go into Ibi and delete the duplicates, Ibi will keep automatically adding the photos back as long as the photos still exist in storage on the two different devices.

You will probably want to use “automatic backup” when you first set up your Ibi. That way all of your photos will be automatically copied to Ibi to start you off. But you should turn “automatic backup” off before you start deleting duplicate photos. You will never have a problem with duplicate photos if automatic backup is turned off.+++++

I really wanted to love this keyboard. In fact, I have purchased three of them over the past 18 months. If it weren't for the fact that two of them simply stopped working altogether with the steady red LED problem along with complete lack of function, I would probably have given this deice a 5 star review, and that is all of the variants that exist of this keyboard. When it works, it is a wonderful device. The problem is, there are clearly some major quality issues.

First off, what is it about this keyboard that is so fantastic that makes it so popular if it has so many problems? Answer, it feels wonderful, and when it works, it's a dream. It is the right shape and size even for practically all typically sized hands. Maybe even for some of the more tiny-handed men out there. Microsoft has perfected the bezel curve of the ergonomic keyboard in the Sculpt, and the amount of travel it gives each key is perfect. The feedback of the keys (as in the feel) is perfect as well. The apparently physical quality of the device seems well made (if though it clearly has some design flaws). Even the amount of "clack" that the keyboard makes is satisfying without being obnoxious.

So what's the problem? Aside form the things people have talked about ad nauseam (broken keys, losing that tiny transceiver means the keyboard is useless, etc.. being the seemingly biggest issues) so along with practically all of Microsoft's consumer-grade products, support is nowhere to be found. While MS offers comprehensive support plans for their corporate products, you are on your own with accessories, even if they are expensive bluetooth accessories. They don't even host proper forums for their accessories (there is no category for this on their official forum) and any information elsewhere on the internet about the Sculpt is strangely scant, so trying to find out what the steady red LED means is definitely a no-go. Anything I find is either for another model or simply doesn't map to this condition. Therefore, I can't even find out what the red LED light even means, let alone attempt to resolve the problem. Their phone and chat support offers no meaningful help as they are unfamiliar with the device. Since I have a Mac they balk and say the device isn't supported on a Mac, even though I have been using it for 9 months beforehand without incident. Also, the red LED turns on immediately after the new batteries go in so it's probably nothing to do with signal and a failure of the device itself. This seems further evident since the bottom of the keyboard that is underneath the light actually gets warm to the touch, so I should assume the keyboard is fried. This would be the second Sculpt keyboard that this has happened to in less than a year so this is not an outlier. I don't do anything to my keyboards that would kill them like this. My old Logitech Wave that I keep having to go back to keeps on ticking.

Also, note that apparently USB 3 interferes with the wireless signal between the USB dongle and the keyboard, a problem I have personally experienced when my keyboard strangely stopped receiving input temporarily for a few seconds and then resume. I thought I solved the problem by using an old USB 2 hub to get the dongle physically closer to the keyboard as I thought it was a reception issue that is so common with Bluetooth devices. (I am not even sure if this even uses Bluetooth and it might just be some proprietary RF signal.) But in fact, I later learned that it was the use of a USB 2 port that was far away from my USB 3 ports!

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

I am an Amazon junkie but I also do not like restrictions on products I purchase. During my July 2014 research, I discovered that the Nexus 7 tablet was the highest rated Android next to those more restrictive tablets.

After I received the Nexus, I wondered if I had made the right decision. First, I was surprised that this came with no documentation (other than the business card sized diagram of where all the ports were and a warranty and safety agreement in both English and French). The documentation didn't even say how long I needed to charge the unit. I charged it overnight and then had immense trouble getting this connected.

The router I was connecting to has MAC filtering enabled so I needed the MAC address. However, I couldn't get the MAC address without setting up the device. Also, I couldn't set it up because I couldn't get the MAC address. I could have fussed with the router and turned off MAC filtering/security temporarily but I had to get to work in the morning right after the unit completed charging. I then tried connecting via three other networks (my library for one, my work another, and another Wi-Fi connection). It still would not connect. Because I didn't want to wait until I got home 12 hours later to fuss with my router I wound up asking a tech support person where I work. He connected me via his personal MiFi mobile hotspot.

Apparently, Google Nexus only connects to certain networks if the first time setup has not been done. I tried several open networks. My co-worker's MiFi mobile network connection, although I suspect mine would have connected had I temporarily removed the security on my router, was the only one that would allow me to run the automatic setup so that I could connect. After setup was performed, I was able to get the MAC address from the settings "about" tab. I was also able to connect to the three other networks I tried previously and after inputting the MAC address, I could also connect to my router. It was apparently the initial setup process that prevented the connection.

This Google Nexus would have gotten five stars if they enhanced the user experience by:
1 - Providing a MAC address either on the unit or on a piece of paper for those that have MAC filtering enabled.
2 - Providing a documentation pamphlet with the unit that:
* Tells the user how long they need to charge the unit the first time.
* Explains to the user that setup cannot be run on all networks and sometimes they will get an error message. Therefore, they might say something like "using your own network is advisable" or provide an explanation of why certain networks (including totally open ones that allow all connections) would not work. Perhaps there is some sort of technical protocol that is not available on all networks; I have no idea.

Other than the above, I absolutely love my Google Nexus. I've been using this for almost 6 months and it has met my every expectation. It charges in less than four hours; lasts about 3 hours if I'm constantly using it; lasts about 3-4 days when I'm using it for about 10 minutes daily. I've used this for email, movies, web surfing, pictures, etc. App availability is unending (Kindle, LinkedIn, Battery Doctor, etc., etc.) I tested the screen image next to my co-workers Kindle Fire HD 7" and there is no discernible difference in quality or resolution. Images and movies on this device are superb. If I attach my [[ASIN:B00N4SIIFY APLWL USB 2.0 A to Micro B Cable 6FT-TPE jacket-Blue]] to my laptop, I can both charge the unit and also access files on it from my laptop such as the photos located under Nexus 7\Internal storage\DCIM\Camera directory (that's Computer\Nexus 7\Internal storage\DCIM\Camera in Explorer).

Overall this is a quality tablet that did not disappoint me once I got past the initial installation and lack of documentation headache. In the comments section of my review, I put links to Google documentation I found helpful as well as to the 2014 review I used for my research.

UPDATE Jan 6, 2015 - Right after I wrote this review I had a problem where my Nexus was shutting down automatically and every time I went to use it I had to power it back up. After doing an Internet search I was able to fix this by going to the Play Store app on the Nexus, then selecting "My Apps" and accepting all install updates. There were a few updates that had not installed and this was playing havoc with my system. After I did this, the Nexus remained powered up and has been working fine the last several days.

When I received my review sample I tested it on a legacy system (a ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP) and a phone running Android 4.4.2. I tested the USB 2.0 compatibility on the ThinkPad and USB 3.0 on the phone using an [[ASIN:B00GLKI258 [OTG HUB with SD card reader] Unitek usb3.0 hub with OTG adapter Bus-powered HUB ALL IN ONE USB 3.0 HUB OTG Function]]. As a previous reviewer warned it's not advisable to plug hubs into bubs, but I wanted to text the transfer speed.

In the case of the ThinkPad I plugged in an extra keyboard, mouse, flash drive and camera (the latter for transfers only). The load of devices did not exceed the 500mA that this hub kicks down to for power consumption when connected to USB 2.0 ports. this can support up to 900mA when connected to USB 3.0 ports, but note that it's still only viable for lower power peripherals. Plugging a single USB 3.0 external drive into this into USB 3.0 ports can eat your entire power budget, rendering the other ports in the hub unusable. Be aware that this limitation applies to all unpowered USB hubs, not just this one.

I tested the USB 3 speeds using the set up described about to my Note 3 phone. This hub, even daisy chained into another hub, supported copying 10 GB from the phone to an SD card reader in about 30 seconds. That is blazing fast.

While this is not the prettiest hub on the market (there seems to be a trend towards brushed aluminum these days), it performs per USB specs and has an integrated switch that I like. I had no issues whatsoever with either of the test beds I used. As long as you heed the limitations of unpowered hubs this one is worth considering if you need to expand your ports in a cost effective manner.
