I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

The TOMTOM GO2535 TM WTE is quite attractive with a large screen and smooth appearance but because of its size, this is a heavier GPS than many others. A magnetic plug attaches the power supplies either to a computer with its USB plug or to a car with its accessory power plug. As with most GPS devices, no "home" DC power supply is included. I have found the car mount to be great, easy to attach and remove from the windshield with a simple turn. My only complaint with the mount is that it takes some work to direct the device to a visible position and I fear that it will not last as long as the GPS. The magnetic plug slips into a cutout in the mount, allowing it to remain in position so the GPS can quickly be inserted or removed for safekeeping.
As for the functionality of the GPS, it has some problems, thereby preventing me from giving this a 5 star review. I'll simply list the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Start up time is quick and option to start from last destination can save time if the satellite connection is delayed.
Menu options are easily learned even if at first they seem to include extra steps.
Responds quickly to need for alternate route when a turn is missed.
Ease in moving through functions on screen.
POIs are expansive and easy to discover
Map identifies a location I frequent which is not identified by any other GPS I've used.
Identifies traffic light cameras adequately. Have yet to receive speed camera warning.
Voice commands are intuitive and a little printed card is included if you're in need of prompting.
Connectivity to my Mac is easy and the option to automatically check for updates can save time.

Cons:
Speed is not always accurate. Often has my car going at 10 mph less than actual speed.
When setting a new destination, I've been unable to change the state unless I do it using the voice command. This may be possible, but I haven't had the time to investigate. Since I'm in a metropolitan area and may venture through 2 states and the District of Columbia in less than an hour, it's important for me to access the individual states.
When using phone through the GPS, although I can hear the conversation with no problem, the person on the other end of my call can't hear me clearly. Every time I've used it with a phone, the call has been dropped. I've never had a call dropped otherwise with my phone or other Bluetooth capable device.
Does not recognize voice commands at times.
Voice prompts are very frequent and I'd love to be able to reduce them but not turn it off.
Seldom comes up with the routes I usually take, even with a second try after selecting the Change Route option.

All in all, this is a good GPS navigation device and the lifetime updates are a definite advantage. I haven't traveled the wold with it, but will update my review as necessary with observations internationally. What's interesting is that I still prefer my 3-year-old Navigon for its ease of use, accuracy and lovely displays, with two exceptions. When the time comes for my beloved Navigon to bite the dust, I feel confident that I'll still be happy with this TOMTOM.

When I got this, I was very excited to be able to use it with my tablet. When I want to write anything on my tablet, it is difficult to do at times, so I thought it would be great to use this keyboard with it. Then I realized, it does not work with a tablet as advertised- UNLESS YOU PURCHASE AN ADAPTER CORD

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This keyboard is a nice little keyboard. I love that it has a touch pad as well. The keys are pretty easy to use. They are small but there is enough space around them to make it easier to type. The touchpad also has nice features making it pretty easy to use. There are other controls for devices you might want to use this with. I used this with my tablet as it was my primary reason for obtaining it.

WHAT ADAPTER DID I NEED?
I purchased a USB female to mini USB male cord. That is for the dongle that you put in to make the keyboard connect with the device. The keyboard is still wireless.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
I really like having this. It is still tiny, but I can do some typing on my tablet when I need to without having to constantly backtype and mess with the screen. There is no lag and it works really well so far. The touchpad also works well in most cases depending on what I am trying to do.

THE DONGLE
The little USB dongle has to be put into the device you plan to use the keyboard with. That stores in the back of the keyboard so you don't use it if you plan to use this keyboard with multiple devices.

SLEEP
This keyboard will go into sleep mode when not in use for a while to save power. There is a power button to turn it right back on again.

MOUSE
There are multiple ways to use this as a mouse control (pointer). You can use the touchpad or the right and left mouse button have buttons on the keyboard too. They are separated so it is easy to keep them straight when using it.

THE BOTTOM LINE
As long as you make sure to have the adapter cord for anything with mini USB port that you plan to use this with, it will work great even for tablets and phones, at least it does for mine.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. I would have liked to know that this needed an adapter BEFORE I got it so I did not have to wait to find one before I could use it.

One of my favorite Nikon lenses is an old 16mm fisheye from about 1977, I think. It has two problems: it is a fisheye and curves straight lines at the edges and it's a non-CPU lens, like many of my aged old Nikon lenses. Non-CPU means I have to remember to select it from my list of non-CPU lenses using that menu feature of the D800, and that there is no focus assist. It's full frame, however, and now that we're back to shooting full FX 24x36 sensor, the old lenses are making a comeback.

That 16mm fisheye costs a pretty penny today and the 14-24mm Nikon f/2.8 zoom is even more. And I'm sure they are both fine lenses.

So I bought a Samyang/Rokinon 800mm f/8 mirror lens for two bills and said, "that ought to be fun, even if it's not that great a lens for such little money." Funny thing: it's a pretty good lens.

That good purchase experience allowed me to select this 14mm Rokinon f/2.8. It is surprisingly good considering it's one third the cost of its Nikon equivalent. Even wide open at 1.5 feet, it is tack sharp.

The main difference between this and the Nikon is that this Rokinon is a fully manual focus lens while the 14mm Nikon is auto focus, although I'm not sure how accurately a 14mm lens can focus automatically. I've often simply estimated the distance and set the lens to that distance using the barrel markings. The focus ring is a pleasant long throw, with the ring rotating about 270 degrees around the lens from infinity to .28 meters (less than 1 foot). Focus drag feels silky smooth. Focus happens internally -- the front element does not rotate.

This Rokinon has a clickstop f/stop diaphragm. It also has a chip in it, giving it enough smarts to qualify as an AI-S lens. To use it on a D800, you have to set it to minimum aperture (f/22) or you get the flashing "fee" in the viewfinder. Ah, takes me back....

Setting it to f/22 (marked in orange) tells the camera what f/stop the lens is working at and allows control of the f/stop from the front selector wheel on the D800. The focus indicator in the eyepiece also works -- you see the left/right arrows and the little ball that verifies it's in focus. It also automatically records f/stop and focal length data in the metadata with the shot. In other words, it's a real lens, just without auto focus, for one third the cost. Old Nikon AI-S lenses have a little lock that holds the f/stop ring at minimum aperture that's not present on this lens, but the click stops are secure and the f/stop ring stays where you set it.

The front element is radically curved and is protected somewhat by the flower petal shaped built-in lens shade. Be careful: that front element is really exposed to the weather.

The front lens cap is terrific and very well designed. It's a durable hard plastic unit that slips over the flower petal lens shade and snaps securely in place against detents in the the lens shade. You have to squeeze both plastic flush-mount buttons on the front edge of the cap to release it. It won't fall off by accident under any circumstances. Only drawback it that it's about 1-3/8" deep and 3-5/8" diameter, so it doesn't exactly slip into a back pocket when it's off the lens.

The cosmetics of the lens are appealing. Even has a brass/gold colored band around the front that mimics real Nikon lenses. The focus ring rubber grip is good and the the body of the lens, minus the front element, is about the size of a 50mm f/1.4 lens. Focus distances in feet and meters are clearly engraved. One nice thing it has that I wish all lenses had is the focal length clearly and largely printed on the side of the lens so you can tell at a glance what it is. Nice. The mount is precision machined and fits the camera like it should. There are five little electrical contacts that interface with the camera body to communicate exposure info. For transport, it comes with an unpadded velour drawstring pouch. May want something a bit more padded if it's bouncing around inside a camera bag against other gear. But the bag's adequate, folds flat when not in use and is compact.

As for performance, I'm not going to go into lines/per millimeter sharpness. What I can say is that it's great for architectural interiors and wide, WIDE rectilinear shots. And in analyzing a snap of my dog I pushed in on his eye as far as I could looking at the D800's rear screen and could see the finest of eyelashes, showing off both the resolution of the lens and the remarkable resolution of the D800's 36 megapixel sensor. The lens distinguishes itself from all the wide/medium wide 24mm/35mm lenses out there. Do I really need to have a heavy, giant, hyper-expensive zoom lens that zooms 10 whole millimeters from 14mm all the way to 24mm? Not hardly. If I need serious wide angle this 14mm will fill the bill nicely, even wide open.

No filters for it, of course, because the front element is so deeply curved.

I'm particularly interested in using the 14mm for video shoots, which I use the D800 for more than for still photography. I'll be able to see the whole world with this lens, even in the most cramped of situations.

This will be a fun lens. Highly recommended.

I ordered the 'Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts and experiences.
First off, out of the box this Bluetooth Wireless Speaker not only looks interesting but it is beautiful. I say interesting because I have never had a Wireless Speaker like this, and I wonder where would I use it and would it be practical. Well after some time with this device I must first report that it really does sound amazing. The sound is clean and immersive. It is hard to describe the incredible sound sensation while wearing it. It is almost as if you have speakers floating on either side of your head (pointing directly to your ears) and it is nothing like I have experienced before but it is pretty cool. I have been trying to think of how this Speaker would actually fit into my life. It's not like you are wearing headphones that only you can hear. While wearing this speaker, everyone else around you can hear it too but it's just not as immersive as it is to you. It's hard to describe, but what I will say is that it really is an incredible experience. If the volume is down low you can still hear your surroundings yet when you crank it up, surprisingly your surrounding sounds seem to disappear. Personally I have decided that this would be best worn while alone in your home while doing simple household chores. Like doing dishes or folding laundry. The Nomodo U speaker stays put pretty well for the most part due to the rubber neck pad, yet if you are constantly bending over or doing anything where you are moving around a lot and twisting your head and body, it tends to need re adjusted. Sitting in bed listening to Music or listening to an audio book works really well with this device as long as you wont be disturbing your partner. As for watching movies, for me this really doesn't work. I can't find anywhere where it says what version of Bluetooth this is using but I don't think it is Bluetooth 5.0 unfortunately. There are noticeable sync issues and this just gets annoying. Speaking of the Bluetooth, it connects/pairs effortlessly to all of my devices and that is a bonus. I am disappointed however that it uses Micro USB (the cable is included btw) for charging. With this being a new device it should have USB Type C. I always have to mention this with any new devices. Call quality is acceptable. Those on the other end can hear you just fine, as long as you are not in a loud environment. This is pretty typical with most wireless headphones. Overall I do love this device and think it is a great value for what it is.

I am pleased with this print server for a number of reasons:
- administration is web-based and set-up is simple and straightforward if you're experienced - the documentation is a bit too terse for the non-technical (home) user who needs detailed guidance.
- you get two USB ports and one parallel port, making this both flexible and an added value if you plan to locate all of your printers in the same space. The added value stems from the fact that most single-port print servers are in the same price range, and almost all of them only support printers with parallel ports.
- it works in network environments based on Microsoft Windows, Netware, Macintosh, UNIX, or any combination, making it standards-compliant and open. I especially like the step-by-step instructions on the manufacturer's web site for integrating this device into Linux-based LANs. It can also be queried and managed via SNMP in an enterprise network.
I am less pleased with the supporting web site. Although it is rich in useful content and has up-to-date driver downloads, well written FAQs and a wealth of technical information for Linux and UNIX users, the pages do not display properly in Netscape 4x. Considering the excellent UNIX and Linux support for the product and in the FAQs this was a surprise since most of those users will be using Netscape 4x as their browser. This is more of an inconvenience than a problem however.

I received this as a free review sample. The reason why I docked it a star is the active tablet window needs improvement (and that could have been one of the stand-out features if properly designed.) Here is the problem: it's the perfect size for an iPad Air 2, but could not accommodate my Tab 2 10.1 inch tablet. It did hold my Samsung Tab Pro 8.4 (even in an Otterbox Defender case). The vinyl window wrinkles and also reduces sensitivity when you interact with your tablet.

If the active tablet window is unimportant to you, then the rest of this backpack is a winner. Pairing my phone to the bluetooth speakers was as simple as flipping a switch and scanning for it on my phone's settings. And the speakers are loud with better than expected sound quality. I was pleased with that - some thought went into the speakers.

The padding is more than ample for protecting electronics, and there are sufficient pockets for the geekiest geek. What I like, though, is the storage areas are not overly complex. I own a Booq bag that is a storage dream come true, but almost requires a photographic memory to remember were all of the pockets are. This one is designed much simpler, but still efficient and effective.

Construction (except for the active tablet window) is first rate. The tablet window is marred by a difficult zipper, whereas all of the other zippers on this bag are sturdier and smooth. The outer fabric seems tough (I have not had it long enough to make any claims beyond that), and all of the seams are reinforced, straight and tight.

It's very comfortable and can be adjusted to evenly distribute the weight of a fully loaded pack. Considering that the bag itself is somewhat heavy this is a major plus for me.

I do want to note one thing about the backup battery: it is rated at (and stores) the full 4000mAh. However, like all batteries using this one's technology it's only 70% efficient, so expect about 2800mAh of usable capacity. That is not a flaw in this bag, but a reality that I wanted to point out so your expectations are properly set.

Overall, this is a well made bag with some innovative features (battery back-up and bluetooth speakers). If the active tablet window is not an important feature it's definitely worth considering. This one will be replacing my Booq because the storage is there without the complexity.

The WD_Black 1TB D50 Game Dock has quality written all over it. Metal construction for heat dissipation, thunderbolt support, nice RGB lighting, and a fast NVMe drive. It is quite obviously geared toward the PC Gaming crowd, but which segment?

The build of this product screams high-quality gaming accessory. Its outer design is reminiscent of a cargo container and its collection of ports are impressive. Each USB port is well labeled with its speed (4x 10Gb/s Type-A and 2x 10Gb/s Type-C), two thunderbolt ports, one of which outputs 87 watts of power, one displayport, one network port (gigabit), and one 3.5mm headphone jack. Add to this, the 1TB high-performance NVMe drive. All in one sleek-looking, compact container (pun intended).

It is obvious that this dock is geared toward the Gaming Laptop crowd, whether its for gaming or for video/graphics production work, but I find that it really doesn't make sense for me. In my tests, this product does not work without the power adapter (it really should be able to power itself through the thunderbolt port). This means an additional outlet that's drawing power at all times. This would make sense if gaming laptops can actually be powered and charged from the 87w thunderbolt port but I have not seen a gaming pc with discreet graphics that actually accepts anything in that range.

So what other advantage would this product provide? External storage through a fast Thunderbolt connection. At $450, this product provides 1TB of additional storage. Which 2TB NVMe drives available for much less, I would opt to upgrade my internal storage to 2TB instead.

Then that leave the docking station. The ports are all of the high quality and your monitor, network, keyboard, mouse, headset, and speakers can be connected via a single thunderbolt connection. This is convenient, but I don't think this justifies the price as there are many docks out there that work just as well, albeit through a USB 3.1 connection instead.

WD has really done well to package a lot into this dock but is charging a premium for it. Personally, I think that there are just better ways of achieving equal or better results when it comes to upgrading a gaming laptop.

**update**

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Very easy to set-up, app is intuitive to use and follow.
* This is a very complete kit with a hub, 6 entry sensors, 2 motion sensors, and a keypad. You don't need to use everything, or install everything in one day. I started off just my garage door and the front door. Same thing with the extra keypad. There is already a control panel on top of the hub. The idea of they keypad is for quicker access to the control panel. So ideally, the keypad will be next to your bed on a nightstand or something.
* Hub is not obtrusive at all. I have it next to a soda can for size reference.
* Sensors work really well. I was concerned about the garage door sensor because usually I get bad wi-fi in the garage. I put the hub near my living room. The garage sensor worked flawlessly. Anytime you open the door where you've installed a sensor, there is a chime that goes off on the hub. You can disable this chime if you wish.
* No need to subscribe to a service, which is perfect for us. We live in a fairly safe neighborhood, knock on wood. But there are times when everyone is gone, and no cars are parked in the driveway. So these are the times, I'll arm the system.

THE BAD:
------------
* The sensor and the magnet has to be half an inch or less apart. Installation will be tricky for some of you. My front entry door has a raised decorative trim that makes this impossible. I made it work by having the sensor at a weird angle, and half the 3M backing isn't even attached to the trim. I will need to think of a solution for this. Or better yet, ADT should have thought about this ahead of time and given us adapters, spacers, etc.
* If you choose not to subscribe, like in our case, you should understand the system is nothing more than a deterrent. You hope the loud sound will be enough to deter would be criminals. If it's not, then no authorities are coming unless you called them yourselves.
* The instructions assumes we all know the industry lingo For example, "Entry or exit delays." It would have been nice if the manual explained what this means. I had to search online for more info. It's basically the time the system allows for you to properly turn off the alarm before it goes off. That's my understand from YT videos of other brands. I couldn't find an exact "Blue by ADT" video on this matter.
* Whenever you arm the system, it takes forever, like 60 to 90 seconds, and during this time, there is a CHIME that's counting down with the seconds. Once the system is armed, then it shuts up. There doesn't seem to be a way to mute this. You see, I'm a night owl, so I don't need to arm the system until very late like 1 or 2 am. People are asleep at this time, the chimes will wake them up. I have contacted customer service, we'll see what they say.
* The 2 yard signs and stakes are great, but the 4 stickers they give for your windows are tiny. My Brinks windows stickers were bigger.

Overall, I'll rate this 4-Stars. And base on the customer service response, this might go up to 5-Stars, or get bumped down to 3-Stars. There has got to be a way to mute the chimes when arming the system. If there isn't a way, then I will bump the rating down because that would be ridiculous. So, 4-Stars for now.

******* Original review before the drama*******

We've had an older Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in our living room for a couple of years and we've been pretty happy overall. I recently put the Bose 500 version of this sound bar in our master bedroom and was amazed at the difference, so getting this 700 for the living room was a no brainer. I mostly just expected them to connect as a group and have the same sound, but this 700 is better than the 500.

It's a long, narrow, sleek looking unit with glass finishes that makes it almost invisible in front of the Tv. Our Roku fits alongside without drama. The connections are via digital optical cable or the HDMI. Just turn off your TV speakers - not mute, off from the tv settings. You need to use the included wired headset to fully set the speakers for your room's accoustics. I'm using this bar with a 55", 3 years old, Sceptre dumb tv and a Room streaming stick - the connection was immediate and drama free.

You must use the Bose app to get full functionality out of the sound bar. The app let's you connect two or more Bose speakers with the tech and use them all simultaneously as a group to play music or audiobooks etc. The app also starts the set up for the Alexa link and the streaming services like Prime, Tune In, Bluetooth streaming and others. You can also set 6 favorites as one touch launch options.

Alexa works fine through the sound bar, but the response speed is noticably slower than through a regular Echo. I get a glitchy message saying "This unit is unable to perform routines" every time I say "Good morning". Good morning triggers a specific set of actions from Alexa to turn on our bedside lamps, the bathroom lights, turn off our porch lights, give me the weather and then our daily news brief. Despite that glitchy message, every morning, the Bose performs our routine flawlessly. It's weird, but not a big deal really.

The sound quality is excellent and immersive in multiple settings from music to a movie. The app let's you adjust the sound quality and balance with bass, treble and center. You can also set it for dialogue mode to enhance/clarify voices and reduce background noise - this is very handy for the news or a talk show. Take some time to adjust the settings for what your ear really likes and you'll be amazed at the fullness of sound and all the background details.

After two weeks, I'm incredibly pleased with the build quality, looks, sound and full functionality of both the 500 and 700 units. The 700 wins out by a nose over the 500 for us because the sound is bigger, but mostly because the remote control is better. The remote lights up when you lift it and you can find the buttons instantly. I programmed our TV to the Bose remote and it controls the sound bar, channels up and down and power for both the tv and the sound bar. Bottom line is that I am now looking at buying another 700 for the master bedroom and moving the 500 to our guest suite so we'll have the full set.

Honestly, I wish I had a tried a Wifi6 mesh system sooner. This is NIGHT AND DAY difference over my previous D-link router + extender. I thought that since both my router and extender were D-link and had the ability to "communicate" with each other, it would work pretty well, but honestly even when it "worked" it was pretty laggy, and outside on the porch it would drop to single digit speed tests, if anything at all (forget about streaming for backyard movie nights!).
This system, however, is incredible. I'm now getting nearly 200mbps outside where I used to have nothing, and in most of my house I'm hitting my maximum 250mbps that I'm paying for with my internet service. Everything responds quickly and smoothly, and I love the control that the TP link system gives over what devices are connected (it alerts me when a new device connects!) and being able to set restrictions and time limits as well!
The one downside, however, is the physical ports. For starters, there are only 3 of them per unit. If you use ethernet backbone to connect them, that leaves only one on the primary node (one for the internet connection to the modem, and the other going to the second node- only one available for anything else). In my case, I have an ethernet cable going to my desktop for work (the most reliable connection), and another going into a telephony system. The 3 port limitation would have been difficult if I hardwired the satellite, but thankfully I didn't have to. The wireless mesh over 6Ghz actually works quite well so far so I managed with only the 3 ports on the primary one.
That being said, at first I had a major issue with the speed on my hardwired connection. The desktop claimed to only connect at 100mbps. Meanwhile, if I turned on wifi I was pulling 250mbps. That can't be! Many chats to customer support and we couldn't figure it out until I switched ports on the Deco and now I'm getting the full 250 over ethernet. I don't know if it was the port having trouble or just reseating the wire that did it, but I never had that on my previous D-link router, and it had more ports too in case I needed them.

In a nutshell, I got it working, and for what it is supposed to do, I'm VERY very impressed at the performance. But the hardwire hiccup and limitation in number of ports available makes this a 4 instead of 5 star review.

The Lensbaby Edge 80 Optic is one of Lensbaby's "swappable" optics for its line of lenses. It has a focal length of 80mm and features a 12-blade aperture with a range from f/2.8 through f/22. It can function as a regular 80mm f/2.8 lens when facing forward on your camera, but this optic's special feature is that it allows you to employ the usual Lensbaby bend and tilt to reposition your plane of focus along any point not parallel with your camera's sensor plane.

The usual Lensbaby lens tilt allows you to place the point of focus (with varying diffusion all around that point) but did not allow you to change the plane of focus itself. With this optic you can put a "slice of focus" through your image in creative ways. For example, you can highlight a certain aspect of the photo (such as producing a portrait where the eyes are in sharpest focus and everything else is softly blurred), or you can create the "false miniature" effect where the objects photographed take on the appearance of miniature scale models. The optic also has a close focus mode that will allow a close focus distance of 17".

There is a bit of learning curve for this optic. Expect to play around for bit before you get the hang of it. There are some good video tutorials on the Lensbaby site. I included a couple of example photos with this review.

You don't need to swap lenses to get back to "normal." As I mentioned earlier, the Edge 80 behaves like a normal 80mm lens when you aren't employing any of its tilt features. The aperture ring on the optic adjusts smoothly, and focusing and tilt occurs on the lens body itself. The shift from regular focus mode to close focus mode is a little tight -- you have to firmly pull the front edge of the optic outward. But, I imagine that's as it should be to avoid it shifting by itself.

My one source of frustration so far is in detaching the optic from the lens itself. Suffice to say you will need to review Lensbaby's instructions for this, and practice several times before you can successfully detach the optic. My first try took almost half an hour, which is not a delay you would want to experience in the field. I did get better with practice, but it's still a bit of tricky. Older hands might suffer more than younger hands. I've found in practice you can get by with swapping out other Lensbaby optics from the lens without detaching the lens from your camera, but with the Edge 80 optic, you really need to detach the whole lens first in order to get the optic out of the lens. That will allow you to get the best grip on the components when performing the detach maneuver.

Note that the optic in this product listing is not sold with a lens. The Edge 80 only works with the latest line of Lensbaby Lenses (NOT the 1.0, 2.0 or 3G). You need at least one of the current Lensbaby Lenses to use this optic. The optic works with the Muse, Composer, Control Freak and Scout lenses; it can also work with the Composer with Tilt Transformer, but you need to buy the Macro Converters in order to use the Edge 80 optic with that lens. Note too that if you want true macro capability, you will need to buy the Macro Converters anyway, regardless of which Lensbaby lens you have (their earlier Macro accessories will not work with this optic).

Normal in-lens tilt-shift lens are expensive ($1200-$2500). While the Edge 80 does not give you all the features of such a dedicated lens, it is a highly affordable alternative that provides enough capability for many tilt/shift needs. It's a great way to get into this type of photography without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.
